questions.question: Which city served as the seat of federal Parliament before Canberra opened in 1927?
questions.explanation: Parliament sat in Victoria's Parliament House on Spring Street for 26 years while the Victorian parliament moved into the Royal Exhibition Building. The Constitution itself said the capital had to be in NSW but at least 100 miles from Sydney, with Melbourne as the stopgap.
questions.hook: Sydney got the capital's state, Melbourne got the parliament's first 26 years: a fair split in a rivalry.

questions.question: Which Australian city hosted the 2000 Summer Olympic Games?
questions.explanation: Sydney beat Beijing by 45 votes to 43 in the final round of the 1993 IOC vote, and Cathy Freeman lit the cauldron before winning the 400 metres. Melbourne hosted in 1956 and Brisbane is set to host in 2032.
questions.hook: Melbourne '56, Sydney 2000, Brisbane '32: one Games per east-coast capital.

questions.question: What name was given to the site where the First Fleet settled after leaving Botany Bay in January 1788?
questions.explanation: Arthur Phillip found Botany Bay shallow and short of fresh water, moved north into Port Jackson and named the cove after Home Secretary Lord Sydney, raising the flag on 26 January 1788. That date is now Australia Day.
questions.hook: Botany Bay was the plan; Sydney Cove was the fix, eight days after Phillip arrived.

questions.question: Which animal appears alongside the emu on the Commonwealth Coat of Arms?
questions.explanation: The kangaroo and emu hold a shield bearing the six state badges, beneath a gold seven-pointed Commonwealth Star, on arms granted in 1912. A popular story says they were chosen because neither can easily walk backwards.
questions.hook: The two supporters are the two animals that can't back-pedal, so the nation only goes forward.

questions.question: Which court replaced the Privy Council in London as Australia's final court of appeal?
distractors: The Full Court of the Family Court
questions.explanation: Appeals to London were closed in stages: from the High Court in 1968 and 1975, and from state supreme courts by the Australia Acts of 1986. The High Court, set up in 1903, sits in Canberra in a building opened in 1980.
questions.hook: 1986: the year the last legal thread to London was cut.

questions.question: Which Australian state was originally named Van Diemen's Land?
questions.explanation: Abel Tasman named it in 1642 after Anthony van Diemen, governor-general of the Dutch East Indies. The colony became Tasmania on 1 January 1856, partly to shed the convict stigma after transportation ended in 1853.
questions.hook: It swapped the Dutch boss's name for the Dutch sailor's name.

questions.question: Whose government introduced the Goods and Services Tax in July 2000?
questions.explanation: Howard took a 10 per cent GST to the 1998 election and held power despite losing the two-party-preferred vote. John Hewson had lost the 'unlosable' 1993 election proposing a GST, and Keating's famous line was 'if you don't understand it, don't vote for it'.
questions.hook: 'Never ever' in 1995, law in 2000: Howard did what cost Hewson the 1993 election.

questions.question: Which Australian city was devastated by Cyclone Tracy on Christmas Eve 1974?
questions.explanation: Tracy destroyed about 70 per cent of Darwin's homes and killed 66 people. More than 30,000 residents were evacuated, most in the biggest airlift in Australian history, and new building codes for cyclone strength followed.
questions.hook: Christmas Eve 1974: a capital city emptied by air within a week.

questions.question: Which parliament was the first in the world to grant women both the vote and the right to stand for election?
questions.explanation: South Australia's 1894 law gave women both rights; New Zealand had given women the vote in 1893 but not the right to stand until 1919. The Commonwealth followed in 1902, although that law excluded most Aboriginal people.
questions.hook: New Zealand won the vote race; South Australia won the vote-and-stand double.

questions.question: Which mainland Australian state is the smallest by area?
questions.explanation: Victoria covers about 227,000 square kilometres, roughly the size of Great Britain and under a tenth of Western Australia. Tasmania is smaller but is an island, which is the trap in the question.
questions.hook: Smallest on the mainland, second most people: Victoria is Australia's most crowded state.

questions.question: Which Australian state was proclaimed separate from New South Wales in 1859?
questions.explanation: Queen Victoria signed the Letters Patent on 6 June 1859, now Queensland Day, and Governor George Bowen proclaimed the colony in Brisbane on 10 December. Victoria had separated from NSW earlier, in 1851.
questions.hook: Victoria left NSW in 1851, Queensland in 1859: both named after the same queen.

questions.question: Which city is home to Australia's oldest university, founded in 1850?
questions.explanation: The University of Sydney was founded in 1850 and began teaching in 1852; Melbourne followed in 1853. They lead the 'sandstone' universities, the six oldest in each state capital.
questions.hook: Sydney 1850, Melbourne 1853: the university rivalry is older than the football one.

questions.question: Which Victorian gold town grew from tent camp to major city within a few years of 1851?
questions.explanation: Victoria's population rose from about 77,000 to more than 500,000 in the 1850s, and Ballarat and Bendigo became cities almost overnight. The Welcome Stranger, the largest alluvial nugget ever found, was dug up near Dunolly in 1869.
questions.hook: Victoria's population rose about sevenfold in ten years: that is what gold does.

questions.question: Who was the first Australian-born person appointed Governor-General?
questions.explanation: Prime Minister James Scullin insisted on him in 1931 over George V's objections, establishing that the Australian government chooses the Governor-General. Isaacs, a former Chief Justice, was also the first Jewish Governor-General.
questions.hook: Scullin argued with a king to get an Australian in the job.

questions.question: Which item was the last to come off wartime rationing in Australia, in July 1950?
questions.explanation: Coupon rationing began in 1942 to feed troops and Britain; clothing came off in 1948, petrol in February 1950 and butter in June 1950, leaving tea last. Menzies had campaigned in 1949 on ending petrol rationing.
questions.hook: Petrol in February, butter in June, tea in July: the nation's cuppa was freed last.

questions.question: Which Australian state has only one house of parliament?
questions.explanation: Labor abolished Queensland's Legislative Council in 1922 by appointing a 'suicide squad' of members pledged to vote it out of existence. The ACT and NT assemblies are also single-chamber.
questions.hook: The upper house was stacked with members appointed to vote themselves out.

questions.question: Which bird is the official bird emblem of New South Wales?
questions.explanation: The laughing kookaburra was adopted in 1971. NSW also has a separate animal emblem, the platypus, while the lyrebird is on the 10 cent coin.
questions.hook: NSW laughs: the bird emblem is the kookaburra, the platypus is the animal.

questions.question: Which 1987-89 inquiry exposed police corruption in Queensland under Joh Bjelke-Petersen?
questions.explanation: Tony Fitzgerald's inquiry, sparked by Phil Dickie's Courier-Mail reports and the ABC's 'The Moonlight State', led to Police Commissioner Terry Lewis being jailed for 14 years and four ministers being jailed. Bjelke-Petersen was forced out in 1987, and Labor's Wayne Goss won in 1989.
questions.hook: One report sent a police commissioner and four ministers to prison.

questions.question: Which state uses the Hare-Clark proportional system to elect its lower house?
questions.explanation: Tasmania's House of Assembly elects several members per electorate, as does the ACT Legislative Assembly, so minor parties and independents win more seats. It is named for Thomas Hare and Tasmanian attorney-general Andrew Inglis Clark.
questions.hook: Clark was Tasmanian, so his system lives in Tasmania.

questions.question: Which 1920 High Court decision abandoned the doctrines of implied immunities and reserved state powers?
questions.explanation: In Amalgamated Society of Engineers v Adelaide Steamship Co, the court held that federal powers should be read by their natural meaning, not cut down to protect the states. It shifted power to Canberra for a century, and the 1983 Tasmanian Dam case built on it.
questions.hook: One 1920 judgment set Australian federalism's direction: toward Canberra.

questions.question: Which caretaker Prime Minister used his twenty-three days in office to veto a successor in 1968?
questions.explanation: The Country Party leader said he would not serve under William McMahon, which ruled McMahon out and helped John Gorton win the Liberal leadership. McMahon finally became PM in 1971 after McEwen retired.
questions.hook: 23 days was long enough to decide who came next, and who didn't.

questions.question: Which decade's banking collapse and land bust pushed both federation and the labour movement forward?
questions.explanation: Melbourne's land boom collapsed and many banks suspended payments in the 1893 crash, after the great maritime and shearers' strikes of 1890-91. Defeat in the strikes pushed unions into politics, and Labor won 35 NSW seats in 1891.
questions.hook: The 1890s depression built the Labor Party and the case for federation at the same time.

questions.question: Whose government fell in October 1941 when two independents voted against its budget?
questions.explanation: Independents Arthur Coles and Alex Wilson voted with Labor on 3 October 1941, ending Fadden's 40-day government, and John Curtin was sworn in on 7 October. It is the last time a federal government has been forced out by a vote on the floor of the House.
questions.hook: Fadden joked that, like the Flood, he 'reigned for 40 days and 40 nights'.

questions.question: Which two health economists designed the scheme that became Medibank?
questions.explanation: Melbourne economists Dick Scotton and John Deeble published a universal insurance model in 1968. Whitlam adopted it, and the Senate kept blocking it until the 1974 joint sitting passed it.
questions.hook: Two academics designed Medibank, then waited six years for a government to use it.

questions.question: At which former Tasmanian convict settlement did the April 1996 massacre that led to Australia's national gun laws take place?
questions.explanation: A gunman killed 35 people at the Port Arthur historic site on 28 April 1996. Within weeks the new Howard government agreed the National Firearms Agreement with the states, banning rapid-fire rifles and buying back more than 650,000 guns.
questions.hook: A place built to punish became the place that changed the law: 35 dead, 650,000 guns handed in.

questions.question: Near which NSW town did Edward Hargraves announce Australia's first payable gold find in 1851?
questions.explanation: Hargraves, back from the Californian goldfields, found gold at Lewis Ponds Creek near Bathurst in February 1851 and named the site Ophir. Within months bigger strikes at Ballarat and Bendigo drew the rush to Victoria.
questions.hook: Gold started in NSW at Bathurst, but Victoria's Ballarat and Bendigo stole the rush.

questions.question: Which Governor-General's wife announced the name 'Canberra' at the ceremony on 12 March 1913?
questions.explanation: Gertrude, Lady Denman read the name from a card. Rejected suggestions included 'Sydmeladperbrisho', made from bits of the state capitals, and the date is still marked as Canberra Day.
questions.hook: Canberra beat Sydmeladperbrisho, and Lady Denman read it out.

questions.question: Which colour fills the top half of the Aboriginal flag?
questions.explanation: Black stands for Aboriginal people, red for the earth and spiritual connection to the land, and the yellow circle for the sun. The flag was proclaimed a Flag of Australia in 1995, alongside the Torres Strait Islander flag.
questions.hook: People above, earth below, sun in the middle.

questions.question: Which state capital grew from a penal settlement set up at Moreton Bay in the 1820s?
questions.explanation: The penal settlement moved up the Brisbane River, and both the river and the city were named after Governor Thomas Brisbane. Queensland separated from New South Wales in 1859.
questions.hook: Convicts moved up the river, and the city took the governor's name.

questions.question: Which two states suffered the deadly Ash Wednesday bushfires of February 1983?
questions.explanation: The fires on 16 February 1983 killed 75 people, 47 in Victoria and 28 in South Australia, and destroyed more than 2,000 homes in Victoria alone. They followed a severe drought and a day of hot, strong winds.
questions.hook: A drought, a hot wind, and two states burning on a Wednesday.

questions.question: From which South Australian rocket range was Australia's first satellite launched in 1967?
questions.explanation: The research satellite WRESAT went up on 29 November 1967 on a modified American rocket. Woomera had been a joint British and Australian rocket range since 1947, and the satellite took its name from the Weapons Research Establishment that built it.
questions.hook: WRESAT came from Woomera, named for the Weapons Research Establishment.

questions.question: In which NSW town did Henry Parkes deliver his famous 1889 speech calling for a national government?
questions.explanation: Parkes spoke at the Tenterfield School of Arts on 24 October 1889, urging the colonies to form a single federal parliament. The speech gave new energy to the federation movement, which then led to the Constitution Convention of 1891 in Sydney.
questions.hook: Tenterfield School of Arts: where the federation drive was relaunched.

questions.question: Which Riverina town hosted the 1893 conference that proposed a popularly elected convention to write the Constitution?
questions.explanation: At the Corowa Conference, John Quick proposed that voters elect delegates to draft a constitution and then approve it by referendum. That plan was adopted by the colonial premiers in 1895 and became the path to the 1898 and 1899 referendums.
questions.hook: Corowa gave Federation its recipe: elect the drafters, then vote on the draft.

questions.question: Which fine-wooled breed of sheep did John Macarthur help establish in the colony from the 1790s?
questions.explanation: Macarthur bred imported Spanish-descended merino stock at Elizabeth Farm and then Camden. He is credited with sending the first bale of Australian wool to London in 1807, and wool became the colony's leading export in the decades that followed.
questions.hook: Macarthur's merinos put a nation's fortune on the sheep's back.

questions.question: From which English port did the First Fleet sail on 13 May 1787?
questions.explanation: Eleven ships left Portsmouth carrying roughly 750 convicts, with marines and officials, then called at Tenerife, Rio de Janeiro and Cape Town before the 252-day voyage ended at Botany Bay.
questions.hook: From Portsmouth the fleet sailed on a long road south.

questions.question: Which Eora man, captured on Governor Phillip's orders in 1789 and taken to England in 1792, returned to Sydney in 1795?
questions.explanation: Phillip built him a brick hut on the point that still carries his name, now the site of the Opera House. Bennelong returned in 1795, found himself caught between two worlds and died in 1813 at Kissing Point.
questions.hook: Bennelong's hut sat where the Opera House now sits.

questions.question: What name was given to the free settlers and officers who refused to dine with ex-convicts in early New South Wales?
questions.explanation: The exclusives, led by figures such as John Macarthur, wanted the colony run by free gentry and opposed Macquarie's elevation of emancipists. The two camps clashed over juries, land and the right to sit on the bench into the 1830s.
questions.hook: The exclusives locked the dinner-party door to emancipists.

questions.question: Which Hawkesbury town founded by Macquarie in 1810 honours the English anti-slavery campaigner?
questions.explanation: Macquarie planned five towns on higher ground after the river's floods. They were Windsor, Richmond, Wilberforce, Pitt Town and Castlereagh, which he named after royalty, statesmen and reformers.
questions.hook: Of five flood-proof towns, one was named for a freedom campaigner.

questions.question: What did Harold Lasseter claim to have found in central Australia in 1930?
questions.explanation: Lasseter said he had found a rich gold reef, and in 1930 he led an expedition backed by investors to relocate it. The expedition failed, and he died in the Petermann Ranges in 1931. No one has ever found the reef.
questions.hook: Lasseter's reef: a fortune that only one man ever claimed to see.

questions.question: By what name was the settlement now called Darwin officially known until 1911?
questions.explanation: The town was founded in 1869 and named after the British Prime Minister Lord Palmerston. The Commonwealth took over the Northern Territory in 1911, and the town was renamed to avoid confusion with a New Zealand place of the same name.
questions.hook: A prime minister's name until 1911, then Darwin of the Beagle.

questions.question: Where on the South Australian coast did Matthew Flinders meet the French commander Nicolas Baudin in April 1802?
questions.explanation: The two captains, who did not yet know their countries had made peace, met peacefully on 8 April 1802. Flinders named the spot Encounter Bay.
questions.hook: Two captains who had not heard the war was over, one friendly meeting, and a bay named for the surprise.

questions.question: Which Aboriginal guide carried Edmund Kennedy's papers to the rescue ship in 1848, after Kennedy died?
questions.explanation: Kennedy's Cape York expedition met starvation and attacks, and only three of thirteen men survived. Jackey Jackey stayed with Kennedy until he died and then reached the schooner Ariel with his journal.
questions.hook: He stayed with the leader until the end, then walked on alone with the journal.

questions.question: After Edward Eyre's overseer Baxter was killed during the 1841 crossing to Albany, which Aboriginal man completed the journey with him?
questions.explanation: Two other members of Eyre's party killed Baxter and fled with most of the supplies. Eyre and Wylie survived on scraps and a rescue by a French whaler, and they reached Albany after crossing the Nullarbor coast.
questions.hook: Two men ran with the stores, and the one who stayed helped Eyre reach Albany.

questions.question: At which peninsula on Moreton Bay was Queensland's first convict settlement established in 1824?
questions.explanation: The settlement was abandoned within a year because of poor water and attacks, and moved up the Brisbane River in 1825. The Redcliffe site is often said to be Queensland's first European settlement.
questions.hook: The first try was abandoned within a year, and the lasting town sat upriver.

questions.question: Which three words are traditionally given as Ned Kelly's last words on the scaffold in 1880?
questions.explanation: Reports differ on his exact words, but 'Such is life' became the accepted version and is now a stock phrase for shrugging off misfortune. Joseph Furphy borrowed the same phrase for the title of his 1903 novel.
questions.hook: A shrug at the gallows that became a national saying.

questions.question: Which coach company, founded in Melbourne in 1853, carried passengers and mail across the bush for about seventy years?
questions.explanation: Cobb and Co first ran from Melbourne to the goldfields, then spread across eastern Australia and into Queensland and New South Wales, using American-style Concord coaches. Its last regular run was in Queensland in 1924, when motor vehicles and rail took over.
questions.hook: The Wells Fargo of the outback, only it began in Melbourne.

questions.question: Which constellation's stars appear on the Eureka flag?
questions.explanation: The flag shows five white stars arranged as the Southern Cross on a blue field, and was sewn in Ballarat in 1854. The Southern Cross was already a symbol of the colonies, and it later appeared on the Australian national flag as well.
questions.hook: The same five stars a digger saw overhead, stitched to a flag.

questions.question: Which New South Wales town, formerly called Lambing Flat, was the scene of anti-Chinese riots in 1861?
questions.explanation: Thousands of European diggers drove Chinese miners from the goldfield, and the 'Roll Up' banner became the rioters' flag. Troops restored order, and the unrest helped lead to NSW's Chinese restriction laws. The town was renamed after Governor Sir John Young.
questions.hook: The riots left the town with the governor's name.

questions.question: In 1856, which group of Melbourne tradesmen, led by James Stephens, won the eight-hour working day?
questions.explanation: The stonemasons working on the University of Melbourne's building site won eight hours' work for the same pay. Melbourne's Eight Hours Day march began that year on 21 April, and the slogan was eight hours labour, eight hours recreation, eight hours rest.
questions.hook: Eight hours work, eight hours rest, eight hours play, and the masons asked first.

questions.question: At which South Australian port did more than 15,000 Chinese miners land in 1857 to dodge Victoria's poll tax?
questions.explanation: Victoria charged a £10 landing tax on each Chinese passenger, so ship masters dropped them across the border and they walked roughly 400 kilometres to the goldfields. South Australia had no such tax, and Robe's population briefly exploded.
questions.hook: A tax dodge that put a tiny port on the map.

questions.question: Which house on the shore of Sydney Harbour is the prime minister's official Sydney residence?
questions.explanation: Kirribilli House sits on the north shore with views of the Opera House and Harbour Bridge. Next door, Admiralty House serves as the Governor-General's Sydney residence, and the two are often confused.
questions.hook: The PM's harbour house looks across the water at the Opera House.

questions.question: What is the official word-for-word record of parliamentary debates in Australia called?
questions.explanation: The name comes from Thomas Curson Hansard, the London printer who published reports of British parliamentary debates from the early nineteenth century. Federal Hansard has recorded the House and Senate since 1901 and is searchable online.
questions.hook: Named after a London printer, it records every word politicians say.

questions.question: What colour are the seats in the chamber of the House of Representatives?
questions.explanation: The House copies the green benches of the British House of Commons, while the Senate chamber is furnished in red, like the House of Lords.
questions.hook: Green for the people's house, red for the house of review.

questions.question: What name is given to the Governor-General's rarely used powers, such as dismissing a government, that may be exercised without ministerial advice?
questions.explanation: The reserve powers are not set out in detail in the Constitution. They rest on the Constitution's text and on convention, and they include dismissing a government. The most controversial use was the dismissal of the Whitlam government on 11 November 1975.
questions.hook: Powers held in reserve are the Crown's emergency kit.

questions.question: What is the upper house of the New South Wales and Victorian parliaments called?
questions.explanation: Both colonies had upper houses before Federation, and the councils survived as houses of review. The Legislative Assembly is the lower house in both, while 'House of Assembly' is the name used in South Australia and Tasmania.
questions.hook: Council above, Assembly below.

questions.question: In which city did the Federal Convention, with elected delegates, first meet in March 1897?
questions.explanation: Delegates were elected by voters in New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania, and Western Australia sent nominees. Queensland sent no delegates to Adelaide and announced during the Sydney session that it wanted to join. The convention then met in Sydney in late 1897 and Melbourne in 1898 to finish the draft.
questions.hook: Adelaide, Sydney, Melbourne: the three stops to the Constitution.

questions.question: Bob Brown first rose to national prominence campaigning to save which Tasmanian river from being dammed in 1982-83?
questions.explanation: The Franklin Dam blockades saw more than 1,000 people arrested, including Brown, and Hawke's government blocked the dam, a decision upheld by the High Court in 1983. Brown later became the first leader of the Australian Greens in 2005.
questions.hook: Save the Franklin: the blockade that grew the Greens.

questions.question: In which Queensland town was Kevin Rudd born in 1957?
questions.explanation: Rudd was born in Nambour on the Sunshine Coast hinterland. He grew up on a farm near Eumundi, and his father died when Rudd was 11.
questions.hook: From a farm near Nambour to the Lodge.

questions.question: Kim Beazley senior, father of the later Labor leader, held which portfolio in the Whitlam government?
questions.explanation: Beazley Sr was Minister for Education from 1972 to 1975 and was a key figure in the expansion of federal funding for schools. His son, Kim Beazley Jr, later served as Defence Minister and Labor leader.
questions.hook: Father schooled the nation, son defended it.

questions.question: Which Melbourne school did Robert Menzies attend as a teenager?
questions.explanation: Menzies was born in Jeparit in the Wimmera and moved to Melbourne to attend Wesley College before studying law at the University of Melbourne. He was brilliant, winning scholarships, and entered Victorian politics in 1928.
questions.hook: From Jeparit to Wesley, then to the top.

questions.question: What colour name was given to the mostly female independents who won affluent Liberal-held seats such as Kooyong and Goldstein in 2022?
questions.explanation: The 'teals' ran on climate action, integrity in politics and gender equality, with campaign branding blending Liberal blue and green. Monique Ryan took Kooyong from Treasurer Josh Frydenberg and Zoe Daniel won Goldstein.
questions.hook: Liberal blue plus climate green made teal, and it cost the Liberals their heartland.

questions.question: Which tiny Pacific nation hosted an offshore processing centre for asylum seekers under Howard's 2001 'Pacific Solution'?
questions.explanation: The island's detention centre opened in 2001 and received people intercepted at sea, with Papua New Guinea's Manus Island as the second site. Labor closed the centres in 2008, then reopened Nauru and Manus in 2012 under Julia Gillard.
questions.hook: Smallest republic, biggest policy: Nauru became Australia's offshore waiting room.

questions.question: Which animal did the Gunditjmara farm using stone channels and ponds at Budj Bim in south-west Victoria?
questions.explanation: The Gunditjmara engineered channels and weirs across lava flows to trap and smoke short-finned eels, and some of the system is thousands of years old. Budj Bim was World Heritage listed in 2019.
questions.hook: Budj Bim's lava made the channels and the Gunditjmara made the eel farm.

questions.question: The Arrernte people are the traditional owners of the country around which Central Australian town?
questions.explanation: Alice Springs is known to the Arrernte as Mparntwe, and the Arrernte language has several dialects.
questions.hook: Alice Springs is Mparntwe first: the town sits on Arrernte country.

questions.question: The Yolngu people live in which region of the Northern Territory?
questions.explanation: Yolngu, meaning 'people', live across north-east Arnhem Land in communities such as Yirrkala and Galiwin'ku. The band Yothu Yindi, led by Mandawuy Yunupingu, brought Yolngu Matha lyrics into the pop charts with 'Treaty' in 1991.
questions.hook: Arnhem Land is Yolngu country, and Yothu Yindi's 'Treaty' carried Yolngu Matha onto the charts.

questions.question: Perth sits on the traditional country of which Aboriginal people?
questions.explanation: The Noongar homelands cover the whole south-west corner of Western Australia, and Perth is Whadjuk Noongar country. The South West Native Title Settlement between the Noongar people and the WA government covers this region.
questions.hook: Noongar country is the whole south-west corner, not just Perth.

questions.question: Neville Bonner, the first Indigenous member of federal parliament, represented which state in the Senate from 1971?
questions.explanation: Bonner, a Bundjalung man, was chosen by the Queensland parliament to fill a casual vacancy and sat for the Liberals until 1983. He lost his seat that year as an independent after being dropped from the Liberal ticket.
questions.hook: Bundjalung man, Queensland senator, first through the door in 1971.

questions.question: Which settlement was placed under martial law in 1824 during the Wiradjuri resistance led by Windradyne?
questions.explanation: Governor Brisbane declared martial law in August 1824 after fighting and killings around the new settlement of Bathurst. Windradyne was the Wiradjuri leader at the centre of that resistance.
questions.hook: Windradyne's resistance around Bathurst brought martial law to the town in 1824.

questions.question: Charles Perkins in 1966 became the first Aboriginal man to graduate from which university?
questions.explanation: Perkins graduated with a Bachelor of Arts from the University of Sydney. In 1984 he became the first Aboriginal person to head a Commonwealth department, the Department of Aboriginal Affairs.
questions.hook: Perkins studied at Sydney, then led the 1965 Freedom Ride through the towns of country New South Wales.

questions.question: Which area of eastern Singapore became the main prison camp for Australian soldiers captured when the island fell in February 1942?
questions.explanation: About 15,000 Australians were taken prisoner at Singapore, and thousands were held at Changi before being sent to work camps such as the Burma-Thailand Railway. The Changi name became shorthand for the wider captivity experience of Australian prisoners of the Japanese.
questions.hook: Singapore fell on 15 February 1942, and Changi became a name for captivity.

questions.question: Which British innovation, first used on the Somme in 1916, largely failed to support the Australian attack at First Bullecourt in April 1917 and left the infantry exposed?
questions.explanation: The tanks broke down or were knocked out early, and the attack went in without an artillery bombardment, so the Australian 4th Brigade lost about 2,300 men, per Peter Burness of the Australian War Memorial. Tanks worked far better alongside infantry at Hamel in 1918.
questions.hook: A machine that failed at Bullecourt, then helped win the war once it was used properly.

questions.question: Which Presbyterian minister founded the Australian Inland Mission that grew into the Royal Flying Doctor Service?
questions.explanation: John Flynn set up the Australian Inland Mission, whose medical air service grew into the Royal Flying Doctor Service, bringing doctors to remote outback communities by plane.
questions.hook: Flynn of the Inland put a doctor in the sky.

questions.question: Pauline Hanson was first elected to Parliament in 1996 for which Queensland seat?
questions.explanation: Hanson was the Liberal candidate for Oxley in 1996 but was disendorsed, then won the seat as an independent. In 1998 she won Blair for One Nation.
questions.hook: The seat she won after being disendorsed.

questions.question: Which critic coined the phrase 'the cultural cringe' in a 1950 essay about Australian attitudes to local culture?
questions.explanation: Arthur Angell Phillips argued that Australians tended to assume local work was inferior to work from overseas, especially Britain. Donald Horne's The Lucky Country followed in 1964 and is often confused with it.
questions.hook: Phillips named the cringe in 1950, before anyone else could.

questions.question: Which is the largest country in the world by land area?
questions.explanation: Russia covers about 17.1 million square kilometres, roughly 1.7 times second-placed Canada and more than Antarctica, spread across eleven time zones. The next favourite follow-up is the second-largest country, Canada, which beats the US and China only because of its vast area of lakes.
questions.hook: Russia is so wide that when Kaliningrad has breakfast, Kamchatka is already having dinner.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Canada?
questions.explanation: Queen Victoria chose Ottawa in 1857 as a compromise between English-speaking Toronto and French-speaking Montreal (and Quebec City), and because it sat further from the American border. Toronto is the largest city, which is why it is the most common wrong answer.
questions.hook: Ottawa sits on the river between Ontario and Quebec, splitting the English–French difference.

questions.question: Which mountain is the highest above sea level?
questions.explanation: Everest's official height, agreed by Nepal and China in 2020, is 8,848.86 metres, on the Nepal–Tibet border. K2 is second at 8,611 metres and Kangchenjunga third; measured base to summit Hawaii's Mauna Kea is taller, and measured from Earth's centre Ecuador's Chimborazo wins.
questions.hook: Everest, K2, Kangchenjunga: E, K, K, the top three in order.

questions.question: Which desert is the largest hot desert in the world?
questions.explanation: The Sahara spans about nine million square kilometres across eleven countries, roughly the size of the United States or China. A desert is defined by low rainfall, not heat, so Antarctica is the largest desert overall and the Arctic second; the Arabian is the second-largest hot desert.
questions.hook: 'Sahara' simply means 'desert' in Arabic, so 'Sahara Desert' is really 'Desert Desert'.

questions.question: Which country has the largest population in the world?
questions.explanation: India passed China in 2023 according to UN estimates, with both above 1.4 billion and together holding more than a third of humanity. China's population has been shrinking since 2022, while the United States remains a distant third.
questions.hook: 2023 was the year the crown passed from China to India, and China has been shrinking ever since.

questions.question: What is the capital of New Zealand?
questions.explanation: It replaced Auckland in 1865 after a commission of three Australians picked it for its central position on Cook Strait, partly to calm South Island talk of separation. Auckland is far larger, and Wellington is the southernmost capital of any sovereign state.
questions.hook: Australians chose New Zealand's capital, and they picked the windy middle.

questions.question: Which strait separates mainland Australia from Tasmania?
questions.explanation: It is about 240 kilometres wide and named for surgeon George Bass, who with Matthew Flinders sailed around Tasmania in 1798–99 and proved it was an island. Torres Strait separates Australia from New Guinea, while Cook and Foveaux straits are in New Zealand.
questions.hook: Bass is the low note at the bottom of the map; Torres is up top.

questions.question: Which country is shaped like a boot?
questions.explanation: The peninsula's outline has Calabria as the toe, Puglia as the heel and Sicily as the ball being kicked. Italy also completely surrounds two independent countries, San Marino and Vatican City.
questions.hook: The boot kicks Sicily, and it's carrying two tiny countries in its pocket.

questions.question: Which mountain range separates Europe from Asia in western Russia?
questions.explanation: The range runs about 2,500 kilometres north to south and is the conventional boundary, continued south by the Ural River. Further south the line runs through the Caucasus, whose Mount Elbrus is often named Europe's highest peak.
questions.hook: The Urals divide the continents; the Caucasus gives Europe its roof in Elbrus.

questions.question: Which country spans the most time zones once overseas territories are counted?
questions.explanation: Counting overseas departments and territories from French Polynesia to Réunion and New Caledonia, France spans twelve time zones, thirteen with its Antarctic claim. Russia has the most in one continuous landmass with eleven, and the US also has eleven counting its territories.
questions.hook: France wins on islands, not land: the sun never sets on the French Republic.

questions.question: What is the capital of Kenya?
questions.explanation: It began as a depot on the Uganda Railway in 1899, and its name comes from a Maasai phrase meaning 'cool water'. Nairobi National Park lies within the city limits, so giraffes and lions can be photographed against office towers; Mombasa is the main port.
questions.hook: Nairobi is the rare capital where lions share the skyline.

questions.question: What is the capital of Brazil?
questions.explanation: Purpose-built on the central plateau and inaugurated in 1960, it was planned by Lúcio Costa with buildings by Oscar Niemeyer. Salvador was the colonial capital until 1763, then Rio de Janeiro until Brasília replaced it.
questions.hook: From the air the city plan looks like an aeroplane: Brasília was built to fly the capital inland.

questions.question: In which country does the Mekong River rise?
questions.explanation: It rises on the Tibetan Plateau in Qinghai and runs about 4,900 kilometres through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam to its delta. The Yangtze and Yellow rivers rise on the same plateau, which is why it is called Asia's water tower.
questions.hook: One plateau in Tibet feeds the Mekong, the Yangtze and the Yellow River.

questions.question: Which African country defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa in 1896 to keep its independence?
questions.explanation: Emperor Menelik II's victory kept Ethiopia free through the scramble for Africa, apart from an Italian occupation from 1936 to 1941. Liberia is the other African country usually described as never colonised, and neighbouring Eritrea was an Italian colony.
questions.hook: Adwa 1896: the battle that kept Ethiopia off the colonial map, and why many African flags use its green, gold and red.

questions.question: Which is the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall?
questions.explanation: The Venezuelan falls drop 979 metres in all from the tepui Auyán-tepui, including an unbroken plunge of about 807 metres. They are named after American pilot Jimmie Angel, who crash-landed on top in 1937; South Africa's Tugela Falls is the usual runner-up.
questions.hook: Named for a pilot who landed on top, not for any heavenly angel.

questions.question: What is the capital of Switzerland?
questions.explanation: Swiss law names no capital; Bern is the 'federal city' and seat of government. Zurich is the largest city and financial centre, and Geneva hosts the UN's European headquarters, which is why both are common wrong answers.
questions.hook: Bern is named after a bear, and live bears still have a park there.

questions.question: Which country has Vientiane as its capital?
questions.explanation: Vientiane sits on the Mekong, looking across at Thailand, and Laos is the only landlocked country in South-East Asia. It is also the most heavily bombed country per person in history because of US air raids during the Vietnam War.
questions.hook: The only South-East Asian country with no beach.

questions.question: What is the capital of Morocco?
questions.explanation: Casablanca is far larger and famous from the 1942 film, but the royal palace and government are in Rabat on the Atlantic coast. Fez, Marrakesh, Meknes and Rabat are Morocco's four historic imperial cities.
questions.hook: Casablanca got the film; Rabat got the king.

questions.question: Which country contains the world's largest salt flat?
questions.explanation: The Salar de Uyuni covers more than 10,000 square kilometres at about 3,650 metres and is so flat it is used to calibrate satellites. Beneath it lies one of the world's largest lithium deposits, which Bolivia, Chile and Argentina together dominate as the 'lithium triangle'.
questions.hook: When it rains, Uyuni becomes the world's largest mirror.

questions.question: Which two countries share the Iguazu Falls?
questions.explanation: The falls stretch nearly three kilometres with about 275 separate drops, the biggest being the Devil's Throat. Paraguay meets the other two at the nearby Triple Frontier, but the falls themselves are on the Argentina–Brazil border.
questions.hook: On seeing Iguazu, Eleanor Roosevelt reportedly said 'Poor Niagara'.

questions.question: What is the capital of Vietnam?
questions.explanation: Hanoi became capital of the reunified country in 1976, having been North Vietnam's capital since 1954. Ho Chi Minh City, formerly Saigon, is larger and the commercial hub, and Hue was the imperial capital under the Nguyen dynasty.
questions.hook: The North won the war, so the capital stayed in the North.

questions.question: The geographic term 'delta' was first applied by Herodotus to the mouth of which river?
questions.explanation: The triangle of land where the Nile fans out into the Mediterranean reminded Greek writers of the capital letter delta. Since the Aswan High Dam opened in 1970, far less silt reaches the delta, and parts of the coast are now retreating.
questions.hook: Draw a capital Greek delta, point it south at Cairo, and you have the Nile's mouth.

questions.question: Which country was formerly known as Siam?
questions.explanation: The name changed in 1939, reverted in 1945 and became permanent in 1949; Thailand means 'land of the free'. It is the only South-East Asian country never colonised by a European power, and Siamese cats and the original 'Siamese twins' carry the old name.
questions.hook: 'Land of the free' is the one neighbour that never had a colonial master.

questions.question: What is the capital of Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Abuja was built in the centre of the country and replaced Lagos as capital in 1991, partly to sit on neutral ground between the main ethnic regions. Lagos remains the largest city in Africa by most estimates.
questions.hook: The capital moved inland to be nobody's home turf.

questions.question: What is the capital of Chile?
questions.explanation: Santiago sits in a valley beneath the Andes, but the national congress has met in the port of Valparaíso since 1990. Chile is about 4,300 kilometres long but averages under 180 kilometres wide.
questions.hook: The government sits in Santiago, the parliament by the sea in Valparaíso.

questions.question: Which is the world's driest non-polar desert?
questions.explanation: Parts of northern Chile's Atacama have gone years without measurable rain, and its soils are so Mars-like that NASA tests rovers there. The clear, dry, high skies host the ALMA radio array and the European Extremely Large Telescope under construction.
questions.hook: Dry enough to test Mars rovers, clear enough for the world's biggest telescopes.

questions.question: Which mountain is the highest in Africa?
questions.explanation: The dormant Tanzanian volcano rises 5,895 metres and is the world's tallest free-standing mountain. Mount Kenya is Africa's second-highest, and Kilimanjaro's summit glaciers are expected to vanish within a few decades.
questions.hook: Snow on the equator, but not for much longer.

questions.question: What is the capital of Turkey?
questions.explanation: Atatürk made Ankara the capital in 1923 to break with the Ottoman past and to sit safely in the Anatolian heartland. Istanbul is far larger and straddles Europe and Asia; since 2022 the country has asked the UN to call it Türkiye.
questions.hook: The famous city straddles two continents; the capital is the quieter inland one.

questions.question: Which Australian desert is the largest?
questions.explanation: It spans about 350,000 square kilometres across Western Australia and South Australia, larger than the United Kingdom, and was named by explorer Ernest Giles in 1875 after Queen Victoria. The Great Sandy Desert is second, and the Simpson is known for its parallel red dunes.
questions.hook: Great Victoria beats Great Sandy: the queen outranks the sand.

questions.question: Which country's seat of government, at more than 3,600 metres, is the highest in the world?
questions.explanation: La Paz houses Bolivia's government, while Sucre is the constitutional capital and home of the Supreme Court. Quito in Ecuador, at about 2,850 metres, is the highest official capital that is also the seat of government.
questions.hook: Bolivia splits the job: La Paz up high does the governing, Sucre holds the title.

questions.question: Which US city sits at the confluence of the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers?
questions.explanation: The two rivers join there to form the Ohio, and cheap coal and river transport made Pittsburgh the steel capital of America. With about 446 bridges it is nicknamed the City of Bridges.
questions.hook: Two rivers in, one out, and more bridges than Venice.

questions.question: Which country's realm includes the Faroe Islands and Greenland?
questions.explanation: Both are self-governing parts of the Kingdom of Denmark. Greenland left the European Communities in 1985, mainly over fishing rights, while Denmark stayed in, making it the first territory ever to leave.
questions.hook: Greenland quit Europe's club three decades before Brexit.

questions.question: What is the capital of the Philippines?
questions.explanation: Manila is the capital within the wider Metro Manila region, and it is one of the most densely populated cities on Earth. Neighbouring Quezon City was officially the capital from 1948 to 1976 and still has more people.
questions.hook: The capital isn't even the biggest city in its own metro area.

questions.question: Which African country is the largest by area?
distractors: The Democratic Republic of the Congo
questions.explanation: Algeria became Africa's largest when South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011; more than eighty per cent of it is Sahara. The DR Congo is now second.
questions.hook: Algeria only took the title in 2011, when Sudan split in two.

questions.question: What is the capital of Indonesia?
questions.explanation: Indonesia is building a new capital, Nusantara, on Borneo because Jakarta is overcrowded and sinking, but the move needs a presidential decree that had still not been issued by mid-2026. Indonesia's Constitutional Court confirmed in May 2026 that Jakarta remains the capital until then.
questions.hook: Nusantara is built but not yet the capital, so Jakarta keeps the title for now.

questions.question: Which two seas does the Bosphorus connect?
questions.answer: The Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara
distractors: The Sea of Marmara and the Aegean
The Black Sea and the Aegean
The Black Sea and the Sea of Azov
questions.explanation: The strait runs through Istanbul; beyond the Marmara, the Dardanelles lead on to the Aegean. Together they are Russia's only warm-water route from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean, which is why Gallipoli, on the Dardanelles, mattered in 1915.
questions.hook: Black, Bosphorus, Marmara, Dardanelles, Aegean: north to south in order.

questions.question: Which meridian was chosen in 1884 as zero degrees longitude?
questions.explanation: The International Meridian Conference in Washington chose it because most of the world's sea charts already used Greenwich; France abstained and kept the Paris meridian for decades. The modern GPS zero line actually runs about 100 metres east of the brass line at the observatory.
questions.hook: Tourists straddle the brass line at Greenwich, but their phones say zero is a short walk east.

questions.question: Which country lies immediately south of Egypt?
questions.explanation: The two share a long desert border and argue over the Halaib Triangle on the Red Sea coast. Sudan has more ancient pyramids than Egypt, built by the kingdom of Kush at sites like Meroë.
questions.hook: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt: an easy point most people lose.

questions.question: Which two countries share the island of Hispaniola?
distractors: The Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico
questions.explanation: French-speaking Haiti occupies the western third and in 1804 became the first Black-led republic after a successful slave revolt. The Spanish-speaking Dominican Republic holds the rest, and the border is visible from space because Haiti has lost far more of its forest.
questions.hook: One island, two languages, and a border you can see from orbit in the tree line.

questions.question: Which two countries are doubly landlocked, surrounded entirely by other landlocked countries?
questions.explanation: To reach the sea from either you must cross at least two borders. Liechtenstein sits between Switzerland and Austria, and Uzbekistan is surrounded by Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Turkmenistan.
questions.hook: Two borders minimum before you smell salt water.

questions.question: What is the capital of Kazakhstan?
questions.explanation: The capital moved from Almaty in 1997; the city was renamed Nur-Sultan in 2019 after the first president and changed back to Astana in 2022. Its name simply means 'capital' in Kazakh, and Almaty remains the largest city.
questions.hook: Akmola, Astana, Nur-Sultan, Astana: check the date on the question.

questions.question: Which country has the most UNESCO World Heritage Sites?
questions.explanation: After the 2026 committee session in Busan, Italy had 62 sites to China's 61, each having added one that year. Germany, France and Spain follow some way behind, and the list now totals 1,273 sites.
questions.hook: Italy and China are neck and neck; everyone else is a distant third.

questions.question: Which strait separates the North and South Islands of New Zealand?
questions.explanation: About 22 kilometres wide at its narrowest, it funnels westerly winds, making it one of the roughest stretches of water in the world. Foveaux Strait separates the South Island from Stewart Island, and Cook named the strait after himself in 1770 on his first voyage.
questions.hook: Cook between the two big islands, Foveaux down to the little one.

questions.question: Which African lake has shrunk by roughly ninety per cent since the 1960s?
questions.explanation: Shared by Chad, Cameroon, Niger and Nigeria, it is so shallow that drought and irrigation shrank it dramatically. The loss of water fed poverty and conflict in the region, including the rise of Boko Haram.
questions.hook: Four countries share a lake that is now a tenth of what their grandparents knew.

questions.question: Which city contains an entire sovereign state within its boundaries?
questions.explanation: Vatican City, created by the 1929 Lateran Treaty, sits wholly inside Rome, making Rome the capital that surrounds another capital. Nice, the likely trap, is next to Monaco rather than around it, and San Marino is enclosed by Italy but not by any city.
questions.hook: Two capitals, one inside the other.

questions.question: Which Australian lake is the country's lowest point and only rarely fills?
questions.explanation: Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre sits about 15 metres below sea level at the bottom of a basin covering about a sixth of Australia. It has filled to capacity only a handful of times since European settlement, most famously in 1974, and when it does it draws huge flocks of pelicans.
questions.hook: When it fills, pelicans arrive from the coast within days, and nobody is sure how they know.

questions.question: Which city was officially known as Constantinople until 1930?
questions.explanation: Founded as the Greek colony Byzantium, it was renamed for the emperor Constantine in 330 CE and fell to the Ottomans in 1453. Turkey's 1930 postal law made 'Istanbul' the only accepted name, from a Greek phrase meaning 'to the city'.
questions.hook: Byzantium, Constantinople, Istanbul: three names, one city, sixteen centuries.

questions.question: The Ghan railway runs from Adelaide to Darwin via which town, roughly halfway?
questions.explanation: The line reached Alice Springs in 1929 but was not extended to Darwin until 2004, completing a trip of about 2,979 kilometres. The Ghan is named after the Afghan cameleers who carried supplies through the interior before the railway.
questions.hook: The Ghan is short for Afghan, after the cameleers who got there first.

questions.question: Which river flows through the centre of Paris?
questions.explanation: It runs about 775 kilometres from Burgundy to the English Channel at Le Havre, and the Île de la Cité, home of Notre-Dame, sits in the middle of it. The Loire is France's longest river, and the Marne joins the Seine just east of Paris.
questions.hook: The Seine is the river of Paris; the Loire is the long one lined with châteaux.

questions.question: Which is the longest river in Australia?
questions.explanation: It runs about 2,500 kilometres from the Australian Alps to the sea near Goolwa in South Australia and forms most of the NSW–Victoria border. The Darling, Murrumbidgee and Lachlan are its longest tributaries, and the Murray–Darling Basin covers about a seventh of the continent.
questions.hook: Murray is the main road; the Darling and the Murrumbidgee are its side streets.

questions.question: What is the capital of Papua New Guinea?
questions.explanation: It is on the south coast of New Guinea facing Australia, and was named in 1873 by Captain John Moresby after his father. PNG became independent from Australia in 1975, and Lae is its second city and main industrial port.
questions.hook: Captain Moresby named the harbour after his dad.

questions.question: On which Japanese island does Mount Fuji stand?
questions.explanation: The 3,776-metre volcano sits on the border of Shizuoka and Yamanashi prefectures, about 100 kilometres south-west of Tokyo. It last erupted in 1707, and Honshu is the largest of Japan's four main islands, home to Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka.
questions.hook: Honshu means "main province": the main island holds the main mountain.

questions.question: Which is the only South American country with coastlines on both the Pacific and the Caribbean?
questions.explanation: Colombia's two coasts are separated by Panama, which was part of Colombia until 1903. The US backed Panama's independence and then built the Panama Canal across it.
questions.hook: Colombia lost the canal zone and kept the two coastlines.

questions.question: In which country is Aconcagua, the highest mountain outside Asia?
questions.explanation: It rises 6,961 metres in Mendoza province, just east of the Chilean border, and is one of the Seven Summits, the highest peaks on each continent. Ojos del Salado, the highest volcano on Earth, is second in South America and sits on the Argentina–Chile border.
questions.hook: Almost 7,000 metres and walkable without ropes, yet the thin air kills climbers.

questions.question: Which African kingdom changed its name from Swaziland in 2018?
questions.explanation: King Mswati III announced the change on the fiftieth anniversary of independence in April 2018; Eswatini means 'land of the Swazis' in siSwati. It is one of the world's last absolute monarchies, and it borders only South Africa and Mozambique.
questions.hook: It was only ever the Swazis' land; the new name just says so in their own language.

questions.question: Under the 2023 Falepili Union treaty, Australia offers a special migration pathway to citizens of which Pacific nation threatened by rising seas?
questions.explanation: The treaty, in force since 2024, lets up to 280 Tuvaluans a year move to Australia and commits Australia to help if Tuvalu faces a disaster. Tuvalu's highest point is under five metres above sea level, and the country earns a large share of its income from leasing its '.tv' internet domain.
questions.hook: Tuvalu makes money from '.tv' while its land slowly goes under water.

questions.question: Which two rivers have formed the border between Germany and Poland since 1945?
questions.explanation: The Oder–Neisse line was set at the Potsdam Conference, moving Poland about 200 kilometres west and expelling millions of Germans from the lands east of it. East Germany accepted it in 1950, and a reunited Germany confirmed it by treaty in 1990.
questions.hook: Poland was shifted west in 1945, and the Oder and Neisse mark where it stopped.

questions.question: Which Australian external territory in the Indian Ocean is famous for its mass migration of red crabs?
questions.explanation: Tens of millions of crabs march from the forest to the sea to breed at the start of the wet season, and roads are closed for them. The island was named by an English captain on Christmas Day 1643, and it is closer to Jakarta than to Perth.
questions.hook: Once a year Christmas Island turns red, and the roads belong to crabs.

questions.question: Which city is the capital of the Northern Territory?
questions.explanation: Darwin was named Port Darwin in 1839 by Commander John Clements Wickham of HMS Beagle, after Charles Darwin, who had sailed on the Beagle's earlier voyage. It was bombed by Japan in 1942 and flattened by Cyclone Tracy on Christmas Day 1974, then rebuilt.
questions.hook: Darwin the city carries the name of Darwin the naturalist, and it has been rebuilt from ruins twice.

questions.question: Which Australian capital city is nicknamed the City of Churches?
questions.explanation: Adelaide was founded in 1836 as a free colony without convicts, and many early settlers were nonconformist Protestants who built numerous churches. Its tidy grid was laid out by Colonel William Light and is ringed by parklands.
questions.hook: A free settlement with no convicts, planned by a colonel and filled with steeples.

questions.question: Which river splits the Iraqi capital, Baghdad, into its eastern and western halves?
questions.explanation: The caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad on the Tigris in 762, and it became the centre of the Abbasid golden age. The Tigris and Euphrates together define Mesopotamia, meaning the land between the rivers.
questions.hook: Mesopotamia is Greek for between the rivers, and Baghdad sits on one of them.

questions.question: On which river is the city of Hobart built?
questions.explanation: The Derwent widens into a deep estuary at Hobart, giving the city a sheltered deep-water harbour. The city was founded in 1804 and is the country's second-oldest capital after Sydney.
questions.hook: Sydney is the oldest capital, and Hobart on the Derwent comes right after.

questions.question: On which Greek island is the Minoan palace of Knossos?
questions.explanation: Knossos, near Heraklion, was the centre of the Bronze Age Minoan civilisation, and Arthur Evans excavated it from 1900. Crete is the largest of the Greek islands.
questions.hook: Arthur Evans dug up a palace that many link to the Minotaur's labyrinth.

questions.question: Which city is the capital of Texas?
questions.explanation: The city was named after Stephen F. Austin, known as the Father of Texas, and became the capital of the independent Republic of Texas in 1839. Houston is bigger and Dallas better known, so both are common wrong answers.
questions.hook: The biggest cities in Texas are all wrong; the capital is named for the founder.

questions.question: Which one country has coastlines on both the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea?
questions.explanation: Russia reaches the Black Sea near Sochi and the Caspian in Dagestan. The Volga-Don Canal links the Volga, which drains to the Caspian, with the Don, which drains through the Sea of Azov to the Black Sea. Turkey borders the Black Sea but not the Caspian, while Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan border the Caspian but not the Black Sea.
questions.hook: Only one country borders both seas, and a canal links their river systems.

questions.question: Which is the southernmost state capital on the Australian mainland?
questions.explanation: Melbourne lies at about 37.8 degrees south, well below Adelaide at 34.9 and Sydney at 33.9. Only Hobart, on the island of Tasmania, is further south among Australian capitals.
questions.hook: Melbourne is the capital closest to Antarctica, bar Hobart across Bass Strait.

questions.question: Which is the smallest country on mainland Africa?
questions.explanation: It covers about 11,300 square kilometres and is a thin strip along the Gambia River, entirely surrounded by Senegal apart from its short Atlantic coast. Only island nations such as Seychelles are smaller on the continent.
questions.hook: A country shaped like a river with Senegal wrapped around it.

questions.question: Which Great Lake lies entirely within the United States?
questions.explanation: The other four Great Lakes are shared with Canada. Michigan connects to Lake Huron through the wide Straits of Mackinac, and some geographers treat the two as a single lake.
questions.hook: Four lakes cross the border; Michigan stays home.

questions.question: Which city is the constitutional capital of the Netherlands, even though the government sits in another city?
questions.explanation: The Dutch constitution names Amsterdam as the capital, and the monarch is sworn in at the Nieuwe Kerk there. The cabinet, parliament and Supreme Court all work in The Hague, which is why the two are so often confused.
questions.hook: Amsterdam wears the crown, but The Hague does the work.

questions.question: Which city is the capital of Belgium?
questions.explanation: Brussels is officially bilingual in French and Dutch and forms its own region inside Flemish Belgium. It also houses the European Commission and the Council of the EU, so it is often called the unofficial capital of Europe.
questions.hook: Same name as the sprout, and the same city that runs Europe's paperwork.

questions.question: Which capital city straddles the Vltava River and is overlooked by a vast hilltop castle complex?
questions.explanation: The medieval Charles Bridge, started in 1357, crosses the Vltava here, and Prague Castle is listed by Guinness as the largest ancient castle complex in the world. The city is the capital of Czechia, formerly part of Czechoslovakia.
questions.hook: Charles Bridge crosses the Vltava beneath the castle.

questions.question: Which city is the capital of Jamaica?
questions.explanation: Kingston was founded in 1692 for survivors of the earthquake that sank much of nearby Port Royal, and it sits on one of the largest natural harbours in the Western Hemisphere. It is also the heart of reggae, with Bob Marley's old home turned into a museum.
questions.hook: Reggae's capital began as an earthquake refuge.

questions.question: Which city was declared the capital of Wales in 1955?
questions.explanation: Wales had no official capital before 1955. In December 1955 the government said it would regard Cardiff as the capital, after most local authorities backed it in a poll. Cardiff had grown rich on 19th-century coal exports, and the Senedd, the Welsh parliament, now meets in Cardiff Bay.
questions.hook: Coal built Cardiff, and a 1955 announcement made it the capital.

questions.question: Which capital on the Dâmbovița River holds the Palace of the Parliament, one of the heaviest buildings in the world?
questions.explanation: Dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu had the huge palace built in the 1980s, demolishing a large part of the historic centre to make room. Interwar Bucharest was nicknamed 'Little Paris' for its boulevards and architecture.
questions.hook: Ceaușescu's giant palace crowds the little river.

questions.question: Which city is the capital of Croatia?
questions.explanation: Zagreb lies near the Sava River beneath the wooded Medvednica mountain, far from the sea. Tourists flock to coastal Split and Dubrovnik, but Zagreb has been Croatia's capital since independence in 1991 and is its largest city.
questions.hook: Zagreb keeps its feet dry while the coast gets the fame.

questions.question: Which Bolivian city is the country's constitutional capital and home to its Supreme Court?
questions.explanation: Sucre is named after Antonio José de Sucre, the independence hero and Bolivia's second president. Its whitewashed colonial centre is a UNESCO World Heritage site, though the government works from La Paz.
questions.hook: Sucre keeps the title; La Paz keeps the government.

questions.question: Which Pacific port is Ecuador's largest city, even though Quito is the capital?
questions.explanation: The city lies on the Guayas River estuary, Ecuador's main commercial and shipping hub, and is far hotter than the Andean capital. Quito holds the government, while Guayaquil holds the money and the biggest population.
questions.hook: Quito governs; Guayaquil trades.

questions.question: Which city was the capital of Soviet Ukraine until 1934?
questions.explanation: Soviet Ukraine's government sat in Kharkiv from 1919, and the capital only moved to Kyiv in 1934. Kharkiv's huge Freedom Square is one of the largest city squares in Europe.
questions.hook: Ukraine's capital wandered east to Kharkiv, then back to Kyiv.

questions.question: Which southern city was Poland's royal capital until the court moved to Warsaw around 1596?
questions.explanation: King Sigismund III Vasa shifted the court north to be nearer his other crown in Sweden and Lithuania. Polish monarchs were still crowned at Wawel Castle in Kraków until 1734, and the Old Town was in UNESCO's very first World Heritage list in 1978.
questions.hook: Kings kept their crowns in Kraków long after the court left.

questions.question: Which Peloponnese port city was the capital of Greece from 1829 until Athens took over in 1834?
questions.explanation: Nafplio is overlooked by the Venetian Palamidi fortress, and the first governor of independent Greece, Ioannis Kapodistrias, was assassinated here in 1831. King Otto arrived in 1833 and soon moved the capital to Athens.
questions.hook: Greece's first capital sat under the Palamidi fortress.

questions.question: Which small river flows beneath central Brussels, largely covered over in the 1860s and 1870s?
questions.explanation: Mayor Jules Anspach had the Senne arched over after polluted water caused cholera outbreaks, and grand boulevards were built on top. The river still runs in a tunnel under the city centre and emerges to the north.
questions.hook: The Senne is the river Brussels buried.

questions.question: Which river was dammed in the thirteenth century to give the Dutch capital its name?
questions.explanation: A settlement on the Amstel is recorded around 1275 as Amstelredamme, 'dam on the Amstel', and received toll privileges at about that time. The river is still the city's main waterway, and the old dam is now the square called Dam.
questions.hook: Amstel plus dam makes Amster-dam.

questions.question: Which Costa Rican city served as the colonial capital until 1823?
questions.explanation: Founded in 1563, Cartago lost the capital to San José after a short civil war in 1823. Severe earthquakes in 1841 and 1910 damaged it repeatedly, and its basilica is now a major pilgrimage site.
questions.hook: Cartago was first; San José came later.

questions.question: Which capital sits on the Cap-Vert peninsula, near the westernmost point of mainland Africa?
questions.explanation: The point, Pointe des Almadies, lies just north-west of the city centre. Dakar gave its name to the famous rally, which began in Paris but ran to Dakar for many years.
questions.hook: Dakar sticks out into the Atlantic like Africa's chin.

questions.question: Which planned city south of Kuala Lumpur has housed Malaysia's federal government offices since the late 1990s?
questions.explanation: It was built from the mid-1990s and named after Tunku Abdul Rahman Putra, the first prime minister. Kuala Lumpur remains the official national capital, while Putrajaya is the administrative centre.
questions.hook: Putra's city: the admin capital built in the palm-oil plantations.

questions.question: Which Australian state is made up of one large island and many smaller ones south of the mainland?
questions.explanation: Tasmania covers about 68,000 square kilometres, making it Australia's smallest state by area, and is separated from Victoria by the roughly 240-kilometre-wide Bass Strait. Its capital is Hobart, and it has the smallest population of the six states.
questions.hook: Tassie is the lone island state, the little one at the bottom of the map.

questions.question: Which Australian state is officially nicknamed the Sunshine State?
questions.explanation: Queensland earned the nickname for its warm climate and strong tourism pitch, and it appears in the state's promotion. Brisbane is its capital, though the Gold Coast and Cairns draw many of the visitors.
questions.hook: Queensland gets the sun, and the slogan to prove it.

questions.question: Which Australian state has the largest population?
questions.explanation: About a third of all Australians live in New South Wales, most of them around Sydney, which is the nation's biggest city. Victoria is second and Queensland third, with Western Australia fourth despite being the largest state by area.
questions.hook: First colony, first on the population ladder.

questions.question: Which Queensland tourist strip is home to Surfers Paradise?
questions.explanation: The Gold Coast stretches south from Brisbane to the New South Wales border at Coolangatta and is Australia's largest non-capital city. It is known for its high-rise beachfront, theme parks and surf breaks like Burleigh Heads.
questions.hook: Surfers Paradise sits in the south, where the towers meet the surf.

questions.question: Which mountain range west of Sydney is famous for the Three Sisters rock formation?
questions.explanation: The Three Sisters overlook the Jamison Valley at Katoomba. The range gets its blue haze from fine oil droplets released by eucalypt forests, and it sits within a World Heritage area.
questions.hook: Eucalyptus oil in the air paints the mountains blue.

questions.question: Which far-north Queensland city is the usual gateway to the Daintree rainforest?
questions.explanation: Cairns has an international airport and sits about 110 kilometres south of the Daintree. Its tourism trade is built on boat trips to the Great Barrier Reef and the Kuranda scenic railway and Skyrail through the hills behind the city.
questions.hook: Cairns is where reef trips and rainforest trips both begin.

questions.question: Which Kimberley town is famous for Cable Beach and camel rides at sunset?
questions.explanation: Broome sits on the Indian Ocean in the north of Western Australia and was once the pearling capital of the world. Its tides are among the largest in Australia, and a natural rock-and-mud illusion called the Staircase to the Moon appears over Roebuck Bay.
questions.hook: Broome is where the camels walk into the sunset.

questions.question: Canberra was chosen as the site of the national capital as a compromise between which two rivals?
questions.explanation: The Constitution required a capital in New South Wales but at least 100 miles from Sydney. Melbourne hosted Parliament until it moved to Canberra in 1927, and the site was picked in 1908 on the Molonglo Plain.
questions.hook: Neither big city won, so a sheep paddock in the middle did.

questions.question: Tennant Creek, between Alice Springs and Darwin, lies on which highway?
questions.explanation: The Stuart Highway runs 2,834 kilometres from Port Augusta in South Australia to Darwin, roughly following John McDouall Stuart's 1862 route. Tennant Creek, about 500 kilometres north of Alice Springs, is a major stop on the highway.
questions.hook: Stuart's 1862 route is now a highway from the bottom to the Top End.

questions.question: The Mornington Peninsula curls between Port Phillip and which other Victorian bay?
questions.explanation: The peninsula lies south-east of Melbourne with the sheltered Port Phillip on one side and Bass Strait's open ocean on the other. Western Port holds French Island, and Phillip Island sits at its mouth.
questions.hook: Peninsula in the middle, Port Phillip one side, Western Port the other.

questions.question: Wilsons Promontory, the southernmost point of the Australian mainland, is in which Victorian region?
questions.explanation: Gippsland is the large eastern and south-eastern region of Victoria, running from the Latrobe Valley's coal country to the East Gippsland coast. Locals call Wilsons Promontory simply the Prom, and it is one of the state's most popular national parks.
questions.hook: The Prom sticks out of Gippsland like the toe of Victoria.

questions.question: Launceston sits where the North Esk and South Esk rivers join to form which river?
questions.explanation: The Tamar flows about 70 kilometres north from Launceston to Bass Strait, in a drowned river valley that is actually an estuary for most of its length. The city is Tasmania's second-largest, after Hobart.
questions.hook: Two Esks meet and the Tamar starts at Launceston.

questions.question: The Super Pit gold mine, one of Australia's largest open-cut mines, sits beside which Western Australian city?
questions.explanation: Kalgoorlie-Boulder is in the Goldfields about 600 kilometres east of Perth, where Paddy Hannan found gold in 1893. The Super Pit joined many smaller mines along the Golden Mile into one giant pit.
questions.hook: Hannan's find grew into a hole big enough to show up in satellite photos.

questions.question: The Port of Newcastle in New South Wales is one of the world's biggest export ports, for which commodity?
questions.explanation: The Hunter Valley's coal travels by rail to Newcastle's terminals, which shipped about 143 million tonnes in 2022. Newcastle was founded as a penal settlement in 1804.
questions.hook: The Hunter's coal rolls by rail to Newcastle's wharves.

questions.question: Ranked by population, which state comes third behind New South Wales and Victoria?
questions.explanation: Queensland has more than 5 million residents, well ahead of fourth-placed Western Australia on roughly 2.9 million. It is also the second-largest state by area, and many of its people live outside Brisbane.
questions.hook: Podium order runs NSW, Victoria, Queensland.

questions.question: HMAS Creswell, the Royal Australian Navy's college, stands on which large inlet on the New South Wales south coast?
questions.explanation: The college sits in the Jervis Bay Territory, a small Commonwealth enclave on the New South Wales coast. Land was set aside in 1915 to give the new national capital its own seaport, though the port was never built.
questions.hook: Canberra's sea-door is Jervis Bay, with a naval college inside.

questions.question: Katherine Gorge in the Northern Territory is known by which Jawoyn name?
questions.explanation: Nitmiluk means 'cicada place' and is Jawoyn land, jointly managed with the Parks and Wildlife service. The Katherine River carves through thirteen sandstone gorges before reaching the town of Katherine, about 320 kilometres by road south of Darwin.
questions.hook: Nitmiluk, the cicada place, is Katherine's gorge.

questions.question: The Margaret River wine region lies on a ridge between which two capes?
distractors: Cape Jervis and Cape Du Couedic
questions.explanation: The strip of land runs about 100 kilometres from Cape Naturaliste in the north to Cape Leeuwin in the south, where the Indian and Southern oceans meet. Cape Leeuwin is the south-western tip of the continent.
questions.hook: Naturaliste up top, Leeuwin at the bottom, wine in the middle.

questions.question: Which Pilbara port, mainly shipping iron ore, was Australia's largest by tonnage in 2024-25?
questions.explanation: Port Hedland handled 577.7 million tonnes in 2024-25, more than any other Australian port, and the Pilbara Ports Authority calls it the world's largest bulk export port. Trains carry ore from inland mines such as Mount Whaleback at Newman, and the town has some of the world's largest tides.
questions.hook: Hedland is the Pilbara's iron ore pipe to the world.

questions.question: Whitehaven Beach, famed for its almost pure silica sand, lies on which island?
questions.explanation: The beach stretches about seven kilometres along the island's eastern side and has sand that is almost 99 per cent silica, so it stays cool underfoot. Whitsunday Island is the largest of the 74 Whitsunday islands and has no resort.
questions.hook: Whitehaven's sand is among the whitest in the world.

questions.question: Off the coast of which state does Kangaroo Island lie?
questions.explanation: It lies south-west of Adelaide across Backstairs Passage and is the third-largest island in Australia, after Tasmania and Melville Island. It is known for sea lions, koalas and Remarkable Rocks.
questions.hook: Kangaroo Island is South Australia's big offshore getaway.

questions.question: The Australian mainland's most easterly point, where the sun rises first, is found on which headland?
questions.explanation: The headland near Byron Bay is topped by a lighthouse that opened in 1901. Cape Howe, on the Victorian border, is a common wrong guess.
questions.hook: Byron Bay is where Australia's mainland sees the sun first.

questions.question: Karijini National Park, known for deep red gorges, lies in which region of Western Australia?
questions.explanation: The gorges cut through the Hamersley Range and show banded iron formations about 2.5 billion years old. The same iron-rich rock is what makes the Pilbara the centre of Australia's iron ore industry.
questions.hook: The Pilbara's red rock is both gorge scenery and iron ore.

questions.question: Old Faithful, a geyser famous for erupting about every 90 minutes, is in which US national park?
questions.explanation: Yellowstone, set up in 1872, is generally regarded as the world's first national park, and it sits above a vast volcanic hotspot that powers more than half of the world's geysers. Old Faithful can throw water about 40 metres into the air.
questions.hook: Old Faithful keeps time in the stone-yellow park of Yellowstone.

questions.question: Which European country's coastline is most famous for its deep, glacier-carved fjords?
questions.explanation: Norway's Sognefjord stretches about 200 kilometres inland and is the longest in the country. Glaciers gouged these steep-sided inlets during the ice ages, and the sea later flooded them as the ice melted; Sweden, Finland and Denmark have none on that scale.
questions.hook: Fjord is a Norwegian word, so look to Norway.

questions.question: Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America, lies in which US state?
questions.explanation: Badwater Basin is about 86 metres below sea level, the lowest point in North America, in Death Valley. The valley is among the hottest places on Earth. Death Valley National Park is mostly in California but also reaches into Nevada, which is why Nevada is the common wrong guess.
questions.hook: Badwater sits in California, but the park it belongs to reaches over into Nevada.

questions.question: Transylvania lies inside the great curve of which country's Carpathian Mountains?
