questions.explanation: The Carpathians arc about 1,500 kilometres through central and eastern Europe, and more of them lie in Romania than in any other country. Bram Stoker set Dracula in this region without ever having visited it.
questions.hook: The Carpathian arc cradles Transylvania, Dracula's homeland.

questions.question: The Appalachian Trail ends at the top of Mount Katahdin in which US state?
questions.explanation: The trail runs about 3,500 kilometres from Springer Mountain in Georgia and crosses 14 states. Katahdin is 1,606 metres high and Maine's tallest peak, standing in Baxter State Park.
questions.hook: Georgia to Katahdin: the 14th and last state is Maine.

questions.question: Which Antarctic volcano, on Ross Island, is the southernmost active volcano on Earth?
questions.explanation: At 3,794 metres, Erebus has had a persistent lava lake for decades and was named in 1841 for a Royal Navy ship that James Clark Ross sailed. Mount Terror, nearby, is the other peak named for his ships.
questions.hook: Erebus, ship of Ross, burns at the bottom of the world.

questions.question: The name Himalaya comes from Sanskrit words meaning abode of what?
questions.explanation: The Sanskrit words are hima, meaning snow, and alaya, meaning dwelling. The range stretches about 2,400 kilometres and holds ten of the world's fourteen peaks above 8,000 metres.
questions.hook: Hima is snow, alaya is home: the home of snow.

questions.question: The Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau tower over which Swiss region of the Alps?
questions.explanation: The Eiger's 1,800 metre north face, first climbed in 1938, is a notorious test for climbers, and a railway tunnels through the Eiger and Mönch to Jungfraujoch at 3,454 metres. The Bernese Oberland includes the resort town of Interlaken.
questions.hook: Ogre, Monk and Maiden: the Oberland trio.

questions.question: Niagara Falls lies on the border between New York State and which Canadian province?
questions.explanation: The Niagara River drains Lake Erie into Lake Ontario, and the falls are the drop along the way, with the cities of Niagara Falls on each side of the border. The Canadian city is in Ontario, which also contains Toronto and Ottawa.
questions.hook: Niagara's Canadian side is Ontario, the same province as Toronto.

questions.question: Which great American river flows past New Orleans into the Gulf of Mexico?
questions.explanation: It rises in northern Minnesota and drains all or part of 31 US states and two Canadian provinces. The Missouri and Ohio are its two biggest tributaries, but the lower Mississippi carries their water on to the sea.
questions.hook: Much of the American heartland drains into the Mississippi on its way to New Orleans.

questions.question: On which river does the German city of Cologne stand?
questions.explanation: Cologne's twin-spired Gothic cathedral stands beside the river, which flows about 1,230 kilometres from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea. The Rhine is Europe's busiest inland waterway and runs through the industrial Ruhr region.
questions.hook: Cologne's cathedral spires look straight down on the Rhine.

questions.question: Which huge reservoir was created by the building of Egypt's Aswan High Dam?
questions.explanation: Completed in 1970, the dam flooded a long stretch of the Nile Valley, including part of Sudan, and forced the moving of temples such as Abu Simbel. It is named after Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser, who championed the project.
questions.hook: Nasser built the dam and the lake took his name.

questions.question: Lake Titicaca straddles the Andes on the border between Peru and which other country?
questions.explanation: At about 3,800 metres above sea level it is often called the highest navigable lake in the world, with floating islands built by the Uru people from reeds. Bolivia's capital La Paz is only a short distance from its southern shore.
questions.hook: Peru and Bolivia share the roof-of-the-world lake.

questions.question: Which two national capitals stand on opposite banks of the Congo River?
questions.explanation: They face each other across a stretch of the river known as Malebo Pool, only a few kilometres apart. Kinshasa is in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Brazzaville in the Republic of the Congo.
questions.hook: Two Congos, two capitals, one stretch of water.

questions.question: At which city do the Blue Nile and White Nile meet to form the main Nile?
questions.explanation: Khartoum is the capital of Sudan, and the junction lies beside the city, where the Blue Nile arrives from Ethiopia's Lake Tana and the White Nile from the lakes of central Africa. The two are named for their colours: the Blue Nile carries most of the silt.
questions.hook: Khartoum is where the two Niles become one.

questions.question: In 1982 Britain fought a short war with Argentina over which group of South Atlantic islands?
questions.explanation: Argentina invaded on 2 April 1982, and British forces retook the islands by mid-June, in about ten weeks. Argentina calls them Las Malvinas, while the capital, Stanley, sits on East Falkland, and sheep farming and fishing drive the local economy.
questions.hook: Falklands to Britain, Malvinas to Argentina, one 1982 war.

questions.question: Which tropical island, shared between Indonesia and an independent nation to its east, is the largest in the tropics?
questions.explanation: At about 785,000 square kilometres it is the world's second-largest island, after Greenland, and holds some of the planet's richest rainforest and highest linguistic diversity, with more than 800 languages spoken in Papua New Guinea alone.
questions.hook: Second on the world list, first among tropical islands.

questions.question: Which country governs Easter Island, famous for its giant stone moai statues?
questions.explanation: Chile annexed the island in 1888, and it lies about 3,500 kilometres off the Chilean coast, among the most isolated inhabited places on Earth. Its Polynesian name is Rapa Nui, and the nearly 900 moai were carved from volcanic tuff.
questions.hook: Polynesian carvers, a Chilean island since 1888.

questions.question: The flightless dodo, extinct by the late 1600s, was native to which Indian Ocean island?
questions.explanation: Dutch sailors arrived in 1598, and within about 80 years the bird was gone, hunted and displaced by introduced pigs, rats and monkeys. The dodo now appears on Mauritius's coat of arms, and the island, once French and British, became independent in 1968.
questions.hook: Dodo today, Mauritius coat of arms forever.

questions.question: The Canary Islands, off the north-west coast of Africa, belong to which country?
questions.explanation: Though only about 100 kilometres from Morocco, the seven main islands are an autonomous Spanish region. Tenerife's volcano, Teide, at 3,715 metres, is Spain's highest point, and the name comes from the Latin word for dogs, not from birds.
questions.hook: Closer to Morocco, but the passport says Spain.

questions.question: Which sea between China and the Korean Peninsula is named for the silt carried in by the Huang He?
questions.explanation: The river, itself called the Yellow River, carries so much loess sediment that the water turns a muddy colour. The sea is quite shallow, averaging only about 44 metres deep, and its tides are among the largest in the region.
questions.hook: Muddy river in, muddy sea out.

questions.question: The 2004 Boxing Day tsunami was triggered by an earthquake off the coast of which Indonesian island?
questions.explanation: The magnitude 9.1 quake struck on 26 December 2004 and sent waves across the Indian Ocean, killing more than 220,000 people in over a dozen countries. Aceh, at the northern tip of Sumatra, was the worst hit.
questions.hook: Sumatra shook, and the whole Indian Ocean rang.

questions.question: What name did the military government give Burma in 1989?
questions.explanation: The ruling junta also renamed the capital Rangoon as Yangon. Myanmar is in fact the formal Burmese-language name of the country, but opponents of the junta, and for many years governments such as those of the United States and Britain, kept using Burma.
questions.hook: Same country, two names: one for the formal Burmese, one for the everyday.

questions.question: Which African country's territory includes the Sinai Peninsula, which lies in Asia?
questions.explanation: The Suez Canal is conventionally treated as the boundary between Africa and Asia, so the Sinai side lies in Asia and makes Egypt a transcontinental country. Israel held the peninsula from 1967 until it was returned under the 1979 peace treaty, completed in 1982.
questions.hook: Egypt reaches across the canal into Asia.

questions.question: Which South American country's name honours the explorer who reached the Americas in 1492?
questions.explanation: The name was popularised by the revolutionary Francisco de Miranda and used by Simon Bolivar for Gran Colombia, formed in 1819. After that union broke up, the present country later adopted Colombia as its permanent name in 1886.
questions.hook: Spelt with an o, not a u, for the navigator whose name it borrows.

questions.question: Which Spanish town in the Pyrenees is an exclave completely surrounded by French territory?
questions.explanation: Under the 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees Spain ceded 33 villages to France, but Llívia held the status of a town and was kept, which left it cut off from the rest of Spain.
questions.hook: A town kept by a technicality: it counted as a town, not a village.

questions.question: Andorra has two co-princes: the French president and the Catholic bishop of which Catalan diocese?
questions.explanation: The arrangement dates from a 1278 agreement settling a dispute between the bishop and the Count of Foix, whose rights later passed to the French head of state. The bishop lives in La Seu d'Urgell in Spain, so one of Andorra's two heads of state is a priest.
questions.hook: A prince who is also a bishop, on Spain's side of the hills.

questions.question: What was Burkina Faso called before it was renamed in 1984?
questions.explanation: President Thomas Sankara chose the new name, which means 'land of upright people' in two local languages, Mooré and Dyula. Upper Volta had been named after the upper reaches of the Volta River, which rises within its borders.
questions.hook: From a river's upper reaches to the land of the upright.

questions.question: Ceuta and Melilla, two Spanish cities on the north coast of Africa, share a land border with which country?
questions.explanation: They are the European Union's only land borders with Africa, and Spain has held Melilla since 1497 and Ceuta since the 1600s. Morocco claims both, along with a few small islands off its coast, though Spain regards them as integral parts of its territory.
questions.hook: The only places where Europe's land border runs straight into Africa.

questions.question: Which city is the capital of the US state of California?
questions.explanation: It sits where the American and Sacramento rivers meet, and became the capital in 1854 after the Gold Rush brought thousands of settlers inland. Los Angeles and San Francisco are far bigger, which is why they are the usual wrong guesses.
questions.hook: Gold Rush money moved the capital to the river, not the coast.

questions.question: Which city, not New York City, is the capital of New York State?
questions.explanation: Albany on the Hudson River has been the capital since 1797, and it was first settled by the Dutch in the early 1600s, long before New York became an English colony. New York City has more than 8 million people, while Albany has about 100,000.
questions.hook: The biggest city rarely holds the capital: think Albany, not Manhattan.

questions.question: Which city is the capital of the Canadian province of Saskatchewan?
questions.explanation: It was named in honour of Queen Victoria (regina is Latin for queen) in 1882 and sits on flat prairie. Saskatoon is the larger of the two big cities in the province, which makes it the common mistake.
questions.hook: Queen city on the prairie: Regina is Latin for queen.

questions.question: Patagonia, the windswept southern tip of South America, is shared between which two countries?
questions.explanation: The region spans the Andes and the steppe east of them, with the larger share in Argentina. Its famous sights include Torres del Paine in Chile and the Perito Moreno Glacier in Argentina.
questions.hook: The Andes split Patagonia: Chile on the left, Argentina on the right.

questions.question: Which Illinois city, not Chicago, is the state capital?
questions.explanation: It was where Abraham Lincoln practised law and lived for nearly 25 years before becoming president, and he is buried there. The capital moved from Vandalia to Springfield in 1839 partly thanks to his lobbying as a state legislator.
questions.hook: Lincoln's home town is the capital, not the Windy City.

questions.question: In which Indian city does the white marble Taj Mahal stand beside the Yamuna River?
questions.explanation: Emperor Shah Jahan built the mausoleum in the 1630s and 1640s for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Agra was then the Mughal capital, and the monument sits on the river's southern bank.
questions.hook: Agra: the Taj is the city's grand marble love letter.

questions.question: Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world, is found in which country?
questions.explanation: The Khmer king Suryavarman II built it in the early 12th century, first as a Hindu temple to Vishnu and later a Buddhist site. It is so central to national identity that it appears on Cambodia's flag.
questions.hook: Angkor Wat sits on Cambodia's national flag.

questions.question: The Alhambra, a hilltop palace and fortress of the Moorish rulers, overlooks which Spanish city?
questions.explanation: The Nasrid dynasty built most of the complex in the 13th and 14th centuries. Granada fell to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492, ending Muslim rule in Spain, and the snowy Sierra Nevada rises behind it.
questions.hook: Granada: the last Moorish stronghold keeps its red fortress.

questions.question: Which city is nicknamed the Big Apple?
questions.explanation: The name was popularised in the 1920s by New York racing writer John J. Fitz Gerald, who borrowed it from horse-racing slang. A 1970s tourism campaign revived it.
questions.hook: The Big Apple began as horse-racing slang.

questions.question: Which American city on Lake Michigan is nicknamed the Windy City?
questions.explanation: The nickname probably refers more to the city's boastful politicians than its weather, although the breeze off the lake is real. Chicago was rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1871 and gave the world the skyscraper.
questions.hook: Chicago: windy from the lake and from the loud politicians.

questions.question: Which is the most populous city in South America?
questions.explanation: The city proper had more than 11 million people at the 2022 census, and the wider metropolitan area has over 20 million, making it among the largest in the Southern Hemisphere. Rio is better known abroad, but Brazil's economic heart is São Paulo.
questions.hook: São Paulo is Brazil's business engine; Rio is its party.

questions.question: Which city on the Huangpu River is the largest city proper in China and home to the Bund waterfront?
questions.explanation: The city proper had more than 24 million people at the 2020 census, and its port has been the world's busiest container port for well over a decade. Beijing is the capital, but Shanghai has more people in its city proper.
questions.hook: Shanghai is the biggest city proper; Beijing only has the government.

questions.question: Which island is the largest of the Inner Hebrides, reached by road bridge from the Scottish mainland?
questions.explanation: The Skye Bridge opened in 1995 and links the island to Kyle of Lochalsh. It is famous for the jagged Cuillin mountains and the Old Man of Storr rock pinnacle.
questions.hook: Skye: the Cuillin ridge you cross a bridge to climb.

questions.question: Which is the largest and southernmost of the three Baltic states, with Vilnius as its capital?
questions.explanation: In 1990 it became the first Soviet republic to declare independence. In the late Middle Ages the Grand Duchy of Lithuania was one of the largest states in Europe, reaching the Black Sea.
questions.hook: Lithuania: biggest Baltic, first to leave the USSR.

questions.question: Which treeless biome, with permanently frozen ground beneath the soil, rings the top of the world?
questions.explanation: The frozen layer is called permafrost, and it stops tree roots from growing deep, so only mosses, lichens and low shrubs survive. The word comes from a Sami term for a treeless hill, and the tundra stretches across northern Canada, Alaska and Siberia.
questions.hook: Tundra: too cold for trees, so only lichens and mosses.

questions.question: Which type of tropical grassland, dotted with scattered acacia trees and home to lions, zebras and elephants, covers much of East Africa?
questions.explanation: It has a warm climate with a long dry season and a wet season, which drives the great animal migrations. Fires and grazing animals stop forest from taking over, and Africa holds the largest savannas, though others lie in Australia and South America.
questions.hook: Savanna: grass, a few trees, and a big cat watching.

questions.question: Which floating sheet of frozen fresh water, the biggest in the Antarctic, honours the British naval officer who found it in 1841?
questions.explanation: James Clark Ross, a Royal Navy officer, sighted this vast ice barrier from the sea in 1841, and its seaward face is a cliff tens of metres high. In 1911 Amundsen's base was on the shelf itself at the Bay of Whales, while Scott's was on nearby Ross Island, both starting their South Pole attempts from this area.
questions.hook: Ross found a wall of ice the size of a country.

questions.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Mercury is closest but not hottest: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat and makes it the hottest planet at about 465 degrees. Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its night side drops below minus 170.
questions.hook: Mercury, the winged messenger, runs the shortest lap round the Sun: a year of just 88 days.

questions.question: What gas do plants absorb from the atmosphere during photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Using light, plants turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and give off oxygen. They also respire around the clock like animals, using some oxygen, but by day photosynthesis far outpaces it.
questions.hook: Plants breathe in what we breathe out, and hand back the oxygen.

questions.question: What is the largest organ of the human body?
questions.explanation: An adult's skin covers about two square metres and weighs roughly four kilograms. The liver is the largest internal organ and also the heaviest solid one, at around 1.5 kilograms.
questions.hook: Outside champion: skin. Inside champion: liver.

questions.question: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
questions.explanation: Iron oxide dust gives Mars its colour. It also has Olympus Mons, the solar system's tallest volcano at about 22 kilometres, roughly two and a half Everests, and two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos.
questions.hook: Mars is rusty: the whole planet is coated in iron oxide.

questions.question: What is the hardest naturally occurring substance?
questions.explanation: Diamond tops the Mohs scale at 10 because every carbon atom is locked to four others. Graphite, the same element in flat sheets, is soft enough to write with; corundum (ruby and sapphire) is 9.
questions.hook: Diamond and pencil lead are both pure carbon: only the arrangement differs.

questions.question: Which is the largest planet in the solar system?
questions.explanation: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been watched continuously since at least 1830.
questions.hook: Jupiter, king of the gods, is king of the planets: bigger than all the rest put together.

questions.question: What force keeps planets in orbit around the Sun?
questions.explanation: Newton described gravity as a pull between masses in 1687. Einstein's general relativity (1915) recast it as curved spacetime, which explained the slow shift in Mercury's orbit that Newton's maths could not.
questions.hook: Newton called it a force; Einstein called it a dent in spacetime.

questions.question: What is the fastest land animal over a short distance?
questions.explanation: Cheetahs reach roughly 100 to 110 kilometres per hour but only for about 20 to 30 seconds before overheating. The North American pronghorn is the endurance champion, holding high speed for kilometres.
questions.hook: Cheetah for the sprint, pronghorn for the marathon.

questions.question: What is the centre of an atom called?
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons and nearly all the atom's mass in about a hundred-thousandth of its width. Ernest Rutherford, the New Zealander, discovered it in 1911 by firing alpha particles at gold foil.
questions.hook: If an atom were a stadium, the nucleus would be a pea on the centre spot.

questions.question: Which animal is the largest ever known to have lived?
questions.explanation: Blue whales reach about 30 metres and up to around 190 tonnes, heavier than any known dinosaur. Its heart weighs roughly 180 kilograms, and a 2023 claim that the fossil whale Perucetus was heavier was later revised down.
questions.hook: The biggest animal ever is alive now and eats tiny krill.

questions.question: What is the study of fossils called?
questions.explanation: Palaeontology studies ancient life through fossils, while archaeology studies human remains and artefacts. The classic trap is dinosaurs: they are palaeontology, never archaeology.
questions.hook: Dinosaurs go to palaeontologists; pottery goes to archaeologists.

questions.question: Which organ of the human body produces insulin?
questions.explanation: Beta cells in the pancreas's islets of Langerhans make insulin, which lowers blood sugar. Insulin was first used to treat a diabetic patient in Toronto in 1922, earning Banting and Macleod the 1923 Nobel.
questions.hook: Islets of Langerhans: little islands of insulin factories in the pancreas.

questions.question: What is the collective noun for a group of lions?
questions.explanation: A pride is built round related females, who do most of the hunting, with a few males who hold it for a few years. Lions are the only truly social big cat.
questions.hook: Pride of lions, pack of wolves, troop of baboons.

questions.question: Which planet has the most prominent ring system?
questions.explanation: Saturn's main rings are mostly water ice, span about 280,000 kilometres, and are often only tens of metres thick. All four giant planets have rings, but the others are faint and dark.
questions.hook: Rings as wide as most of the Earth-Moon gap, yet thinner than a city block.

questions.question: Which Australian animal lays eggs but feeds its young milk?
questions.explanation: The echidna and platypus are the only living monotremes, egg-laying mammals. They have no nipples: milk seeps from skin patches and the young lap it up, and a baby echidna is called a puggle.
questions.hook: A baby echidna is a puggle: hatched from an egg, raised on milk.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
questions.explanation: Na comes from the Latin natrium, from the mineral natron used in Egyptian mummification. S is sulfur, and potassium's K comes from kalium the same way.
questions.hook: Na from natrium, K from kalium: the pair that trip everyone up.

questions.question: Which sense is most closely linked to memory and emotion in the brain?
questions.explanation: Smell signals run straight to the olfactory bulb, which connects directly to the amygdala and hippocampus, the brain's emotion and memory centres. The other senses route through the thalamus first.
questions.hook: Proust's madeleine: one whiff and a whole childhood comes back.

questions.question: What is the process by which liquid becomes gas at its surface below boiling point?
questions.explanation: Evaporation happens at any temperature because the fastest molecules escape from the surface, taking heat with them. That is why sweat cools you and why a wet towel dries on a mild day.
questions.hook: Sweat works because evaporation steals heat as it goes.

questions.question: Which protein gives skin and connective tissue its structural strength?
questions.explanation: Collagen is the most abundant protein in mammals, about a quarter to a third of all protein. Keratin makes hair and nails, elastin lets tissue spring back, and myosin powers muscle contraction.
questions.hook: Collagen for strength, elastin for stretch, keratin for hair and nails.

questions.question: Which moon of Saturn has a dense atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane?
questions.explanation: Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere and the only body besides Earth known to have stable surface liquids. The Huygens probe landed there in 2005, and NASA's Dragonfly drone is due to launch for it in 2028.
questions.hook: Titan has rain, rivers and lakes, but of methane rather than water.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
questions.explanation: Ohm's law states voltage equals current times resistance. The volt measures potential difference, the ampere current and the watt power, and the ohm's symbol is the Greek capital omega.
questions.hook: V = IR: volts equal amps times ohms.

questions.question: Which element has the atomic number 1?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element, about three quarters of ordinary matter by mass. Helium, atomic number 2, is second, and together they make up about 98 per cent.
questions.hook: Hydrogen is number one on the table and number one in the universe.

questions.question: What is the term for animals that are active at dusk and dawn?
questions.explanation: Crepuscular comes from the Latin crepusculum, twilight. Kangaroos and wombats are crepuscular, which is why dawn and dusk are the riskiest times to drive in the bush.
questions.hook: Kangaroos on the road at dusk: that is crepuscular behaviour.

questions.question: Which particle carries a negative electric charge?
questions.explanation: J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897, the first subatomic particle found. The positron is its antimatter twin with positive charge, predicted by Dirac and found by Carl Anderson in 1932.
questions.hook: The positron is the electron's evil twin: same mass, opposite charge.

questions.question: What is the name of the galaxy containing our solar system?
questions.explanation: The Milky Way is a barred spiral about 100,000 light years across with 100 to 400 billion stars. The Magellanic Clouds are satellite galaxies visible only from the Southern Hemisphere, easily seen from outback Australia. A 2025 study cut the odds of a collision with Andromeda to about a coin flip within 10 billion years.
questions.hook: Galaxy comes from the Greek galaxias, 'milky': our Milky Way named them all.

questions.question: Which acid is found in the human stomach?
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid keeps the stomach at a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5, killing germs and activating the enzyme pepsin. A mucus lining stops it digesting the stomach itself.
questions.hook: It's the same acid hardware stores sell as 'spirits of salt' for cleaning concrete.

questions.question: What is the collective noun for a group of jellyfish?
questions.explanation: Smack is the traditional term; scientists call a sudden population surge a bloom. A shiver is sharks, a pod is dolphins or whales and a shoal is fish.
questions.hook: A smack of jellyfish, which is what a sting feels like.

questions.question: Which planet rotates on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees?
questions.explanation: An ancient giant collision probably knocked Uranus over, so each pole gets about 42 years of sunlight then 42 of darkness. It was the first planet found by telescope, by William Herschel in 1781.
questions.hook: Uranus rolls round the Sun like a barrel instead of spinning like a top.

questions.question: What is the medical term for the kneecap?
questions.explanation: The patella is a sesamoid bone, one that grows inside a tendon, in this case the quadriceps tendon. The scapula is the shoulder blade, the clavicle the collarbone and the sternum the breastbone.
questions.hook: Patella sounds like 'plate': the little plate over your knee.

questions.question: Which type of rock forms from cooled magma or lava?
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks include granite (cooled slowly underground) and basalt (cooled fast at the surface). Sedimentary rock forms from compressed layers and metamorphic from rock changed by heat and pressure; conglomerate is a type of sedimentary rock.
questions.hook: Igneous from the Latin ignis, fire, as in ignition.

questions.question: Which element is the most abundant in the Earth's crust?
questions.explanation: Oxygen makes up about 46 per cent of the crust by mass, locked into silicate and oxide minerals. Silicon is second at about 28 per cent, while iron dominates the planet as a whole because of the core.
questions.hook: Nearly half of every rock is oxygen, just not the kind you can breathe.

questions.question: What is the name for an animal that eats both plants and meat?
questions.explanation: Bears, pigs, crows and humans are classic omnivores. Detritivores such as earthworms feed on dead and decaying matter, recycling nutrients into soil.
questions.hook: Omni means 'all': an omnivore eats all of it.

questions.question: What is the largest species of shark?
questions.explanation: Whale sharks grow to about 18 metres and filter-feed on plankton. Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia is one of the best places on Earth to swim with them, from about March to July.
questions.hook: The two biggest sharks both eat plankton: size and menace are unrelated.

questions.question: Which gland in the neck produces hormones that regulate metabolism?
questions.explanation: The thyroid makes thyroxine, which needs iodine; deficiency causes goitre. Since 2009 Australian bread has had to be made with iodised salt to prevent it.
questions.hook: Aussie bread is iodised for the sake of this one butterfly-shaped gland.

questions.question: Which planet has a day longer than its year?
questions.explanation: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once but only 225 to orbit the Sun. It also spins backwards, so the Sun rises in the west.
questions.hook: On Venus you'd celebrate a birthday before the day was out.

questions.question: What is the scientific name for the voice box?
questions.explanation: The larynx houses the vocal folds, and its cartilage forms the Adam's apple. The pharynx is the throat above it, the trachea the windpipe below and the oesophagus the food pipe behind.
questions.hook: Laryngitis loses your voice, pharyngitis gives you a sore throat.

questions.question: Which subatomic particle was discovered at CERN in 2012?
questions.explanation: The Higgs boson confirms the field that gives fundamental particles their mass. Peter Higgs and François Englert shared the 2013 Nobel; the top quark was found at Fermilab in 1995.
questions.hook: Predicted 1964, found 2012: a forty-eight-year wait for the 'God particle'.

questions.question: Which Australian marsupial has a backwards-facing pouch?
questions.explanation: A rear-opening pouch stops soil filling it while the mother digs. Koalas, a wombat's closest living relatives, also have one; wombats are also famous for cube-shaped droppings.
questions.hook: Diggers need rear-facing pouches or the joey gets a face full of dirt.

questions.question: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Mercury melts at minus 39 degrees. Gallium melts at about 30 degrees, so it liquefies in your hand, and bromine is the only other element liquid at room temperature, a non-metal.
questions.hook: Gallium melts in your palm, but only mercury is liquid on the shelf.

questions.question: What is the term for a group of organisms interbreeding in a particular area?
questions.explanation: A community is all the populations of different species in an area, an ecosystem adds the physical environment, and a biome is a large climate-and-vegetation zone such as desert or rainforest.
questions.hook: Population, community, ecosystem, biome: each one wider than the last.

questions.question: What is the closest star to Earth after the Sun?
questions.explanation: Proxima is a red dwarf about 4.24 light years away and part of the Alpha Centauri triple system. Too faint to see by eye, it hosts Proxima b, a planet in its habitable zone; Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky.
questions.hook: Proxima means 'nearest' in Latin, the clue is in the name.

questions.question: Which blood vessel carries blood away from the heart?
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away and veins bring it back. The pulmonary artery is the odd one out, carrying oxygen-poor blood to the lungs, so 'arteries carry oxygenated blood' is the classic wrong rule.
questions.hook: A for artery, A for away.

questions.question: What is the study of the weather called?
questions.explanation: The name comes from Aristotle's Meteorologica, from the Greek for 'things high in the air'. Climatology studies long-term averages; Australia's Bureau of Meteorology was founded in 1908.
questions.hook: Nothing to do with meteors: the Greek root just means 'things up high'.

questions.question: Which two elements make up common table salt?
questions.explanation: Sodium is a metal that reacts violently with water and chlorine a toxic gas, yet bonded they form sodium chloride. Potassium chloride, a real distractor, is sold as a salt substitute.
questions.hook: An explosive metal plus a poison gas equals a table condiment.

questions.question: What is the term for the number of protons in an atom?
questions.explanation: The atomic number fixes which element an atom is. The mass number counts protons plus neutrons, and isotopes are versions of one element with different neutron counts, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14.
questions.hook: Protons decide the element; neutrons only decide the isotope.

questions.question: Which Australian bird is the world's second-tallest?
questions.explanation: Emus stand up to about 1.9 metres, behind only the ostrich, and can run at about 50 kilometres per hour. The 1932 'Emu War' saw soldiers with machine guns fail to cull them in WA.
questions.hook: The emu lost only one war: it beat the army in 1932.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: One newton accelerates one kilogram at one metre per second squared, about the weight of a small apple. The joule measures energy, the pascal pressure and the watt power.
questions.hook: A newton is about one apple's weight, fittingly.

questions.question: Which organ filters waste from the blood to produce urine?
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter about 180 litres of blood plasma a day through about a million nephrons each, returning nearly all of it. They also control blood pressure and trigger red cell production.
questions.hook: 180 litres filtered a day, and you only notice about one and a half of them.

questions.question: What is the name for the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing escapes?
questions.explanation: The singularity is the theoretical point of infinite density at the centre. The Event Horizon Telescope's 2019 image of M87's black hole shows a dark shadow ringed by glowing gas, not the horizon itself.
questions.hook: Horizon: like the edge of your view, you can't see past it.

questions.question: Which gas is responsible for the smell of rotten eggs?
questions.explanation: Humans can smell hydrogen sulfide at a few parts per billion, but at high concentrations it paralyses the sense of smell, which makes it deadly in sewers. Natural gas is odourless; the smell is added mercaptan.
questions.hook: You smell it at tiny doses and stop smelling it at lethal ones.

questions.question: What is the term for an animal with a backbone?
questions.explanation: Vertebrates are a subgroup of chordates, which also include backbone-less sea squirts and lancelets. About 95 per cent or more of animal species are invertebrates, most of them insects.
questions.hook: Nearly all animals have no backbone: vertebrates are the rare case.

questions.question: Which planet is the densest in the solar system?
questions.explanation: Earth's average density is about 5.5 grams per cubic centimetre thanks to its big iron core; Mercury is a close second. Saturn is the least dense, less than water.
questions.hook: Earth is the densest planet; Saturn would float in a big enough bath.

questions.question: What is the largest muscle in the human body?
questions.explanation: The gluteus maximus extends the hip and keeps the trunk upright when running. It is unusually large in humans compared with other apes, possibly an adaptation for endurance running.
questions.hook: Maximus by name, maximus by size.

questions.question: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix during replication?
questions.explanation: Helicase separates the two strands, primase lays short RNA primers, DNA polymerase builds the new strands and ligase seals the gaps. PCR tests skip helicase and use heat to separate strands instead.
questions.hook: Helicase unzips the helix, primase starts, polymerase builds, ligase glues.

questions.question: What is the name of the effect where light shifts to longer wavelengths as sources recede?
questions.explanation: Edwin Hubble used redshifts in 1929 to show distant galaxies are receding faster the further away they are, building on Georges Lemaître's 1927 work. It is the light version of the Doppler effect.
questions.hook: It's the Doppler effect for light: a passing siren drops in pitch, a receding galaxy drops into red.

questions.question: What is the invisible substance, detected only by its gravity, that makes up about 85 per cent of all matter in the universe?
questions.explanation: Dark matter is inferred from galaxies spinning too fast and from gravitational lensing, but its particle has never been detected. Dark energy is a separate mystery that drives the accelerating expansion of space.
questions.hook: Dark matter holds galaxies together; dark energy pushes the universe apart.

questions.question: What is the term for the temperature at which a magnet loses its magnetism?
questions.explanation: Above it, heat scrambles the aligned magnetic domains; iron's Curie point is about 770 degrees. Cooling lava locks in Earth's field below it, which is how seafloor stripes recorded magnetic reversals.
questions.hook: Named for Pierre Curie, not Marie: he studied magnetism before radioactivity.

questions.question: Which part of the brain coordinates balance and fine motor control?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum, Latin for 'little brain', holds about 80 per cent of the brain's neurons in about a tenth of its volume. Alcohol impairs it early, which is why roadside sobriety tests check balance.
questions.hook: Little brain, big job: it makes a drunk walk wobble.

questions.question: What is the name for a sudden, often repeated brightening caused when a white dwarf ignites gas pulled from a companion star?
questions.explanation: A nova is a thermonuclear flash on a white dwarf's surface that leaves the star intact, so it can recur. A supernova destroys a star, and a kilonova is the flash from two colliding neutron stars.
questions.hook: Nova means 'new' because it looked like a new star; it's really an old one flaring.

questions.question: Which hormone regulates the sleep-wake cycle?
questions.explanation: The pineal gland releases melatonin as light fades. Blue light from screens suppresses it, and in Australia melatonin tablets for adults aged 55 and over can be bought from pharmacists without a prescription.
questions.hook: Melatonin is the darkness hormone: it rises when the lights go down.

questions.question: What is the name for the boundary between the Earth's crust and mantle?
questions.explanation: Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovičić found it in 1909 when earthquake waves suddenly sped up at depth. The Gutenberg discontinuity separates mantle from outer core, and the Lehmann discontinuity marks the inner core.
questions.hook: The Moho for crust to mantle, Gutenberg for mantle to core.

questions.question: Which element is named after the Greek word for 'lazy'?
questions.explanation: Argon was named for its chemical inertness when Rayleigh and Ramsay found it in 1894. Ramsay and Morris Travers then isolated neon ('new'), krypton ('hidden') and xenon ('stranger') in 1898.
questions.hook: Argon lazy, neon new, krypton hidden, xenon stranger.

questions.question: Which blood cells are responsible for clotting?
questions.explanation: Platelets are fragments broken off giant bone-marrow cells called megakaryocytes and live only about 10 days. Aspirin makes them less sticky, which is why it is used to prevent heart attacks.
questions.hook: Platelets are little plates that stack up to plug a leak.

questions.question: What is the name of the theoretical particle that mediates gravity?
questions.explanation: The graviton remains hypothetical because gravity has never been reconciled with quantum mechanics. Photons carry electromagnetism, gluons the strong force and W and Z bosons the weak force.
questions.hook: Every other force has a confirmed carrier; gravity's is still missing.

questions.question: Which layer of the Earth is liquid?
questions.explanation: The inner core is solid despite being hotter, because the pressure is too great for melting. Swirling molten iron in the outer core generates Earth's magnetic field; the mantle is solid rock that creeps slowly.
questions.hook: The hotter inner core is solid: pressure beats temperature down there.

questions.question: Which scale do seismologists now use to report the size of large earthquakes?
questions.explanation: Charles Richter's 1935 scale saturates for big quakes, so the moment magnitude scale (1979) replaced it. Each whole step releases about 32 times more energy; Mercalli and Rossi-Forel measure shaking felt, not size.
questions.hook: News reports still say Richter; seismologists moved on in the 1970s.

questions.question: Which animal has the most complex eyes known, with up to sixteen photoreceptor types?
questions.explanation: Humans have three colour receptor types; mantis shrimp have about 12 for colour plus others for ultraviolet and polarised light. A 2014 study at the University of Queensland found they are actually poor at telling similar colours apart.
questions.hook: Sixteen receptor types, but it seems to see colour worse than we do, not better.

questions.question: What is the term for a solution that resists changes in pH?
questions.explanation: A buffer pairs a weak acid with its salt to mop up added acid or alkali. Blood is buffered by bicarbonate to stay between pH 7.35 and 7.45; outside that range is acidosis or alkalosis.
questions.hook: A buffer is a shock absorber for pH.

questions.question: What is the name for the pigment that makes plants green?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green. In autumn it breaks down, revealing yellow and orange carotenoids that were there all along; anthocyanins add the reds and purples.
questions.hook: Chloros is Greek for green, phyllon for leaf: 'green leaf'.

questions.question: What is the name of the process by which cells engulf external material?
questions.explanation: White blood cells such as macrophages use phagocytosis to swallow bacteria. Exocytosis is the reverse, pushing material out, and osmosis is water crossing a membrane.
questions.hook: Phago means 'eating' in Greek: the cell literally swallows.

questions.question: Which acid is the main component of vinegar?
questions.explanation: Vinegar is about four to eight per cent acetic acid, from the Latin acetum, vinegar. Formic acid is in ant stings, lactic acid in sour milk and working muscle, and citric acid in lemons.
questions.hook: Formic acid is named for ants: formica is Latin for ant.

questions.question: Which NSW radio telescope, the star of the film The Dish, relayed most of the Apollo 11 moonwalk to world TV?
questions.explanation: Honeysuckle Creek near Canberra sent the first minutes including Armstrong's first step, then Parkes took over for most of the 2.5-hour broadcast to about 600 million viewers. The dish now also carries the Wiradjuri name Murriyang.
questions.hook: Honeysuckle got the first step, Parkes got the rest.

questions.question: Which condition results from a deficiency of thiamine, vitamin B1?
questions.explanation: Beriberi spread when polished white rice replaced brown rice in Asia, as polishing strips out thiamine. Pellagra comes from lack of niacin (B3), rickets from lack of vitamin D and scurvy from lack of vitamin C.
questions.hook: Polishing rice removed the vitamin and caused the disease.

questions.question: What is the name for the point in an orbit closest to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Earth reaches perihelion in early January, during the southern summer, so distance does not cause seasons; axial tilt does. Perigee and apogee are the nearest and farthest points of orbits round Earth, as with the Moon.
questions.hook: Peri means near, ap means far; helion for the Sun, gee for the Earth.

questions.question: What is the term for the smallest possible unit of any physical property?
questions.explanation: Max Planck introduced energy quanta in 1900 to solve the black-body radiation problem, calling it an act of desperation. A photon is the quantum of light, as Einstein showed in 1905.
questions.hook: A 'quantum leap' is actually the smallest possible jump, not a giant one.

questions.question: Which Australian marsupial predator became extinct in the twentieth century?
questions.explanation: The last known thylacine died at Hobart's Beaumaris Zoo in September 1936, two months after the species was protected. Numbats eat termites rather than hunting prey, and devils are threatened by a contagious facial cancer.
questions.hook: Protection arrived two months before the last one died.

questions.question: What do honeybees collect from flowers and turn into honey?
questions.explanation: Bees drink sugary nectar, add enzymes and fan it with their wings until most of the water evaporates. Pollen is collected too, but as protein food for larvae, not for honey.
questions.hook: Pollen feeds the babies; nectar fills the honey pot.

questions.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Fe?
questions.explanation: Fe comes from the Latin ferrum, which also gives 'ferrous' and 'ferric'. Iron is the most common element in Earth by mass because of the core, and Australia is the world's biggest iron ore exporter, mostly from WA's Pilbara.
questions.hook: Ferrum, ferrous, ferry-to-the-Pilbara: Fe is iron.

questions.question: What kind of animal is the Komodo dragon?
questions.explanation: It is the world's largest living lizard, up to about three metres long, found on a few Indonesian islands. It is a monitor, the same family as Australia's goannas, and its bite carries venom.
questions.hook: A Komodo dragon is a giant goanna.

questions.question: Which organ in the human body produces bile?
questions.explanation: The liver makes bile, and the gall bladder only stores and concentrates it. Bile emulsifies fats in the small intestine, and people can live normally after having their gall bladder removed.
questions.hook: The gall bladder is the storage shed; the liver is the factory.

questions.question: As of 2026, which planet has the most confirmed moons?
questions.explanation: Saturn passed Jupiter in 2023 and a batch of 128 new moons in 2025 put it far ahead; by March 2026 the count was 285 against Jupiter's 101. Most are tiny captured rocks only a few kilometres across.
questions.hook: Saturn wins on rings and on moons, by a mile.

questions.question: What is the Latin name of the constellation known as the Southern Cross?
questions.explanation: Crux is the smallest of the 88 constellations and appears on the Australian and New Zealand flags. The two Pointers beside it, Alpha and Beta Centauri, belong to Centaurus.
questions.hook: Crux means cross; the Pointers belong to the Centaur.

questions.question: Which dwarf planet, discovered in 2005 and more massive than Pluto, prompted the 2006 redefinition of a planet?
questions.explanation: Eris is about 27 per cent more massive than Pluto, though New Horizons showed Pluto is slightly wider. Named after the Greek goddess of strife, it forced the vote that demoted Pluto.
questions.hook: Eris, goddess of discord, started the fight that cost Pluto its title.

questions.question: Which element, officially named in 2016, has the highest atomic number on the periodic table?
questions.explanation: Oganesson is element 118, named after Russian nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian, only the second living person to have an element named after him. It completes row seven; no element 119 or 120 has yet been made.
questions.hook: The last element, 118, ends in -on like the other noble gases.

questions.question: Which unit of astronomical distance equals about 3.26 light years?
questions.explanation: A parsec is the distance at which a star would shift by one arcsecond of parallax as Earth orbits the Sun. The astronomical unit is the Earth-Sun distance, about 150 million kilometres.
questions.hook: Han Solo bragged of doing the Kessel Run in 12 parsecs: a distance, not a time.

questions.question: Which element is the most electronegative, pulling electrons harder than any other?
questions.explanation: Fluorine tops the Pauling scale at about 4.0, so it reacts with almost everything. It is added to Australian tap water as fluoride, and bonded to carbon it forms the non-stick coating Teflon.
questions.hook: Fluorine is the most grabby element on the table: top right, minus the noble gases.

questions.question: Which microbes built the living stromatolites of Shark Bay in Western Australia?
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria trap sediment in layered mats, and their ancient relatives pumped the oxygen into Earth's early atmosphere. Hamelin Pool at Shark Bay has the world's most diverse living stromatolites.
questions.hook: Cyano means blue-green: the blue-green algae that made our oxygen.

questions.question: Which mineral, from the Jack Hills in Western Australia, holds the oldest dated fragments of Earth's crust?
questions.explanation: Zircon crystals about 4.4 billion years old show that crust and probably water existed soon after Earth formed. Zircon survives erosion and traps uranium, which makes it ideal for dating.
questions.hook: Zircon is a time capsule: tough, and a built-in uranium clock.

questions.question: Which planet has the fastest winds measured in the solar system?
questions.explanation: Neptune's winds reach about 2,000 kilometres per hour, faster than the speed of sound on Earth. Voyager 2 flew past in 1989, and it remains the only spacecraft to visit.
questions.hook: The coldest, furthest planet is also the windiest.

questions.question: Which is the tallest living land animal?
questions.explanation: A giraffe can stand about five metres tall, yet its neck has the same seven vertebrae as ours, each one enormously stretched. Its tongue is dark purple and around 45 centimetres long.
questions.hook: Seven neck bones, same as you, just much longer.

questions.question: Which greenhouse gas is released in large amounts by cattle and sheep belching?
questions.explanation: Methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide per tonne, though it breaks down in the air within about a dozen years. Australian researchers have shown a red seaweed, Asparagopsis, can sharply cut it from cattle.
questions.hook: Cow burps are a climate issue, and seaweed is the proposed fix.

questions.question: Which part of the eye gives it its colour?
questions.explanation: The iris is a ring of muscle that widens or narrows the pupil to control light. Its colour depends on the amount of melanin, and blue eyes contain no blue pigment at all, just scattered light.
questions.hook: Iris was the Greek goddess of the rainbow: the coloured part.

questions.question: Which type of electromagnetic radiation has the shortest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Gamma rays come from radioactive decay and cosmic explosions, and carry the most energy of any light. At the other end, radio waves can be longer than a football field.
questions.hook: Shortest wave, biggest punch; longest wave, gentlest touch.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux density?
questions.explanation: A fridge magnet is about five thousandths of a tesla, and an MRI scanner uses one of a few tesla. The weber measures total magnetic flux and the gauss is an older unit, one ten-thousandth of a tesla.
questions.hook: MRI machines are rated in tesla, and a 3-tesla scanner has twice the field of a 1.5-tesla one.

questions.question: Which radioactive element, number 95, is the active ingredient in most household ionisation smoke alarms?
questions.explanation: Americium-241 gives off alpha particles that let a tiny current flow through the air, and smoke interrupts that current and triggers the alarm. It was first made in 1944 by Glenn Seaborg's team.
questions.hook: Named for the Americas, just as europium is named for Europe.

questions.question: Which coloured ring of muscle in the eye adjusts the size of the pupil?
questions.explanation: The iris widens the pupil in dim light and narrows it in bright light. The amount of pigment in it decides whether eyes look brown, green or blue.
questions.hook: The iris is the eye's camera aperture.

questions.question: What is the hardest substance in the human body, covering the crown of each tooth?
questions.explanation: Enamel is about 96 per cent mineral, harder than bone, but it contains no living cells and cannot regrow once worn or eaten away by acid. Fluoride helps strengthen it.
questions.hook: Enamel is armour you can never regrow.

questions.question: Which muscle at the back of the upper arm straightens the elbow, opposing the biceps?
questions.explanation: Muscles can only pull, so they work in opposing pairs. As the triceps contracts the biceps relaxes, and the triceps has three heads, as its name says.
questions.hook: Tri means three heads; it pushes while the biceps pulls.

questions.question: Which protein makes up hair and fingernails?
questions.explanation: Hair and nails are made of dead, hardened cells packed with keratin, which is why cutting them does not hurt. The same protein forms the outer layer of skin, as well as horns and claws in other animals.
questions.hook: Keratin: the hard stuff in your hair and nails.

questions.question: Which organ is covered in tiny bumps called papillae, many of which hold taste buds?
questions.explanation: An adult tongue carries thousands of taste buds, each holding dozens of receptor cells that are replaced roughly every one to two weeks. Different regions do not specialise in single tastes, despite the old tongue map.
questions.hook: Bumps on the tongue are the taste welcome mat.

questions.question: Which light-sensitive cells in the retina work best in dim light but cannot detect colour?
questions.explanation: Each eye has about 120 million rods but only around 6 million cones. This is why colours fade to greys at night, and why dark-adapting takes about half an hour.
questions.hook: Rods for the night shift, in black and white.

questions.question: Which clear front window of the eye provides roughly two-thirds of its focusing power?
questions.explanation: The cornea has no blood vessels and gets oxygen directly from the air and tears. The lens does the remaining fine-tuning, and corneal transplants were among the first successful organ grafts.
questions.hook: Cornea: the eye's built-in front lens.

questions.question: Which fist-sized organ under the left ribs removes worn-out red blood cells and can be lost without being fatal?
questions.explanation: The spleen also stores white blood cells and platelets and helps fight infection. People without one are more prone to certain serious infections, so doctors recommend extra vaccinations.
questions.hook: The spleen: a blood recycler you can live without.

questions.question: To which part of the large intestine is the appendix attached?
questions.explanation: The caecum is the pouch where the small intestine meets the large. Appendicitis is a common emergency, and the appendix may serve as a store of helpful gut bacteria.
questions.hook: The appendix dangles off the caecum.

questions.question: Which pair of tubes carries urine from the kidneys down to the bladder?
questions.explanation: Each ureter is about 25 centimetres long and pushes urine along with muscle waves. The urethra is the single tube that carries urine out of the bladder.
questions.hook: Ureters travel up top; urethra exits.

questions.question: Roughly how long does a red blood cell live before it is removed?
questions.explanation: With no nucleus, red cells cannot repair themselves and wear out after roughly 120 days, with the bone marrow making about two million new ones every second.
questions.hook: Four months of delivery runs, then retirement.

questions.question: Edward Jenner's 1796 experiments with cowpox led to the first vaccine against which disease?
questions.explanation: Jenner inoculated a boy with cowpox material from a dairymaid and later showed he resisted smallpox. The word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow. Smallpox is the only human disease that has been wiped out worldwide.
questions.hook: A cow gave us the word vaccine.

questions.question: Which vitamin, made in the body from the orange pigment beta-carotene in carrots, supports night vision?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A is needed to make rhodopsin, the light-sensitive pigment in the retina's rod cells. Too little causes night blindness, and a lack remains a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness in poorer countries.
questions.hook: Carrots help you see in the dark.

questions.question: Which mineral, plentiful in milk and cheese, forms most of the hard structure of bones and teeth?
questions.explanation: About 99 per cent of the body's calcium is stored in the skeleton, bound with phosphate. The remainder helps muscles contract and nerves fire, so the body will draw on bone if blood levels drop.
questions.hook: Bones are built from the dairy aisle.

questions.question: Which Sydney heart surgeon, born in Shanghai, helped develop an artificial heart valve and was murdered in 1991?
questions.explanation: Chang worked at St Vincent's Hospital and helped develop the St Vincent's heart valve prosthesis. He also pushed heart transplants forward in Australia. The Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute in Sydney carries on his work.
questions.hook: A valve designer with an institute named for him.

questions.question: Which hormone, released during childbirth and breastfeeding, triggers labour contractions and milk let-down?
questions.explanation: It is made in the hypothalamus and released by the pituitary gland. Oxytocin is also linked to social bonding and trust, though its effects on human behaviour are more modest than the popular cuddle-hormone label suggests.
questions.hook: The hormone that gets things moving and bonded.

questions.question: SSRI antidepressants work by raising levels of which neurotransmitter, made mostly in the gut?
questions.explanation: About 90 per cent of the body's serotonin sits in the digestive tract, where it helps regulate gut movement. The brain makes only a small share. SSRIs block its reabsorption by neurons so more stays available between them.
questions.hook: Most of the mood chemical is in your gut.

questions.question: An iron rod blasted through the head of railway foreman Phineas Gage in 1848, damaging which part of his brain?
questions.explanation: Gage survived, but friends said his personality changed. His case offered early evidence that the frontal lobes help control planning, judgement and social behaviour. Exactly how much his character changed is still debated.
questions.hook: The rod hit the planning department.

questions.question: Caffeine keeps people alert by blocking receptors for which sleep-promoting chemical that builds up during the day?
questions.explanation: Adenosine accumulates as brain cells burn energy and gradually makes us drowsy. Caffeine has a similar shape and sits in its receptors without activating them. It does not remove the sleep pressure, which returns when the caffeine wears off.
questions.hook: Caffeine plugs the tired-signal sockets.

questions.question: Iron rusts when it is exposed to water and which gas in the air?
questions.explanation: Rust is hydrated iron oxide, formed when iron, water and oxygen react together. Salt speeds the process up, which is why cars near the sea corrode faster than those inland.
questions.hook: No oxygen, no rust: iron rots by breathing.

questions.question: The 'lead' in a pencil is actually made of which crystalline form of carbon?
questions.explanation: Graphite is arranged in flat layers that slide off onto paper as you write. The name comes from the Greek 'graphein', to write, and clay is mixed in to control how hard the pencil is.
questions.hook: Graphite: the layers that write.

questions.question: The Statue of Liberty is green because of a weathered coating on which metal?
questions.explanation: The statue is made of thin copper sheets, and over the following decades air and moisture turned the surface into a green patina. That layer protects the metal beneath from further corrosion.
questions.hook: Lady Liberty went green like an old penny.

questions.question: Which substance gives lemons and limes their sharp, sour taste?
questions.explanation: Citrus juice is about five to six per cent citric acid, which is why it works as a natural cleaner for kettles and limescale. It is also added to soft drinks and lollies as a preservative and sour flavour.
questions.hook: Citrus has citric: the name gives it away.

questions.question: Which state of matter has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container?
questions.explanation: Liquid particles stay close together but can slide past one another, so liquids pour yet resist being squashed. A gas, by contrast, spreads out to fill any space it is given.
questions.hook: Liquids pour but will not squash.

questions.question: Mixing baking soda with vinegar fizzes because it releases which gas?
questions.explanation: The acid in the vinegar reacts with the sodium bicarbonate to make carbon dioxide, water and a salt. The same gas makes cakes rise when baking soda meets an acidic ingredient such as buttermilk.
questions.hook: The science-fair volcano runs on carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Ordinary steel is made by adding small amounts of which non-metal to iron?
questions.explanation: Less than two per cent carbon makes iron far stronger and less brittle, and more carbon makes it harder but more fragile. Cast iron has a higher carbon content than steel, which is why it cracks rather than bends.
questions.hook: A pinch of carbon turns iron into steel.

questions.question: Galvanised steel, used for Australian corrugated roofing and fences, is coated with which metal?
questions.explanation: Zinc protects steel in two ways: it forms a barrier, and it corrodes in preference to the iron beneath even where the coating is scratched. This sacrificial protection is why galvanised iron lasts decades.
questions.hook: Zinc takes the rust so the steel doesn't have to.

questions.question: What name is given to the hydrogen isotope whose nucleus holds one proton and one neutron?
questions.explanation: Deuterium is sometimes called heavy hydrogen, and water made with it is called heavy water. Ordinary hydrogen, protium, has no neutron, while tritium has two and is radioactive.
questions.hook: Deuterium: hydrogen with a neutron buddy.

questions.question: Which radioactive noble gas can seep from uranium-bearing rocks into buildings?
questions.explanation: Radon forms as radium decays in rock and soil, and it can collect in poorly ventilated basements. It is the heaviest of the noble gases that occur naturally and has no stable isotope.
questions.hook: Radon rises from the radium below.

questions.question: Charles Goodyear's vulcanisation toughened natural rubber by heating it with which element?
questions.explanation: The sulfur forms cross-links between the long rubber molecules, making the material stronger and stopping it going sticky in heat or brittle in cold. Goodyear patented the process in 1844.
questions.hook: Sulfur links the rubber chains tight.

questions.question: Which metal's salts give fireworks and road flares their deep red colour?
questions.explanation: Burning strontium compounds give off a vivid crimson light. Barium makes green, copper makes blue and sodium makes yellow, and pyrotechnicians mix these to get other shades.
questions.hook: Strontium: the red in the sky.

questions.question: The symbol Cu for copper comes from the Latin name for which Mediterranean island, once a major source of the metal?
questions.explanation: The Romans called the metal aes Cyprium, 'metal of Cyprus', which was shortened to cuprum. Cyprus was mined for copper from the Bronze Age, and the island's name may in turn come from the metal.
questions.hook: Cu is for Cyprus.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek thinker is said to have leapt from his bath shouting 'Eureka!' after spotting how water was displaced?
questions.explanation: Archimedes realised that an object dunked in water pushes aside its own volume of liquid, which let him test whether a crown was pure gold. His buoyancy rule explains why heavy steel ships still float.
questions.hook: Archimedes: the bath that launched a thousand floating ships.

questions.question: Which colour of visible light has the shortest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Violet light has a wavelength of roughly 400 nanometres, while red is near 700 nanometres, so violet is a little over half the length of red. Shorter wavelengths scatter more strongly, which is also why the daytime sky looks blue rather than red.
questions.hook: Violet is the short end of the rainbow stick.

questions.question: What is the name for a sound that bounces off a distant cliff and returns to your ears?
questions.explanation: Sound travels at about 343 metres per second in air, so an echo needs a surface roughly 17 metres away or more for your ear to hear it as a separate sound. Bats and dolphins use echoes to find their way.
questions.hook: Shout at a cliff and your own voice answers back.

questions.question: Which unit is printed on a light globe to show how much electrical power it uses?
questions.explanation: One watt is one joule of energy used each second. The unit honours James Watt, the Scottish engineer whose steam engine improvements helped power the Industrial Revolution.
questions.hook: A 60 watt globe uses 60 joules every second.

questions.question: In which unit is the frequency of a sound wave measured?
questions.explanation: One hertz is one wave cycle per second. Humans hear roughly 20 to 20,000 hertz, and the unit honours Heinrich Hertz, who first demonstrated the radio waves that James Clerk Maxwell had predicted.
questions.hook: Hertz counts the wiggles, decibels count the loudness.

questions.question: In a primary rainbow, which colour appears on the outer edge of the arc?
questions.explanation: Raindrops bend red light slightly less than violet, so red emerges at a higher angle of about 42 degrees. A fainter secondary rainbow sometimes appears outside, with its colours in reverse order.
questions.hook: Red on the roof, violet on the inside track.

questions.question: Which form of heat transfer warms your face when you stand a few metres from a campfire?
questions.explanation: Infrared radiation travels as electromagnetic waves and needs no material in between, which is how the Sun warms Earth across empty space. Conduction needs contact, and convection needs a moving fluid such as air or water.
questions.hook: Radiation reaches you with nothing in the middle.

questions.question: In the word laser, which word does the letter S stand for?
questions.explanation: Laser stands for light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Excited atoms are triggered to release identical light particles, producing a narrow beam of nearly one colour that stays tightly focused.
questions.hook: Lasers: light amplified by stimulated emission.

questions.question: What is the brightest star in Earth's night sky?
questions.explanation: Sirius, the Dog Star, shines so brightly because it is both luminous and close, only about 8.6 light years away. Polaris, the North Star, is often assumed to be the brightest but is only moderately bright.
questions.hook: Sirius, the Dog Star, outshines every other star.

questions.question: Which constellation, named after a hunter of Greek myth, is marked by a distinctive belt of three bright stars?
questions.explanation: The belt of Orion points toward Sirius in one direction and the red star Aldebaran in the other. From Australia, Orion appears upside down compared with the view from Europe, so the hunter looks like he is standing on his head.
questions.hook: Three in a row: follow Orion's belt to find Sirius.

questions.question: What is the name for the event when the Moon passes directly between Earth and the Sun and blocks its light?
questions.explanation: A total solar eclipse is possible because the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so the two look almost the same size in our sky. Totality is seen only along a narrow path.
questions.hook: Sun hidden by Moon: solar eclipse.

questions.question: Which planet is the hottest in the solar system, thanks to a runaway greenhouse effect?
questions.explanation: Venus has a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere with surface pressure about 90 times that of Earth. It traps heat, holding the surface near 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
questions.hook: Venus wears a blanket of CO2 and bakes under it.

questions.question: In many Aboriginal sky stories, which bird is outlined by the dark dust lanes stretching across the night sky?
questions.explanation: The Emu in the Sky is made of dark clouds rather than bright stars, with the head near the Southern Cross. Its changing position through the year signals when emus lay eggs, a calendar used by some Aboriginal groups.
questions.hook: Look for the dark shapes, not the bright dots: the sky emu.

questions.question: What is the name for a piece of space rock that survives its fiery fall and lands on the ground?
questions.explanation: In space the rock is a meteoroid, and the streak of light it makes while burning up in the atmosphere is a meteor. Only a fragment that actually reaches the ground is called a meteorite, such as those found on the Nullarbor Plain.
questions.hook: Meteoroid in space, meteor in the sky, meteorite on the ground.

questions.question: Spring tides, the biggest of each month, occur around which two lunar phases?
questions.explanation: At new and full moon the Sun, Moon and Earth line up, so the Sun's pull adds to the Moon's. At the quarter phases the two pulls partly cancel, producing the weaker neap tides. The name has nothing to do with the season.
questions.hook: Lined up means bigger: spring tides at new and full.

questions.question: What is the glowing outer atmosphere of the Sun, visible as a pearly halo during a total solar eclipse, called?
questions.explanation: The corona is millions of degrees hotter than the surface below it, a puzzle astronomers are still working on. It is normally drowned out by the Sun's glare, so totality is one of the few chances to see it with the naked eye.
questions.hook: Corona is Latin for crown, and it crowns the eclipsed Sun.

questions.question: Which gas, at heights of about 100 kilometres, produces the most common green glow of an aurora?
questions.explanation: Charged particles excite oxygen atoms, which release green light at lower altitudes. Rarer red glows come from oxygen much higher up, while nitrogen produces blue and purple fringes at the bottom edge of the display.
questions.hook: Green curtains are oxygen, blue fringes are nitrogen.

questions.question: Which dog became the first animal to orbit the Earth, aboard a Soviet spacecraft in November 1957?
questions.explanation: Laika was a stray found on the streets of Moscow and flew on Sputnik 2, which had no way of returning to Earth. Belka and Strelka became the first animals to orbit and come home alive, in 1960.
questions.hook: Laika went first; Belka and Strelka were the ones who made it back.

questions.question: Which law of motion explains why a rocket moves forward by throwing exhaust gas backwards?
distractors: Kepler's first law of planetary orbits
questions.explanation: Newton's third law says every action has an equal and opposite reaction. A rocket does not push against the air, which is why it works even better in the vacuum of space.
questions.hook: Gas goes down, rocket goes up: action and reaction.

questions.question: Which American space station fell back to Earth in July 1979, scattering debris across the Western Australian outback near Esperance?
questions.explanation: The local shire jokingly fined NASA 400 dollars for littering. Skylab had been launched in 1973 and housed three crews.
questions.hook: Skylab dropped in on Esperance and got a littering fine.

questions.question: What was the name of the lunar module that carried Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to the Moon's surface in 1969?
questions.explanation: Eagle touched down in the Sea of Tranquillity with under half a minute of fuel to spare, and Armstrong's first words from the surface were 'Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.'
questions.hook: The Eagle has landed: Eagle is the lunar module, Columbia the command module.

questions.question: From which Queensland town did Gilmour Space attempt the first orbital launch of an Australian-built rocket in July 2025?
questions.explanation: The Eris rocket lifted off from the Bowen Orbital Spaceport but flew only briefly before it fell back and crashed. It was a test flight and the company planned more launches.
questions.hook: Bowen's rocket flew only briefly, but it was a start.

questions.question: What is molten rock called once it erupts onto the Earth's surface?
questions.explanation: The same molten rock is called magma while it is still underground. Lava from Hawaiian volcanoes can flow at over 1,000 degrees Celsius and cools into basalt.
questions.hook: Underground it's magma; once it escapes, it's lava.

questions.question: What name is given to a tropical cyclone that forms in the north-western Pacific Ocean?
questions.explanation: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are the same kind of storm with different regional names. Those in the Atlantic and north-eastern Pacific are hurricanes, and those near Australia are simply cyclones.
questions.hook: Same storm, three names, depending on which ocean it's in.

questions.question: Which fossil fuel is formed mostly from the remains of ancient swamp forests?
questions.explanation: Most coal began as plant matter buried in swamps around 300 million years ago, in the Carboniferous period, then compressed over time. Oil and gas mostly came from tiny sea creatures.
questions.hook: Coal is old forest, squashed for 300 million years.

questions.question: Which gemstone is Australia's national gemstone?
questions.explanation: Fields at Coober Pedy, Lightning Ridge and Andamooka supply the great majority of the world's precious opal.
questions.hook: Australia digs most of the world's opal out of the outback.

questions.question: Which layer of the Earth is the thickest?
questions.explanation: The mantle is about 2,900 kilometres thick and makes up roughly 84 per cent of Earth's volume. The crust is a thin skin by comparison, only 5 to 70 kilometres deep.
questions.hook: The crust is just the apple's skin; the mantle is the flesh.

questions.question: Which climate pattern, with warmer than normal water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific, tends to bring drier conditions to eastern Australia?
questions.explanation: During El Niño the trade winds weaken and rain-bearing warm water shifts away from Australia towards South America. The opposite phase, La Niña, tends to bring floods to the east.
questions.hook: El Niño brings the dry; La Niña brings the wet.

questions.question: Uluru is mostly made of which type of rock?
questions.explanation: The rock is a coarse sandstone laid down hundreds of millions of years ago and later tilted almost vertical. Its red colour comes from iron minerals that have rusted on the surface.
questions.hook: Uluru is a rusted, upended sandstone slab.

questions.question: Which gemstone made the Argyle mine in the Kimberley famous for its rare pink examples?
questions.explanation: Argyle was the source of most of the world's pink diamonds until it closed in 2020. At its peak it was also one of the largest diamond producers by volume, though mostly of small brown stones.
questions.hook: Argyle: the pink diamond mine of the Kimberley.

questions.question: At which research station was the lowest air temperature ever measured at ground level, minus 89.2 degrees Celsius, recorded in July 1983?
questions.explanation: Vostok is a Russian base sitting high on the East Antarctic ice sheet at an elevation of around 3,500 metres. Satellites have since detected colder surface temperatures on remote ice ridges, but those are satellite estimates, not station air readings, so Vostok keeps the ground-station record.
questions.hook: Vostok: the coldest air anyone has measured.

questions.question: Opal is made mostly of which compound, with water making up to about a fifth of its weight?
questions.explanation: Precious opal contains up to about 20 per cent water locked between tiny stacked spheres of silica. Those spheres split light into the flashing colours called play of colour.
questions.hook: Opal is sand and water arranged beautifully.

questions.question: Which marsupial eats little else but the leaves of gum trees?
questions.explanation: Koalas eat only a few of the hundreds of eucalypt species and get most of their water from the leaves. The leaves are low in energy and toxic to most animals, so koalas rest for most of the day.
questions.hook: Gum leaves in, naps out: the koala's whole life.

questions.question: What shape are the droppings of a wombat?
questions.explanation: The only known animal to produce cube-shaped droppings, the wombat uses them to mark territory. The pellets stack on logs and rocks without rolling away, and the shape forms in the last stretch of the intestine.
questions.hook: Wombats stack their poo like building blocks.

questions.question: Australia's barrier fence of more than 5,000 kilometres was built mainly to keep which wild canine out of sheep country?
