questions.explanation: Eris threw the apple inscribed "for the fairest" at Thetis's wedding. Hera offered Paris power, Athena victory, and Aphrodite the most beautiful woman, Helen of Sparta. He chose Aphrodite, and the Trojan War followed.
questions.hook: The Judgement of Paris: choose beauty, get a war.

questions.question: Which Knight of the Round Table's affair with Queen Guinevere helped destroy Camelot?
questions.explanation: Lancelot, the greatest knight, was also Galahad's father. When the affair was exposed, Arthur's fellowship split, and Mordred used the chaos to seize the throne. Tristan had a parallel affair with Isolde, wife of King Mark of Cornwall.
questions.hook: Lancelot loved the queen, Tristan loved Isolde: both wrecked a king.

questions.question: Which Trojan hero's journey to Italy is told in Virgil's great Latin epic?
questions.explanation: Aeneas carried his father out of burning Troy, was waylaid in Carthage by Queen Dido, who killed herself when he left, and founded the line that led to Romulus and Remus. Augustus claimed descent from him through Aeneas's son Ascanius, also called Iulus.
questions.hook: Aeneas is Rome's Trojan grandfather, and Julius Caesar's family claimed him.

questions.question: Which festival marks the end of the Ramadan fast?
questions.explanation: Eid al-Fitr, the "festival of breaking the fast", begins when the new moon is sighted. Eid al-Adha, the "festival of sacrifice", comes about two months later at the end of the Hajj and recalls Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son.
questions.hook: Fitr = breaking the fast; Adha = sacrifice.

questions.question: Which Christian festival, 50 days after Easter, marks the Holy Spirit descending on the apostles?
questions.explanation: Acts 2 describes tongues of fire and the apostles speaking in many languages, often seen as the birthday of the Church. Pentecost is Greek for "fiftieth" and began as the Jewish harvest festival of Shavuot. In England it is also called Whit Sunday. Ascension Day is ten days earlier.
questions.hook: Pente = five, as in pentagon: fifty days on from Easter.

questions.question: What was the name of the magic fetter that finally bound the wolf Fenrir?
questions.explanation: After Fenrir broke two iron chains, the dwarves made Gleipnir, a thin ribbon, from six impossible things, including the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard and the roots of a mountain. That is why, as the Prose Edda jokes, those things no longer exist.
questions.hook: Gleipnir is made of things that do not exist, which is why it cannot break.

questions.question: Which Norse god guards the Bifröst bridge and will blow the Gjallarhorn at Ragnarök?
questions.explanation: Heimdall needs less sleep than a bird and can hear wool growing on sheep. His horn announces Ragnarök, where he and Loki kill each other. The Eddic poem Rígsþula makes him the father of the classes of humankind.
questions.hook: Heimdall is the watchman: Idris Elba in the Marvel films.

questions.question: Which ram-headed Egyptian god was said to shape human beings on a potter's wheel?
questions.explanation: Khnum was also the god of the Nile's source, worshipped at Elephantine near Aswan. He shaped each child and its ka, or life force, and placed them in the mother's womb. Amun could also appear as a ram, which makes him the usual wrong answer.
questions.hook: Khnum kneads the clay: picture a ram at a potter's wheel.

questions.question: In the Egyptian judgement of the dead, what was the heart weighed against?
questions.explanation: The feather of Ma'at stood for truth and order. If the heart was heavier with wrongdoing, the monster Ammit, part crocodile, lion and hippo, devoured it. Scarab amulets were placed over the heart to stop it testifying against its owner.
questions.hook: A heart as light as a feather was the only pass to paradise.

questions.question: In Malory's version, which Grail knight was pure enough to achieve the Holy Grail?
questions.explanation: Galahad, Lancelot's son by Elaine, sat safely in the Siege Perilous and achieved the Grail with Percival and Bors, dying in ecstasy at Sarras. In the earlier romances of Chrétien de Troyes and Wolfram von Eschenbach, the Grail hero is Percival.
questions.hook: Lancelot was too sinful, so his son Galahad got the Grail.

questions.question: Which Old Testament prophet was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind with a chariot of fire?
questions.explanation: Elijah's successor Elisha saw him taken and inherited his mantle, the origin of "passing the mantle". A place is set for Elijah at the Passover Seder in case he returns. The film Chariots of Fire takes its title from Blake's hymn "Jerusalem", which borrows the image.
questions.hook: Elijah went up; Elisha picked up the mantle.

questions.question: Which Jewish harvest festival is celebrated by eating meals in temporary huts?
questions.explanation: Sukkot starts five days after Yom Kippur and lasts a week, remembering the Israelites living in shelters in the wilderness after the Exodus. Families build a sukkah with a roof of branches through which the stars can be seen. Purim celebrates Esther, Hanukkah the rededicated Temple.
questions.hook: Sukkah is a hut, Sukkot the week in the huts.

questions.question: Which creature of Greek myth has a human torso growing from the body of a horse?
questions.explanation: Centaurs were usually wild and unruly, famous for brawling at the wedding of Pirithous. Satyrs, the usual mix-up, are part goat. Chiron was the rare wise centaur, and the constellation Centaurus is named for the kind.
questions.hook: Centaur is horse below, human above; satyr is goat below.

questions.question: Which three-headed hound guarded the gates of the Greek underworld?
questions.explanation: Cerberus let souls in but never out. Bringing him up to the surface alive was the twelfth and last labour of Heracles. Orthrus was a two-headed dog and brother of Cerberus, and Garmr is the hound at the gates of the Norse underworld.
questions.hook: Cerberus is the bouncer of Hades: everyone gets in, nobody leaves.

questions.question: Which legendary king was granted the power to turn everything he touched into gold?
questions.explanation: Dionysus granted the wish as thanks for the return of his companion Silenus, but Midas nearly starved when even his food turned to gold. He was cured by washing in the River Pactolus, whose sands were said to carry gold from then on.
questions.hook: Be careful what you wish for: the golden touch also starved him.

questions.question: Which wizard served as adviser to King Arthur?
questions.explanation: Merlin entered the Arthurian story through Geoffrey of Monmouth's History of the Kings of Britain, written around 1136, and was based on the Welsh figure Myrddin. In many tales he arranged Arthur's conception and the sword in the stone.
questions.hook: Merlin is Myrddin with a French accent.

questions.question: Which holy book of Islam do Muslims believe is the word of God revealed to Muhammad?
questions.explanation: It has 114 chapters, called surahs, and was revealed in Arabic over about 23 years, beginning in Ramadan in a cave on Mount Hira near Mecca. The word means "recitation", and the Quran is memorised in full by many Muslims.
questions.hook: Quran means "recitation": it was spoken before it was written.

questions.question: Which deity of the Hindu Trimurti is the creator of the universe?
questions.explanation: Brahma is shown with four faces and rides a swan, yet he has very few temples; the best known is at Pushkar in Rajasthan. Do not confuse him with Brahman, the ultimate reality, or the Brahmins, the priestly caste. Indra is a king of the gods, not one of the three.
questions.hook: Brahma creates, Vishnu preserves, Shiva destroys: B-V-S, in that order.

questions.question: Which skilled mortal weaver was turned into a spider after challenging Athena to a contest?
questions.explanation: The story is told by Ovid in the Metamorphoses. Arachne wove a flawless tapestry showing the gods' misdeeds, and Athena tore it up in rage and transformed her. The Greek word for spider gave us arachnids and arachnophobia.
questions.hook: Arachne is Greek for spider: arachnophobia is fear of her.

questions.question: Which Māori demigod is said to have hauled the North Island of New Zealand from the sea as a giant fish?
questions.explanation: The North Island is called Te Ika-a-Māui, the fish of Māui, and the South Island is his canoe, Te Waka-a-Māui. Māui is also credited with slowing the sun and bringing fire to people. Tāne is the god of forests, Tangaroa of the sea and Ranginui the sky father.
questions.hook: Fish on a hook: the North Island is Māui's catch, the South his canoe.

questions.question: In the Chinese zodiac legend, which animal won the great race set by the Jade Emperor?
questions.explanation: The rat hitched a ride on the ox's back, then jumped ahead just before the finish line to take first place, and the ox came second. In one version the cat, tricked by the rat, missed the race entirely, which is said to explain why cats chase rats.
questions.hook: The rat rode the ox and jumped off at the line: first place by cheating.

questions.question: Which city is the holiest in Islam and the direction Muslims face for daily prayer?
questions.explanation: At its centre stands the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine that Muslims believe was built by Abraham and Ishmael. The direction of prayer is called the qibla. Early Muslims first prayed towards Jerusalem before the direction was changed to Mecca. Medina is the second holiest city.
questions.hook: Mecca is the compass point: Medina is second, Jerusalem third.

questions.question: Which Hawaiian goddess is said to live in the Halemaʻumaʻu crater of Kīlauea?
questions.explanation: Pele is said to have travelled from Tahiti to the Hawaiian islands in search of a home. Volcanologists still use her name for "Pele's hair", thin strands of volcanic glass, and "Pele's tears", small glass droplets. Hiʻiaka is her youngest sister.
questions.hook: Pele's hair and Pele's tears are real volcanic glass named for her.

questions.question: Which knight fatally wounded King Arthur at the Battle of Camlann?
questions.explanation: The tenth-century Welsh annals note that "Arthur and Medraut fell" at Camlann. Mordred began as Arthur's nephew and became his son by incest in later romances. In Malory's telling, Arthur kills him with a spear and is mortally wounded in the same moment.
questions.hook: Camlann: the king and his traitor kill each other.

questions.question: Which ten-headed demon king of Lanka abducted Sita in the Ramayana?
questions.explanation: Rama, aided by the monkey army of Sugriva with Hanuman among its greatest warriors, defeated Ravana and rescued Sita. The festival of Dussehra celebrates the victory, and giant effigies of Ravana are burned. Kumbhakarna was his giant brother, who slept for months at a time.
questions.hook: Dussehra burns giant effigies of Ravana every year across much of India.

questions.question: Which apostle refused to believe in the Resurrection until he could touch Jesus's wounds?
questions.explanation: The episode is in the Gospel of John, and it gave English the phrase "doubting Thomas". Tradition holds that Thomas later travelled to India, and the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their church back to him.
questions.hook: Doubting Thomas needed to touch it before he'd believe it.

questions.question: Which god, famed for defeating the sea-dragon Tiamat, became the chief deity of Babylon?
questions.explanation: In the Enuma Elish, Marduk split Tiamat's body to form the sky and the earth. The poem was recited each spring at the Babylonian New Year festival, Akitu. Ashur was the chief god of Assyria, and Enlil an older Sumerian god of air.
questions.hook: Marduk made the world from the slain Tiamat, and Babylon made him king of the gods.

questions.question: Which Japanese god, brother of Amaterasu, slew the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi?
questions.explanation: In its tail Susanoo found the sword Kusanagi, which became one of the three imperial regalia of Japan. His earlier misbehaviour had driven Amaterasu to hide in a cave, plunging the world into darkness. Raijin is the god of thunder, Hachiman of war and Inari of rice.
questions.hook: Eight heads, eight sake barrels: Susanoo got the serpent drunk, then won a sword.

questions.question: Which hero of the Ulster Cycle defended Ulster single-handedly in the Táin Bó Cúailnge?
questions.explanation: The Ulstermen were struck down by a curse of labour pains, leaving the young Cú Chulainn to hold off Queen Medb's army. His name means "hound of Culann", because he killed Culann's guard dog as a boy and promised to take its place. Fionn and Oisín belong to the separate Fenian Cycle.
questions.hook: The Táin is the Irish Iliad, and Cú Chulainn is its Achilles.

questions.question: Which wise half-horse teacher of Achilles and Jason gave up his immortality after being wounded?
questions.explanation: Chiron was accidentally struck by one of Heracles' poisoned arrows, and the wound could never heal. He gave up his immortality to end his pain and was placed among the stars. He also taught the healer Asclepius, unlike the other centaurs Nessus, Pholus and Eurytion.
questions.hook: The wounded healer: Chiron taught medicine yet could not cure himself.

questions.question: Which Hindu goddess, shown riding a lion or tiger, slew the buffalo demon Mahishasura?
questions.explanation: The gods combined their energies to create Durga when no one else could defeat the demon. Her victory is celebrated at Durga Puja, and UNESCO added Durga Puja in Kolkata to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2021. Kali, often confused with her, is a fierce form of the goddess who sprang from Durga's brow in some tellings.
questions.hook: Durga on a lion, spear in the demon: nine nights of worship, then the festival's finale.

questions.question: Which sacred book of the K'iche' Maya tells the story of the Hero Twins and the creation of humans from maize?
questions.explanation: In the Popol Vuh the twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque defeat the lords of the underworld, Xibalba, in a ball game. The text was written in the 1550s in the K'iche' language using Latin letters. It survives thanks to a copy made by the Dominican friar Francisco Ximénez around 1700.
questions.hook: Popol Vuh means "book of the community": the Maya Genesis.

questions.question: Which blind prophet of Thebes warned Oedipus and later advised Odysseus in the underworld?
questions.explanation: In Book 11 of the Odyssey, Odysseus summons Tiresias' ghost with sacrificial blood to learn how to get home. A famous myth says Hera blinded him and Zeus gave him prophecy as compensation, and another that he lived seven years as a woman.
questions.hook: Tiresias sees the future but not the present: blind in life, still prophesying in death.

questions.question: Which brother of Zeus ruled the realm of the dead?
questions.explanation: After the three brothers drew lots, Hades received the underworld, which took its name from him. He owned a helmet of invisibility made by the Cyclopes, and the Romans knew him as Pluto or Dis.
questions.hook: Hades got the short straw: the dark basement of the cosmos.

questions.question: Which Greek goddess tended the sacred hearth of every home and city?
questions.explanation: Hestia received the first offering at every sacrifice and a public fire burned for her in each Greek city. Colonists carried a flame from the mother city's hearth to light the fire of their new settlement.
questions.hook: Hestia is the pilot light of the Greek world: always burning, never in the story.

questions.question: Which Olympian was the lame blacksmith god who forged weapons for the other gods?
questions.explanation: Hephaestus built the gods' palaces and later forged the armour of Achilles. In one story he was lame because he was hurled from Olympus. His Roman counterpart is Vulcan, which gives us the word volcano.
questions.hook: Hephaestus works the forge under the volcano: Vulcan's Greek twin.

questions.question: Which goat-legged Greek god of shepherds and wild places played the reed pipes?
questions.explanation: Pan lived in Arcadia and was said to startle travellers with sudden cries in lonely places, which gave English the word panic. He chased the nymph Syrinx, who was turned into reeds, and he cut those reeds into his pipes.
questions.hook: Pan pipes were made from a nymph who ran out of options.

questions.question: Which Greek god of love and desire is usually shown with a bow and golden arrows?
questions.explanation: Eros shot arrows that made gods and mortals fall in love, and sometimes leaden ones that caused revulsion. Early poets made him a primordial force, while later ones turned him into Aphrodite's mischievous child. The Romans called him Cupid.
questions.hook: Eros gives us erotic: the arrow-shooter of desire.

questions.question: Which underworld river made souls forget their earthly lives when they drank from it?
questions.explanation: Souls about to be reborn drank from the Lethe, as Plato describes in the Myth of Er. Its name means forgetfulness, and the Greek word for truth, aletheia, literally means not-forgetting. The five underworld rivers also include the Styx.
questions.hook: Lethe = lost memory: the river that wipes your hard drive.

questions.question: Which primordial goddess, the personification of Earth, was mother of the Titans?
questions.explanation: Gaia bore Uranus, the sky, and then lay with him to produce the twelve Titans, the Cyclopes and the Hundred-Handers. She later helped Cronus overthrow her husband. Her Roman equivalent is Terra, and the Gaia hypothesis in science borrows her name.
questions.hook: Gaia is the ground floor of the family tree: everyone descends from her.

questions.question: Which Titaness was the mother of the first generation of Olympian gods?
questions.explanation: Rhea bore Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon and Zeus. Later Greeks linked her with the Anatolian mother goddess Cybele. One of Saturn's moons carries her name, and so does a large flightless South American bird.
questions.hook: Rhea is the Olympians' mum: six kids, one famous trick.

questions.question: Into which deep abyss, far below the underworld, did Zeus hurl the defeated Titans?
questions.explanation: Hesiod says a bronze anvil falling from heaven would take nine days to reach the earth and another nine to reach Tartarus. The Titans were locked in behind bronze gates, guarded by the Hundred-Handers. Tartarus was also a primordial being.
questions.hook: Tartarus is the deepest cell: an anvil needs eighteen days of falling to get there.

questions.question: Which blessed realm of the Greek afterlife was reserved for heroes and those the gods favoured?
questions.explanation: Most ordinary souls drifted to the grey Asphodel Meadows, while the favoured few enjoyed a sunlit paradise in Elysium. Homer placed it at the edge of the world, and the Champs-Élysées in Paris is named after it.
questions.hook: Elysium is first class: everyone else gets the grey Asphodel fields.

questions.question: Which Greek goddess of the dawn rose from the edge of the world each morning ahead of her brother Helios?
questions.explanation: Eos was a daughter of the Titan Hyperion and sister of Helios and Selene. She fell in love with the mortal Tithonus and begged Zeus to make him immortal, but forgot to ask for eternal youth, so he withered until he became a cicada.
questions.hook: Eos was careless: immortality without youth turned her lover into a cicada.

questions.question: Which goddess of crossroads, ghosts and witchcraft carried torches and was often shown with three faces?
questions.explanation: Statues of Hecate stood at three-way crossroads, where Athenians left her offerings of food on the night of the new moon. She helped search for Persephone with torches and became the patron goddess of witches in later tradition.
questions.hook: Hecate watches every fork in the road, and she has three faces to see them all.

questions.question: In the most common Greek account of creation, which yawning void existed before anything else?
questions.explanation: The word originally meant a gap or chasm, not disorder. Gaia, Tartarus and Eros followed it, and Chaos then produced Erebus and Nyx. The modern sense of confusion came much later, from the idea of an unformed state.
questions.hook: Chaos first meant a gaping gap, and everything else filled it.

questions.question: Which primordial sky god became the first ruler of the cosmos, only to be overthrown by his youngest Titan son?
questions.explanation: Uranus hid his children inside Gaia, so she gave Cronus a sickle to ambush him. From the blood and foam where the severed parts fell into the sea, Aphrodite was said to rise. The planet Uranus is the only one named for a Greek god.
questions.hook: Uranus ruled the sky until his own son cut him down to size.

questions.question: Which Trojan prince was carried off by Zeus, in the form of an eagle, to serve as cupbearer to the gods?
questions.explanation: Ganymede was described as the most beautiful of mortals and was granted eternal youth on Olympus. His father received divine horses as compensation. Jupiter's largest moon, the biggest in the Solar System, bears his name.
questions.hook: Ganymede got the best job in heaven: pouring the gods' drinks for ever.

questions.question: Which mortal princess, loved by Eros, was set impossible tasks by his jealous mother?
questions.explanation: Psyche sorted a giant heap of seeds, gathered golden wool and fetched water from the Styx. In the end Zeus made her immortal so she could marry Eros. The tale is best known from Apuleius, and psyche is the Greek word for both soul and butterfly.
questions.hook: Psyche means soul and butterfly: love and the soul finally united.

questions.question: Which primordial goddess of night was so feared that Zeus himself held back from angering her?
questions.explanation: In the Iliad, Hypnos admits he escaped Zeus's wrath only by hiding with his mother Nyx, and the king of the gods did not dare to offend her. She was the mother of Sleep, Death, Doom and the Fates, and her daughter Hemera was the day.
questions.hook: Nyx scared even Zeus: night is older than the king of the gods.

questions.question: Which Titan personified the great river that was thought to encircle the entire world?
questions.explanation: Oceanus married his sister Tethys, and Hesiod credits them with 3,000 river gods and 3,000 Oceanids as children. Unlike most Titans he sat out the war against the Olympians. The English word ocean comes directly from his name.
questions.hook: Oceanus is the ocean itself: the river around the edge of the world.

questions.question: What garment, woven by Athenian women, was presented to the ancient statue of Athena at the Panathenaia?
questions.explanation: The peplos was carried in a grand procession to the Acropolis at the yearly festival, and it is usually thought to be shown on the Parthenon frieze. Every fourth year the Great Panathenaia added athletic contests, with olive oil as the prize.
questions.hook: Pan-Athenaia means all-Athens: everyone joined in giving her a new robe.

questions.question: Which goddess of youth, daughter of Zeus and Hera, was cupbearer to the gods and later wife of the deified Heracles?
questions.explanation: Hebe poured nectar for the Olympians until Ganymede took over the job. When Heracles was received among the gods after his death, he married her and so made peace with Hera. The Romans called her Juventas.
questions.hook: Hebe stands for youth: the root of words like hebephrenia.

questions.question: Which Muse presided over epic poetry and was the mother of Orpheus?
questions.explanation: Her name means beautiful voice. Poets of epic, including Homer and Virgil, appealed to the Muse at the start of their work. Clio ruled history, Erato love poetry and Terpsichore dance. A steam organ with whistles is also called a calliope.
questions.hook: Calliope means beautiful voice, and she is the Muse of epic poetry.

questions.question: What did Ariadne give Theseus so he could find his way out of the Labyrinth?
questions.explanation: Theseus tied one end near the entrance and unwound the ball as he went in to face the Minotaur. After killing it, he simply followed the thread back out. Ariadne had fallen in love with him.
questions.hook: Ariadne's thread: the classic way to escape a maze.

questions.question: Theseus promised his father he would raise white sails on the ship's return if he survived Crete. What colour sails did the ship fly instead, fatally misleading his father?
questions.explanation: The Athenian ships carrying youths to Crete as tribute flew black sails in mourning. Seeing the black sails on the returning ship, King Aegeus assumed his son was dead and threw himself into the sea.
questions.hook: Forget the colour change and a father pays for it.

questions.question: Which Greek hero rescued Andromeda from a sea monster and later married her?
questions.explanation: Andromeda had been chained to a coastal rock as an offering because her mother Cassiopeia boasted that she was more beautiful than the sea nymphs. Perseus, Andromeda, Cassiopeia and the sea monster Cetus all became constellations.
questions.hook: A rescue so famous the whole cast ended up in the night sky.

questions.question: Which Amazon queen's war-belt was the target of Heracles' ninth labour?
questions.explanation: The belt was a gift from her father Ares. In the best-known version, Hera disguised herself and told the Amazons that Heracles was abducting their queen, sparking a fight in which Hippolyta was killed.
questions.hook: Hippolyta lost her belt and, in the best-known version, her life.

questions.question: Which winged creatures kept snatching the food of the blind seer Phineus until the Argonauts drove them off?
questions.explanation: Zeus had punished Phineus for revealing too much about the future. The winged sons of the North Wind, Zetes and Calais, chased the Harpies away, and Phineus repaid the crew with directions past the Clashing Rocks.
questions.hook: Food snatchers with wings: the Harpies spoiled every meal.

questions.question: Which dying centaur gave Deianira blood that later poisoned the shirt of her husband Heracles?
questions.explanation: Heracles had shot Nessus with an arrow dipped in Hydra venom for trying to assault Deianira. Nessus claimed his blood was a love charm. Years later she used it on a tunic, and the Hydra's poison burned Heracles in agony.
questions.hook: Heracles was ultimately brought down by a poisoned shirt, not by an arrow.

questions.question: Which sea monster sat opposite the six-headed Scylla, sucking down the sea and spewing it out three times a day?
questions.explanation: Sailors who steered away from one peril risked the other, and the phrase "between Scylla and Charybdis" still means a choice of two evils. Tradition placed them either side of a narrow strait, usually the Strait of Messina.
questions.hook: A monster on one side, a whirlpool on the other: no good choice.

questions.question: Which queen was turned into a weeping stone after boasting that she had more children than Leto?
questions.explanation: Leto had only the twins Apollo and Artemis, who avenged the insult by killing Niobe's children with their arrows. Grief-stricken, Niobe turned to stone on Mount Sipylus, and the rock was said to weep still.
questions.hook: Niobe's boast cost her everything and left her crying in stone.

questions.question: Whose life was bound to a log that his mother Althaea kept out of the fire, until she threw it in?
questions.explanation: The Fates declared he would live only as long as the log lasted. After Meleager killed her brothers in a row over the boar's hide, Althaea burned the log in anger and he died on the spot.
questions.hook: A son's life hung on a log, and a furious mother held the match.

questions.question: Which three-bodied giant's red cattle did Heracles fetch for his tenth labour?
questions.explanation: Geryon lived on the western island of Erytheia, and his herd was guarded by the herdsman Eurytion and the two-headed dog Orthrus. Tradition says Heracles raised the Pillars of Heracles at the Strait of Gibraltar on his way.
questions.hook: Three bodies, one herd, and the far west of the known world.

questions.question: Which half-woman, half-serpent monster bore Cerberus, the Hydra and the Chimera?
questions.explanation: Her partner was the storm giant Typhon, and many of Greek myth's most famous monsters were their children. The Australian spiny anteater, the echidna, takes its name from her.
questions.hook: Echidna the monster mother shares her name with the spiny egg-layer.

questions.question: Which Trojan prince, the eldest son of King Priam, was killed by Achilles outside his city's walls?
questions.explanation: Hector was Troy's greatest defender and killed Patroclus before Achilles avenged him. Achilles dragged the body behind his chariot, until Priam came in secret to beg for it. The Iliad ends with Hector's funeral.
questions.hook: Hector holds the walls; Achilles ends him, and Priam begs the body back.

questions.question: Which faithful wife of Odysseus kept her suitors waiting by unpicking her weaving every night?
questions.explanation: Penelope said she would choose a husband once she finished a burial shroud for her father-in-law Laertes. She did this for about three years, until a maid betrayed her. She finally tested the returned Odysseus by mentioning moving their bed.
questions.hook: Penelope weaves by day and unpicks by night.

questions.question: Who is traditionally credited with the fables of the tortoise and the hare and the boy who cried wolf?
questions.explanation: Aesop is said to have lived in the 6th century BCE, but the fables were collected and added to by many later writers, and none of his own writing survives. The Greek tales travelled widely and many carry a stated moral at the end.
questions.hook: Aesop's name is on the fable, the moral on the end.

questions.question: What is the name of Odysseus's son, who goes searching for news of his father in the Odyssey?
questions.explanation: Telemachus was a baby when Odysseus left for the war. Athena, disguised as a family friend, urges him to seek news at Pylos and Sparta. On his return he helps his father kill the suitors who had been eating through the household.
questions.hook: Telemachus: a boy who grows into the hero's heir.

questions.question: In the Aesop fable behind the phrase 'sour grapes', which animal cannot reach the bunch it wants?
questions.explanation: After jumping repeatedly, the fox walks away claiming the grapes were probably sour anyway. The phrase now describes pretending you never wanted what you could not get.
questions.hook: The fox can't reach, so the grapes get the blame.

questions.question: Which daughter of Oedipus defied King Creon by burying her brother Polynices?
questions.explanation: Creon forbade burial for Polynices, who had attacked Thebes. Antigone buried him anyway and was sentenced to be walled up alive, and hanged herself. Her sister Ismene hesitated, but then offered to share her punishment.
questions.hook: Family duty against the state: Antigone digs in.

questions.question: Which wife of King Agamemnon murdered him in his bath after his return from the war?
questions.explanation: Clytemnestra was angry that Agamemnon had sacrificed their daughter Iphigenia, and was helped by her lover Aegisthus. Their son Orestes later killed her to avenge his father, which is the story of Aeschylus's Oresteia.
questions.hook: Clytemnestra's revenge was waiting in the bath.

questions.question: Which Spartan king was Helen's husband when Paris carried her off to Troy?
questions.explanation: Menelaus was the younger brother of Agamemnon, who led the expedition. Helen's many suitors had earlier sworn an oath to defend her chosen husband, which is why so many Greek kings joined the war. After Troy, Menelaus and Helen reunited.
questions.hook: Menelaus lost the wife, Agamemnon led the war.

questions.question: Which companion of Achilles went into battle wearing his armour and was killed by Hector?
questions.explanation: Achilles had withdrawn from the fighting over a quarrel with Agamemnon. When Patroclus died in his place, Achilles' grief ended his anger at the Greeks, and he returned to fight and kill Hector.
questions.hook: Patroclus wore the armour; Achilles paid the price.

questions.question: Which queen of Carthage killed herself on a pyre after her lover sailed away?
questions.explanation: In Virgil's Aeneid the gods order Aeneas to leave Carthage for Italy, and Dido, abandoned, curses him and his descendants. Romans read this as the mythical start of their long enmity with Carthage in the Punic Wars.
questions.hook: Dido's pyre is the Punic Wars' first spark.

questions.question: In which Greek citadel did Heinrich Schliemann find the gold 'Mask of Agamemnon' in 1876?
questions.explanation: Schliemann reportedly telegraphed that he had gazed upon the face of Agamemnon. The mask comes from a shaft grave at Mycenae and is dated to roughly 1600 to 1500 BCE, several centuries before the time Greek tradition places the Trojan War. Some scholars have questioned whether it is authentic, and whether it is the mask Schliemann described.
questions.hook: The golden face is older than the king it was named for.

questions.question: Which Athenian playwright, known as the father of tragedy, wrote the Oresteia and is said to have fought at Marathon?
questions.explanation: Aeschylus is credited with adding a second actor, which allowed real dialogue and conflict on stage. He wrote about eighty plays, of which only seven survive. His own epitaph mentions Marathon but not his plays.
questions.hook: Aeschylus: the soldier-poet who gave tragedy its second actor.

questions.question: Which Phaeacian princess found the shipwrecked Odysseus after going to the shore to wash clothes?
questions.explanation: Athena inspired her to go to the river that morning. Nausicaa gave Odysseus clothes and directions to her father's palace. Her people, the Phaeacians, then carried him home to Ithaca in one of their magic ships.
questions.hook: Nausicaa's washing day rescued a king.

questions.question: Which Greek commander, in a burst of glory in the Iliad, wounded both Aphrodite and Ares?
questions.explanation: Athena herself guided his spear at Ares, and the god howled back to Olympus. Diomedes was king of Argos and later, with Odysseus, stole the sacred Palladium statue from Troy, which was said to protect the city.
questions.hook: Diomedes wounded two gods and lived.

questions.question: Which Greek soldier pretended to have been abandoned by his comrades, persuading the Trojans to drag the horse inside?
questions.explanation: Sinon was left behind on purpose. He swore the horse was an offering to Athena and would bring Troy luck. Epeius, by contrast, was the craftsman who built the horse, and Thersites the Greek camp's loud-mouthed critic.
questions.hook: Sinon sold the lie; the Trojans bought it.

questions.question: In Euripides' Bacchae, which young king of Thebes is torn apart by women led by his own mother?
questions.explanation: Pentheus banned the new worship of the god and spied on the women on Mount Cithaeron, dressed as one of them. His mother Agave, in a trance, killed him thinking he was a lion. Cadmus, his grandfather, later mourned him.
questions.hook: Pentheus spied on the revel and became the sacrifice.

questions.question: What is the title of the final play in Aeschylus's Oresteia, in which Orestes is put on trial in Athens?
questions.explanation: Athena sets up a jury of Athenian citizens to try Orestes for killing his mother, and casts the deciding vote to acquit him. The Furies are then persuaded to become the Eumenides, or 'kindly ones'. Libation Bearers is the trilogy's second play.
questions.hook: Furies on trial end up kindly.

questions.question: From which type of choral hymn to Dionysus did Greek tragedy reportedly develop, according to Aristotle?
questions.explanation: Aristotle wrote that tragedy began with the leaders of the dithyramb, sung and danced by a chorus. A paean was addressed to Apollo, an epinicion celebrated an athletic victory, and a threnody was a lament for the dead.
questions.hook: Dithyramb: the wine-god's choir that grew into theatre.

questions.question: Which Roman god, wielder of the thunderbolt, ruled as king of the gods?
questions.explanation: Jupiter Optimus Maximus, meaning best and greatest, was the chief god of Rome and had the grandest temple on the Capitoline Hill. Every new consul sacrificed to him on taking office, and his Greek counterpart is Zeus.
questions.hook: Jupiter is Zeus in a toga, and the sky's loudest bully.

questions.question: Which Roman goddess of wisdom and crafts, said to have sprung from Jupiter's head, shared his Capitoline temple with Juno?
questions.explanation: Jupiter, Juno and Minerva made up the Capitoline Triad, the state's chief gods, worshipped together in the great temple on the Capitoline Hill. Minerva also presided over Rome's schoolteachers, doctors and craftsmen.
questions.hook: Three on the hill: king, queen, and the clever daughter.

questions.question: Which Roman god of the sea carried a trident and shared his Greek equivalent with a famous earthquake-maker?
questions.explanation: Neptune's annual festival, the Neptunalia, fell in the dry heat of July, when Romans built shelters of leafy branches to shade themselves. He later gave his name to the eighth planet.
questions.hook: Neptune's trident is the fork that stirs the waves.

questions.question: Which Roman god of fire and the forge was the husband of Venus?
questions.explanation: Vulcan was a lame craftsman who made weapons for the gods, including Jupiter's thunderbolts. His festival, the Vulcanalia, was held on 23 August to ward off fires, and his name gave us the word volcano.
questions.hook: Venus married the blacksmith and kept Mars on the side.

questions.question: Which Roman goddess of the hunt and the Moon had a famous sacred grove beside Lake Nemi?
questions.explanation: The grove at Nemi was guarded by the Rex Nemorensis, a priest-king who held office by killing his predecessor, a custom that inspired Frazer's The Golden Bough. Diana's Greek counterpart is Artemis.
questions.hook: Diana's grove had a priest who had to murder his way into the job.

questions.question: Which household gods, often shown as dancing youths holding drinking horns, were honoured at the family shrine in a Roman home?
questions.explanation: The Lares watched over the family and its land, and received small offerings of food, wine and garlands at the household shrine.
questions.hook: Lares: the little guardians who got a bite of dinner.

questions.question: Which type of gladiator fought with a weighted net and a trident?
questions.explanation: The retiarius wore little armour and relied on speed, and was often matched against the heavily armed secutor.
questions.hook: Rete is Latin for net: the retiarius is the net man.

questions.question: On which day of each month did the Roman Kalends fall?
questions.explanation: The Kalends was the first day of the month, when debts fell due, and the word gives us calendar. The Nones fell on the 5th or 7th and the Ides on the 13th or 15th, so Romans counted backwards from those markers.
questions.hook: Kalends begins the month; calendar is its child.

questions.question: What is the circular opening at the top of the Pantheon's dome called?
questions.explanation: The oculus is more than eight metres wide and is the only source of light, letting sun and rain fall onto the floor, which has drains. The dome is built of unreinforced concrete and was the world's largest for over 1,300 years.
questions.hook: Oculus is Latin for eye: the building looks up at the sky.

questions.question: After his death, Romulus was said to be worshipped as which god?
questions.explanation: Quirinus was an old Sabine god of the community, and his temple stood on the Quirinal Hill. Romulus was said to have been taken up to heaven in a storm.
questions.hook: Rome's founder ended up as Rome's citizen-god.

questions.question: Which Roman woodland god, identified with the Greek Pan, was said to speak in dreams and rustling leaves?
questions.explanation: Faunus was an ancient king of Latium in some stories, and the plural fauns are his woodland followers. The English word fauna comes from his name, and he was also tied to the Lupercal cave.
questions.hook: Faunus gives us fauna, the animals of the woods.

questions.question: Which emperor reportedly joked on his deathbed, "Dear me, I think I am becoming a god"?
questions.explanation: Suetonius records the joke, which mocked the Roman custom of deifying dead emperors after a Senate vote. Vespasian founded the Flavian dynasty and began the Colosseum, and his son Titus saw it finished.
questions.hook: A dying emperor made a gag about his own godhood.

questions.question: Which emperor made the Sun god Sol Invictus an official state cult in AD 274 and built him a great temple in Rome?
questions.explanation: After defeating Palmyra, Aurelian promoted the Unconquered Sun as the empire's chief god. The festival of the Sun's birthday fell on 25 December. Earlier, Elagabalus had promoted a Syrian sun god in Rome, but with little lasting success.
questions.hook: Aurelian crowned the Unconquered Sun with a December birthday.

questions.question: Which Norse goddess of love and fertility travelled in a chariot drawn by two cats?
questions.explanation: Freyja was the leading goddess of the Vanir, owned the gold necklace Brísingamen and had a cloak of falcon feathers. Her brother Freyr and father Njord were also Vanir, who joined the Aesir gods after a war.
questions.hook: Freyja's cat-powered chariot: the original cat lady of the north.

questions.question: Which Norse goddess, famed for her golden hair, was Thor's wife?
questions.explanation: Loki once cut off Sif's hair as a prank, then had to make amends by commissioning dwarf smiths to forge replacement hair of real gold that grew like natural hair. On the way back, Loki also made a wager with other dwarves, who forged Mjölnir.
questions.hook: Sif's haircut gone wrong gave Thor his hammer.

questions.question: Which Norse sea god, father of Freyr and Freyja, was a Vanir hostage who lived among the Aesir?
questions.explanation: Njord ruled the winds, coastal waters and fishing, and was invoked by sailors. His marriage to the giantess Skadi failed because he hated her mountain home and she hated the screaming gulls of his seaside hall Nóatún.
questions.hook: Njord's marriage: mountains versus seagulls, and nobody won.

questions.question: From the body of which primeval giant did Odin and his brothers shape the world?
questions.explanation: Ymir's flesh became the earth, his blood the seas, his skull the sky and his bones the mountains. Dwarves arose as maggots in his corpse, and the gods set four of them, Nordri, Sudri, Austri and Vestri, to hold up the sky.
questions.hook: The world was butchered from Ymir: flesh to earth, blood to sea, skull to sky.

questions.question: Which fire giant, wielding a flaming sword, sets the whole world ablaze at the end of the Norse cosmos?
questions.explanation: Surtr guards the southern realm of Muspelheim and leads the fire giants across the Bifröst, which breaks under them. The Völuspá says he comes from the south with the 'bane of branches', and the sun shines from his sword.
questions.hook: Surtr is the sword-swinging arsonist who has been waiting since day one.

questions.question: Which daughter of Loki was appointed by Odin to rule over those who died of sickness or old age?
questions.explanation: Her mother was the giantess Angrboða. Snorri describes Hel as half living-skinned and half corpse-blue, with her hall called Éljúðnir. Her name and the English word hell share a Germanic root, though the Norse realm was a cold, damp place, not a fiery one.
questions.hook: Hel and English 'hell' share a root, but her realm was damp and chilly.

questions.question: Which primordial Norse realm of ice and mist lay across the void from the world of fire, Muspelheim?
questions.explanation: According to Snorri, creation began when the heat of Muspelheim met the rime of Niflheim across the chasm Ginnungagap. The melting frost formed the giant Ymir and the cow Auðumbla, who licked the first god out of the ice.
questions.hook: Fire meets ice over an empty gap, and out drips the first giant.

questions.question: Which Norse god of poetry and eloquence was said to have runes carved on his tongue?
questions.explanation: Bragi welcomed fallen warriors to Valhalla with verse and was married to Iðunn, keeper of the apples. The ninth-century skald Bragi Boddason, the earliest named poet of the skaldic tradition, may have given the god his name, though this is a scholarly suggestion rather than a fact.
questions.hook: Bragi, god of verse, had runes carved on his tongue, so his speech was literally written down.

questions.question: What term describes the overlapping-plank method used to build Viking longships?
questions.explanation: Clinker hulls were built shell-first with overlapping oak planks fastened by iron rivets, making them light and flexible enough to flex in rough seas. Their shallow draught let longships row far up rivers to raid inland towns.
questions.hook: Clinker: planks overlap like roof tiles, so the hull bends but does not break.

questions.question: Which dragon does the hero Sigurd kill in the Völsunga saga?
questions.explanation: Fafnir killed his own father for a cursed hoard of gold and turned into a dragon. Sigurd hid in a pit on the dragon's path and stabbed upward, then tasted its blood and understood the speech of birds.
questions.hook: Sigurd digs a pit and the dragon walks over it: a patient plan.

questions.question: Tolkien took the names of Gandalf and most dwarves in The Hobbit from a list in which Old Norse poem?
questions.explanation: The 'Dvergatal' catalogue in the Völuspá names dwarves including Gandalf, Thorin, Dwalin, Fili, Kili, Bifur, Bombur and Dori. In the Norse list Gandalf means 'wand-elf'; Tolkien turned the name onto his wizard.
questions.hook: Gandalf started life as a dwarf's name in a poem about the end of the world.

questions.question: Which goddess was Odin's wife and the queen of Asgard?
questions.explanation: Frigg knew everyone's fate but never told it. She was the mother of Baldr, whose death she tried to prevent, and she lived in the hall Fensalir. She is often linked with Friday, named for either her or Freyja.
questions.hook: Frigg knows the future but keeps quiet: the queen who never spoils the ending.

questions.question: Which Egyptian sun god was said to sail across the sky each day in a boat?
questions.explanation: Ra travelled the heavens in his day-barque, then passed through the underworld at night in a second boat, fighting the serpent Apep so the sun could rise again. Pharaohs from the Fifth Dynasty on called themselves his sons.
questions.hook: Ra rows the sun across the sky by day and fights a snake by night.

questions.question: Which goddess searched Egypt to gather the scattered pieces of her murdered husband Osiris?
questions.explanation: Helped by her sister Nephthys, Isis found the pieces of Osiris's body and, in most tellings, revived him long enough to conceive their son Horus. Her cult later spread around the Roman world, with temples as far as Britain.
questions.hook: Isis was the original jigsaw solver: she put her husband back together.

questions.question: Which Egyptian god, worshipped at Kom Ombo and in the Faiyum, had the head of a crocodile?
questions.explanation: Sobek was a god of the Nile's power and fertility, and the Greeks called the Faiyum city of his cult Crocodilopolis. Priests kept sacred crocodiles in temple pools, adorned with gold earrings, and mummified them when they died.
questions.hook: Sobek the crocodile ruled the riverbank where the Nile bites back.

questions.question: What does the ankh, the Egyptian cross topped with a loop, symbolise?
questions.explanation: Gods are often painted holding an ankh to the nose of a king, offering the breath of life. Egyptian Christians, the Copts, later adapted the sign as an early form of the cross.
questions.hook: Ankh means 'life': the loop is the head, the cross the body.

questions.question: Which insect was sacred in ancient Egypt as a symbol of the rising sun and rebirth?
questions.explanation: Egyptians saw the beetle rolling its ball of dung as a picture of the god Khepri pushing the sun over the horizon. Carved scarab amulets were common, and a large 'heart scarab' was wrapped with mummies to help them pass judgement.
questions.hook: A beetle pushing its ball is the sun being pushed up at dawn.

questions.question: During Egyptian mummification, which organ was usually left in the body while the brain was thrown away?
questions.explanation: The Egyptians thought the heart was the seat of thought and memory, and it was needed for judgement in the afterlife. The liver, lungs, stomach and intestines went into four canopic jars, and the brain was pulled out through the nose with a hook.
questions.hook: They kept the heart and binned the brain.

questions.question: Which Persian poet spent around thirty years composing the Shahnameh, the 'Book of Kings'?
questions.explanation: Finished around 1010 CE, the poem runs to about 50,000 couplets and tells of Persian heroes such as Rostam. Ferdowsi deliberately avoided Arabic words, and the work is credited with helping to preserve the Persian language.
questions.hook: Thirty years of verse saved a language: the Shahnameh.

questions.question: In the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish, humans were fashioned from the blood of which slain god?
questions.explanation: Kingu was the general of Tiamat's monster army. After Marduk defeated her, the gods condemned him and had him executed. Humans were created from his blood to do the work of the gods, a very different start from the gentler tales of other traditions.
questions.hook: Humans were made from Kingu's blood to do the gods' chores.

questions.question: Which Canaanite storm god, whose myths appear on tablets found at Ugarit, rode the clouds and brought the rains?
questions.explanation: The Ugarit tablets, excavated at Ras Shamra in Syria in the late 1920s, tell how Baal defeated the sea god Yam, then died at the hands of Mot (death) and returned. His name means 'lord', and later Hebrew writers used it as a term for rival gods.
questions.hook: Baal means 'lord': the storm god who died and came back.

questions.question: What was the unusual source of the iron in the blade of a dagger buried with Tutankhamun, shown by analysis in 2016?
questions.explanation: The blade's high nickel and cobalt content matches iron meteorites. The Egyptians called iron 'metal from the sky', and at that time worked iron was rare and highly prized.
questions.hook: Tut's dagger fell from the sky: iron was space metal.

questions.question: Which Memphite creator god and patron of craftsmen was said to have created the world by thinking it in his heart and speaking it?
questions.explanation: This idea comes from the 'Memphite Theology', carved on the Shabaka Stone. The Greeks matched Ptah with their smith god Hephaestus, and the sacred Apis bull of Memphis was his living form.
questions.hook: Ptah spoke the world into being from his heart.

questions.question: Which Egyptian air god stood on the earth and held up the sky goddess to separate heaven from earth?
questions.explanation: Shu and his sister Tefnut were the first children of Atum, and they were the parents of the earth god Geb and the sky goddess Nut. Shu is shown as a man with an ostrich feather on his head, kneeling beneath the arched body of Nut.
questions.hook: Shu is the cosmic prop holding sky and earth apart.

questions.question: In the Ramayana, which devoted servant of Rama carried a whole mountain of healing herbs to the wounded Lakshmana?
questions.explanation: Unable to tell which herb was the right one, Hanuman lifted the entire Himalayan peak and flew it to Lanka. He is the son of the wind god Vayu and is worshipped for strength and loyalty, especially on Tuesdays.
questions.hook: When in doubt about which herb, Hanuman just brings the mountain.

questions.question: In the Chinese novel Journey to the West, which disciple of the monk Xuanzang steals the peaches of immortality and fights with a magic staff?
questions.explanation: Sun Wukong is the Monkey King, born from a stone and able to do 72 transformations and somersault 108,000 li in one leap. The novel was written by Wu Cheng'en in the 16th century and is based on a real monk's pilgrimage to India.
questions.hook: Wukong is the Monkey King; Zhu Bajie is the pig, so the animals are easy to sort.

questions.question: Which Hindu goddess of learning and the arts is usually shown holding a veena, a stringed instrument?
questions.explanation: Saraswati is shown in white, seated on a lotus or riding a swan, and is the consort of Brahma. Students honour her on Vasant Panchami in spring, often placing their books and instruments before her image for blessing.
questions.hook: White sari, white swan, and a veena instead of a phone.

questions.question: Which bird is the vehicle of Kartikeya, the Hindu god of war and son of Shiva?
questions.explanation: Kartikeya, also called Murugan and Skanda, rides the peacock Paravani and carries a spear called the vel. He is especially venerated in Tamil Nadu and by Tamil communities overseas, including in Australia and Singapore.
questions.hook: The war god's ride is the showiest bird going.

questions.question: Which fierce Hindu goddess is shown with a garland of skulls and her tongue stuck out after battle?
questions.explanation: Kali sprang from Durga's brow in the fight with the demon Raktabija, whose spilled blood created new demons. She drank every drop to end the threat, then danced in such frenzy that Shiva lay down beneath her feet to calm her.
questions.hook: Kali danced so hard that her husband had to lie down under her feet.

questions.question: Which avatar of Vishnu appeared as half man and half lion to kill a king who could not be slain by man or beast?
questions.explanation: King Hiranyakashipu had been granted a boon that he could die neither by day nor night, indoors nor outdoors. Narasimha killed him at dusk, on a threshold, across his lap, rescuing the king's devout son Prahlada.
questions.hook: Dusk, doorway, lap: Narasimha found the loopholes in every rule.

questions.question: In the Mahabharata, which great archer, secretly the eldest son of Kunti, fights for the Kauravas against his own brothers?
questions.explanation: Karna was born to Kunti and the sun god Surya before her marriage, and she abandoned him in a basket on a river. Raised by a charioteer, he became Arjuna's great rival and learned his true parentage only on the eve of the war.
questions.hook: Karna learned on the eve of war that his brothers were his family, and fought them anyway.

questions.question: In Hindu philosophy, which of the yoga paths is the way of loving devotion to a chosen deity?
questions.explanation: The Bhagavad Gita describes several paths to liberation, and bhakti is the one open to anyone regardless of learning. Devotional singing, called kirtan, and the poet-saints of medieval India helped spread it across the subcontinent.
questions.hook: Bhakti is the heart path; jnana is the head path.

questions.question: Where, in a deer park near Varanasi, did the Buddha deliver his first sermon?
questions.explanation: There he spoke to five former companions, setting the wheel of dharma in motion and teaching the middle path. The Dhamek Stupa and the lion capital that is now India's national emblem both come from Sarnath.
questions.hook: Bodh Gaya is where he woke up; Sarnath is where he first spoke.

questions.question: What is the name for the paradoxical riddle, such as the sound of one hand clapping, that Zen teachers set students?
questions.explanation: Zen students meditate on a koan to move past ordinary logic. The tradition is most associated with the Rinzai school, and the riddle's purpose is a sudden insight rather than a clever answer.
questions.hook: A koan has no neat answer, only a better question.

questions.question: Which legendary figure is traditionally said to have founded the first Korean kingdom, Gojoseon, in 2333 BCE?
questions.explanation: According to the myth, Dangun's mother was a bear who became a woman after eating only mugwort and garlic in a cave. His father was Hwanung, a son of the sky god, and South Korea's National Foundation Day on 3 October recalls the legend.
questions.hook: A bear who ate garlic became a mother, and her son founded Korea.

questions.question: The Kumbh Mela rotates between Haridwar, Ujjain, Nashik and which city at the meeting of the Ganges and Yamuna?
questions.explanation: The four sites are where drops of the nectar of immortality fell during a battle between gods and demons. Prayagraj, once called Allahabad, hosts the largest gatherings; the 2025 Maha Kumbh there drew hundreds of millions of visitors.
questions.hook: Four drops of nectar fell, so four cities take turns.

questions.question: In the Book of Genesis, what was the name of the paradise garden where Adam and Eve first lived?
questions.explanation: Genesis places Eden somewhere in the east, watered by a river that split into four, and names the Tree of Life and the Tree of Knowledge among its trees. Gethsemane, by contrast, is the olive garden where Jesus prayed before his arrest.
questions.hook: Eden is the garden they lost; Gethsemane is the one where Jesus prayed.

questions.question: Which of Adam and Eve's sons killed his brother Abel?
questions.explanation: Cain, a farmer, killed his shepherd brother Abel out of jealousy when God favoured Abel's offering. He was marked and sent to wander, and Eve later bore a third son, Seth, from whom Noah descends in the Genesis genealogy.
questions.hook: Cain and Abel: the first murder, and the first fight over a gift.

questions.question: According to Genesis, which bird did Noah send out from the ark that came back with an olive leaf?
questions.explanation: Noah first released a raven, which flew back and forth until the waters dried, then sent a dove. Its second return with a freshly plucked olive leaf told him the flood was receding, which is why the dove with an olive branch became a symbol of peace.
questions.hook: Raven first, dove second: the olive leaf is the first good news after the flood.

questions.question: What weapon did the young David use to bring down the giant Goliath?
questions.explanation: David refused King Saul's armour and sword, choosing five smooth stones from a brook and his shepherd's sling. One stone struck Goliath on the forehead, and David then used the giant's own sword to cut off his head.
questions.hook: Five stones in the bag, one in the forehead: David fought as a shepherd, not a soldier.

questions.question: In the Book of Judges, what did Delilah have cut from Samson's head to rob him of his strength?
questions.explanation: Samson was a Nazirite, vowed from birth never to cut his hair, and his strength lay in that vow. After Delilah had his seven locks shaved, the Philistines blinded him and set him to grind grain, until his hair grew back and he pulled down their temple.
questions.hook: Seven locks, one razor: Samson's vow was the real source of his strength.

questions.question: Which of the seven deadly sins is traditionally defined as laziness or idleness?
questions.explanation: The Church's list of seven runs: pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, wrath and sloth. Sloth began as the monks' 'acedia', a spiritual listlessness and neglect of duty, before it came to mean plain laziness.
questions.hook: Sloth is the sin that does nothing, and the animal that does almost nothing.

questions.question: According to the Gospel of Matthew, which gifts did the Magi bring to the infant Jesus?
questions.explanation: Matthew never says how many Magi there were; the tradition of three comes from counting the gifts. Gold was read as a sign of kingship, frankincense of divinity and myrrh, an embalming resin, of death.
questions.hook: Three gifts, not three men: king, God and burial in one gift basket.

questions.question: Which apostle denied knowing Jesus three times on the night of his arrest, before the cock crowed?
questions.explanation: Jesus had predicted the denial at the Last Supper, and Peter wept bitterly when the cock crowed. After the resurrection, Jesus asked him three times whether he loved him, and the Catholic Church counts Peter as the first pope.
questions.hook: Three denials, three questions: Jesus gave Peter one chance for each.

questions.question: In the Book of Revelation, what colour is the horse ridden by the horseman who is given power to take peace from the earth?
questions.explanation: The four horsemen of the Apocalypse ride in order of conquest on a white horse, war on a red one, famine on a black one with a pair of scales, and death on a pale horse. Red stands for the bloodshed of war.
questions.hook: White conquers, red fights, black starves, pale kills: the colours run from bad to worst.

questions.question: What is the name of the ritual meal and service held at home on the first night of Passover?
questions.explanation: Seder means 'order', and the service follows a fixed sequence told in the Haggadah, with matzah, bitter herbs, four cups of wine and a retelling of the exodus. Children traditionally ask the Four Questions, beginning with why this night differs from all other nights.
questions.hook: Seder means order: a meal where the order of service is the point.

questions.question: What is the name of the meal Muslims eat before dawn to prepare for the day's fast during Ramadan?
questions.explanation: Suhoor is eaten before the dawn prayer, and the fast is then broken at sunset with iftar, often beginning with dates. Eidi is the gift of money given to children at Eid, and sadaqah is voluntary charity.
questions.hook: Suhoor is the pre-dawn meal; iftar is the sunset one.

questions.question: Whom do Shia Muslims regard as Muhammad's rightful immediate successor, being his cousin and son-in-law?
questions.explanation: Sunnis accept Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali as the first four 'rightly guided' caliphs, in that order. Shia hold that Muhammad appointed Ali, husband of his daughter Fatima, and name him the first Imam, a split dating from 632 CE.
questions.hook: Shia means 'party of Ali': the name is the argument.

questions.question: In which city is the Prophet's Mosque, which houses the tomb of Muhammad?
questions.explanation: Muhammad built the mosque after his move to Medina in 622, and he was buried beside it in 632. It is the second holiest site in Islam after the Great Mosque of Mecca, and its green dome marks his tomb.
questions.hook: Mecca is where he was born; Medina is where he is buried.

questions.question: The Talmud is made up of the Mishnah and which later body of commentary?
questions.explanation: The Mishnah is the written record of Jewish oral law, compiled around 200 CE, and the Gemara is the rabbis' discussion of it. Two versions exist, the Jerusalem Talmud and the longer, more authoritative Babylonian Talmud.
questions.hook: Mishnah is the rule, Gemara is the argument about the rule.

questions.question: In Genesis, the Tower of Babel was built on a plain in which land?
questions.explanation: Shinar is generally identified with Babylonia, in southern Mesopotamia. God scattered the builders and confused their single language into many, the biblical explanation for why people speak different tongues.
questions.hook: Shinar is the Bible's name for Babylonia: the tower rose where Mesopotamia's ziggurats did.

questions.question: According to the Book of Esther, what was Esther's Hebrew name?
questions.explanation: Hadassah means myrtle, and the name Esther was used when she became the Persian king's queen. Her cousin Mordecai urged her to speak to the king against Haman's plot to destroy the Jews, an event celebrated at Purim.
questions.hook: Hadassah is the Jewish girl; Esther is the Persian queen.

questions.question: Which wealthy landowner of Bethlehem married Ruth the Moabite in the Old Testament?
questions.explanation: Ruth followed her widowed mother-in-law Naomi to Bethlehem and gleaned grain in Boaz's fields. Their son Obed was the grandfather of King David, which puts a Moabite woman in the ancestry of David and of Jesus.
questions.hook: Ruth gleaned in Boaz's field and ended up in David's family tree.

questions.question: Which Abbasid caliph founded the city of Baghdad in 762?
questions.explanation: Al-Mansur built the Round City on the Tigris as his capital, and Baghdad later became a centre of learning. His grandson Harun al-Rashid and great-grandson Al-Ma'mun, who patronised the House of Wisdom, are tied to its golden age.
questions.hook: Mansur laid the round city; Harun and Ma'mun made it famous.

questions.question: Which fearsome creature of Aboriginal tradition was said to haunt swamps and waterholes, and was reported by many early colonists?
questions.explanation: The word is usually traced to the Wemba-Wemba language of Victoria. Colonists in the 1800s reported bunyip sightings and even displayed supposed skulls, and the word later became Australian slang for a fake or impostor.
questions.hook: If it lives in the billabong and bellows at night, blame the bunyip.

questions.question: What word describes the animal, plant or natural feature that an Aboriginal person or clan has a spiritual bond with and a duty to protect?
questions.explanation: A totem links a person or group to an ancestral being and to a part of Country. Totems carry responsibilities, such as caring for the species or place, and often come with rules about whether it may be hunted or eaten.
questions.hook: Your totem is the kin you look after, and it looks after you.

questions.question: Which Maori god rules the ocean and everything that lives in it?
questions.explanation: Tangaroa is one of the children of Ranginui and Papatuanuku, the sky father and earth mother. His name is a cousin of the Hawaiian Kanaloa and the Samoan Tagaloa, a sign of how widely Pacific stories travelled.
questions.hook: Tangaroa, tides and tuna: the sea belongs to him.

questions.question: In the 2021 Census, which answer to the religion question was given by the most Australians, at about 39 per cent?
questions.explanation: No religion has been the most common answer since 2016, when it passed Catholic for the first time, at around 30 per cent against about 23 per cent for Catholic. By 2021 it had risen to about 39 per cent, while Catholic had fallen to about 20 per cent.
questions.hook: The most common answer to the religion question is no religion.

questions.question: Which creator spirit of the Kulin nations, around Melbourne, takes the form of a wedge-tailed eagle?
questions.explanation: Bunjil is said to have created the first people and given the law. His companion and rival Waa, the crow, appears in many of the same stories, and the pair reflect the two moieties of the Kulin people.
questions.hook: Eagle Bunjil makes and Crow Waa makes trouble.

questions.question: Which legendary Polynesian navigator is traditionally credited with first discovering Aotearoa after sailing from Hawaiki?
questions.explanation: Kupe is said to have chased a giant octopus across the Pacific and found Aotearoa. Many iwi trace their canoe ancestry to the later voyages from Hawaiki.
questions.hook: Kupe chased an octopus and found a country.

questions.question: The mysterious Min Min Light, seen over outback plains, is most associated with roads near which Queensland town?
questions.explanation: The glowing lights are reported to follow or approach travellers at night, and sightings were recorded by both Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal people. The name comes from the former Min Min Hotel near Boulia, and one theory blames a mirage, though the case remains unsettled.
questions.hook: Boulia: the town at the end of the light.

questions.question: In which English forest did Robin Hood and his Merry Men supposedly hide from the Sheriff of Nottingham?
questions.explanation: Sherwood Forest in Nottinghamshire was a royal hunting forest, and the earliest Robin Hood ballads from the 15th century place him there. The Major Oak, a vast ancient tree, is nicknamed his hideout, though that tale is a later invention.
questions.hook: Sherwood sits right beside Nottingham, so the sheriff's patrols never had far to go.

questions.question: According to legend, which creatures did St Patrick drive out of Ireland?
questions.explanation: The story first appears centuries after Patrick's death. Ireland probably never had snakes at all: it was cut off from Britain by rising seas after the last Ice Age, before snakes could cross. Many scholars read the tale as a symbol of banishing paganism.
questions.hook: Ireland had no snakes to begin with: the ice age and the sea did Patrick's work.

questions.question: In Irish legend, Fionn mac Cumhaill gained all knowledge by sucking which part of his body after burning it on a cooking salmon?
questions.explanation: The poet Finnegas spent years trying to catch the Salmon of Knowledge, but young Fionn, his servant, was the one who burned his thumb while cooking it. Whenever Fionn needed wisdom afterwards, he put his thumb in his mouth.
questions.hook: Thumb in mouth, answer in head: the cheapest oracle in Ireland.

questions.question: Which Gaelic festival on 1 May marks the start of summer, traditionally celebrated with bonfires?
questions.explanation: Herds were driven between two fires to protect them before being moved to summer pasture. Beltane sits opposite Samhain on the old Celtic calendar and is still celebrated, notably with a large fire festival on Calton Hill in Edinburgh.
questions.hook: Beltane means 'bright fire': cattle walk between the flames for luck.

questions.question: Which Irish goddess, later Christianised as a saint, is honoured on 1 February at the festival of Imbolc?
questions.explanation: Brigid was linked with poetry, healing and smithcraft, and St Brigid of Kildare later took on many of her traditions. A rush cross woven for her feast day still hangs in many Irish homes.
questions.hook: Brigid's cross of woven rushes keeps the house safe all year.

questions.question: The legendary siren Lorelei is said to lure sailors to their deaths from a cliff above which European river?
questions.explanation: The Lorelei rock stands at a narrow, dangerous bend of the Rhine near St Goarshausen. The legend was largely shaped by the poet Clemens Brentano and made famous by Heinrich Heine's poem, which was set to music and became a German folk song.
questions.hook: The Lorelei is a poet's invention, not an ancient myth.

questions.question: Vlad the Impaler, an inspiration for Dracula, ruled which principality?
questions.explanation: Vlad III ruled Wallachia, in modern Romania, off and on in the 15th century and was known for impaling his enemies on stakes. His father, Vlad II, was called Dracul after the Order of the Dragon, which makes Dracula 'son of the dragon'.
questions.hook: Dracula means 'son of the dragon': a family name, not a vampire's.

questions.question: What was the name of the Irish hero Cú Chulainn in his childhood, before he took the name meaning 'hound of Culann'?
questions.explanation: As a boy Sétanta killed the great guard dog of the smith Culann, then offered to take its place until a replacement was raised. He became Cú Chulainn, 'Culann's hound', and went on to defend Ulster single-handed in the Táin Bó Cúailnge.
questions.hook: He killed the guard dog, so he became the guard dog.

questions.question: In Arthurian tradition, Morgan le Fay is the half-sister of Arthur, daughter of Igraine and which duke?
questions.explanation: Gorlois, Duke of Cornwall, was killed after Uther Pendragon magically took his form to sleep with Igraine, and Arthur was the result. Morgan's later part in the legend ranges from healer to enemy, depending on the author.
questions.hook: Same mother as Arthur, but a different father and a lot more grudge.

questions.question: In 1191 monks at which abbey claimed to have discovered the grave of King Arthur?
questions.explanation: The monks announced they had dug up a tomb with a lead cross bearing Arthur's name, a convenient find after a fire had wrecked the abbey. Glastonbury was soon identified with the legendary island of Avalon, though it is not now an island.
questions.hook: A burned abbey needed pilgrims, and then they found a king.

questions.question: In which country was St Patrick, patron saint of Ireland, actually born?
questions.explanation: Patrick was born in Roman Britain, the son of a Christian deacon. At about 16 he was seized by Irish raiders and enslaved as a shepherd, escaped after six years, and later chose to return as a missionary.
questions.hook: Ireland's patron saint arrived there as a slave and returned as a bishop.

questions.question: Which colossal tentacled sea monster of Scandinavian legend was said to drag whole ships beneath the waves?
questions.explanation: Bishop Erik Pontoppidan of Bergen described the Kraken in 1752 as a creature the size of an island, and sightings of giant squid probably inspired it. Tennyson wrote a poem about it in 1830, and Leviathan is the sea monster of the Hebrew Bible instead.
questions.hook: Kraken: the Norwegian word for the monster that looks like a floating island.

questions.question: Which fictional Himalayan paradise appears in James Hilton's 1933 novel Lost Horizon?
questions.explanation: Hilton's hidden lamasery, where people barely age, was so influential that US President Franklin Roosevelt named his presidential retreat Shangri-La; it is now called Camp David. The word has since become a general term for an earthly paradise.
questions.hook: Shangri-La: the Himalayan hideaway where nobody ages.

questions.question: Which mythical animal is the national animal of Scotland?
questions.explanation: Scottish kings used the unicorn in their royal arms for centuries, valuing its image as a fierce creature that could not be tamed. When James VI of Scotland also became James I of England in 1603, the Scottish unicorn was made a supporter of the royal arms, taking the place of the Tudor dragon.
questions.hook: Scotland picked a beast nobody could capture, which suits the national mood.

questions.question: Which trickster spider is the hero of folktales told across West Africa and the Caribbean?
questions.explanation: Anansi stories began with the Akan people of Ghana, and enslaved Africans carried them to Jamaica and the wider Caribbean, where the spider became a symbol of cunning against stronger opponents. Anansi is said to have won all the world's stories from the sky god and given them to humankind.
questions.hook: Anansi, the spider who outwits bigger foes and owns every story.

questions.question: Which Greek goddess of victory gives her name to a famous sportswear brand?
questions.explanation: The company began in 1964 as Blue Ribbon Sports and was renamed Nike in 1971. The winged goddess was often shown crowning athletes, and the Winged Victory of Samothrace in the Louvre is her most famous statue. The brand's swoosh suggests a wing.
questions.hook: Nike's swoosh is the goddess of victory's wing.

questions.question: Which Aztec ruler welcomed Hernán Cortés into the capital in November 1519?
questions.explanation: Moctezuma II was held captive by the Spaniards and died in 1520, in circumstances still disputed. Cuauhtémoc was the last Aztec ruler, who surrendered in 1521. Atahualpa was the Inca emperor Pizarro captured in 1532, and Ahuitzotl was Moctezuma's uncle and predecessor.
questions.hook: Moctezuma met Cortés; Cuauhtémoc made the last stand.

questions.question: Which Inca god of the sun was considered the divine ancestor of the Sapa Inca?
questions.explanation: The Sapa Inca, or "unique emperor", was believed to be Inti's son. Cusco's Coricancha, the Temple of the Sun, was covered in gold sheets. Mama Quilla was the moon goddess and Illapa the god of thunder and weather.
questions.hook: Inti is the sun, and the emperor was his son.

questions.question: Which Maya creator god, usually shown as a toothless old man, was the patron of writing and learning?
questions.explanation: Itzamna was said to have invented writing and books and was often depicted with scribes. Chaac was the god of rain, Ah Puch was a god of death, and Ek Chuah was the patron of merchants and cacao.
questions.hook: Itzamna is the old scribe at the dawn of Maya writing.

questions.question: Which Inca creator god was said to have risen from Lake Titicaca and made the sun, moon and stars?
questions.explanation: In the myth Viracocha first made a dark world and a race of giants, then destroyed them with a flood and made people from stone. The Spanish reported that he walked off west across the Pacific, promising to return, so some early chroniclers linked him to the Spaniards.
questions.hook: Viracocha: out of the lake, shaped the sky, walked off over the waves.

questions.question: In Yoruba religion, which orisha of thunder and lightning wields a double-headed axe?
questions.explanation: Shango was said to be a king of the Yoruba city of Oyo who became a god. His cult travelled with enslaved Yoruba to Cuba, Brazil and Trinidad, where he is identified with Saint Barbara. Ogun is the orisha of iron and war, and Yemoja a mother of waters.
questions.hook: Shango is the Yoruba Thor with a double axe.

questions.question: In Haida tradition, from what did the trickster Raven coax the first humans on a beach?
questions.explanation: The Haida of Haida Gwaii, off the British Columbia coast, tell how Raven found timid creatures inside a giant clamshell and talked them out. Bill Reid's sculpture of this scene, The Raven and the First Men, is displayed at the University of British Columbia's Museum of Anthropology.
questions.hook: Raven talked the first people out of a clamshell.

questions.question: Which cannibalistic spirit of Algonquian folklore embodies winter, famine and greed?
questions.explanation: Cree, Ojibwe and other Algonquian peoples told of the Wendigo as a warning against greed and selfishness in hard winters. The Skinwalker is a Navajo figure, Mishipeshu an underwater panther of the Great Lakes, and the Pukwudgie a small trickster of Wampanoag stories.
questions.hook: The Wendigo is winter hunger turned into a monster.

questions.question: Which spirit beings, impersonated by masked dancers and represented by carved cottonwood dolls, are central to Hopi religion?
questions.explanation: Kachinas are believed to live in the San Francisco Peaks in Arizona for half the year and visit the Hopi villages in the other half to bring rain. The carved dolls are given to children to teach them about the spirits. The Yei are Navajo holy people, and Manitou is an Algonquian term for a spirit force.
questions.hook: Kachinas: masked dancers who bring the rain.

questions.question: Which trophy do Australia and England contest in Test cricket?
