questions.explanation: The name comes from a mock obituary in London's Sporting Times after Australia won at The Oval in 1882, saying English cricket had died and its ashes would go to Australia. The tiny urn itself stays at Lord's, and Australia won the 2025-26 series at home 4-1.
questions.hook: A joke death notice in a newspaper created cricket's oldest rivalry.

questions.question: Which country has won the most FIFA men's World Cups?
questions.explanation: Brazil has five titles (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002), Germany and Italy four each and Argentina three. Brazil is the only nation to have played at every tournament, and Spain won the 2026 final 1-0 over Argentina for its second title.
questions.hook: Five stars on the yellow shirt, one for each title.

questions.question: In tennis, what term describes a score of zero?
questions.explanation: A popular theory links it to the French l'oeuf, 'the egg', for the shape of a zero, though some historians prefer 'playing for love' (for nothing). Cricket's equivalent, a duck, also comes from an egg.
questions.hook: Tennis has an egg and cricket has a duck's egg: both zeros are egg-shaped.

questions.question: Which sport is played at Wimbledon?
questions.explanation: The All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club began as a croquet club and added tennis in 1875, holding the first championships in 1877. It is the only grand slam still played on grass and keeps a strict all-white dress code.
questions.hook: The club was a croquet club first, which is why croquet is still in its name.

questions.question: Which rugby league series is contested each year between New South Wales and Queensland?
questions.explanation: It began in 1980 because Queensland-born stars playing in Sydney had been lining up against their home state. Players are picked for the state where they first played senior football, and the winning side holds the Origin Shield.
questions.hook: You play for where you started, not where you live: that is the whole 'origin' idea.

questions.question: Which country invented the modern game of cricket?
questions.explanation: It grew up in south-east England by the sixteenth century, and the Marylebone Cricket Club, founded in 1787, still writes the Laws of Cricket at Lord's. The first international match, though, was the USA v Canada in 1844.
questions.hook: The laws of cricket have lived at Lord's since 1788.

questions.question: What is a score of three under par on a single golf hole called?
questions.explanation: One under is a birdie, two under an eagle and four under a condor, which has been recorded only a handful of times. Americans often call the albatross a 'double eagle'.
questions.hook: Birdie, eagle, albatross, condor: the bird gets bigger as the score gets lower.

questions.question: In cricket, what is a score of zero by a batsman called?
questions.explanation: The name comes from 'duck's egg', for the round shape of a zero. Out first ball faced is a golden duck, and out without facing a ball at all (usually run out) is a diamond duck.
questions.hook: Golden duck: first ball. Diamond duck: no ball faced at all.

questions.question: What piece of equipment is used to hit the ball in badminton?
questions.explanation: Badminton, tennis and squash use racquets, table tennis uses a bat (Americans say paddle), and croquet a mallet. A badminton smash has been clocked at over 500 km/h, the fastest projectile in any racquet sport.
questions.hook: The shuttlecock leaves the racquet faster than any other racquet-sport projectile.

questions.question: In which sport would you perform a 'slam dunk'?
questions.explanation: US college basketball banned the dunk from 1967 to 1976, a rule widely believed to target the dominant Lew Alcindor, later Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. He became the NBA's all-time top scorer anyway, a record LeBron James broke in 2023.
questions.hook: College basketball banned it for nine years to slow down one player.

questions.question: Which Australian was known as the 'Rocket' in tennis?
questions.explanation: He is the only player to win the calendar-year grand slam twice, as an amateur in 1962 and as a professional in 1969. The Australian Open's main court is Rod Laver Arena, and the Laver Cup is named after him.
questions.hook: The only person to win all four slams in one year, twice.

questions.question: Which trophy do Australia and New Zealand contest in rugby union?
questions.explanation: It was donated by New Zealand Governor-General Lord Bledisloe and first contested in 1932. New Zealand has held it every year since 2003, and the Webb Ellis Cup is the Rugby World Cup trophy.
questions.hook: Australia last held it in 2002, the longest drought in the fixture's history.

questions.question: Which national league replaced Australia's half of the trans-Tasman ANZ Championship in 2017?
questions.explanation: When the ANZ Championship split, Australia started Super Netball and New Zealand the ANZ Premiership. The Constellation Cup is the annual Test series between the Diamonds and Silver Ferns, and Suncorp's naming rights ended after the 2026 season.
questions.hook: One trans-Tasman league became two in 2017: Super Netball here, ANZ Premiership there.

questions.question: Which professional boxing division has no upper weight limit?
questions.explanation: Cruiserweight tops out at 200 pounds (90.7 kg), and heavyweight is everyone above it. Amateur and Olympic boxing use 'super heavyweight' for the unlimited class instead.
questions.hook: Heavyweight is the only professional division with no ceiling.

questions.question: Which country won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930?
questions.explanation: Uruguay hosted and beat Argentina 4-2 in the final in Montevideo. The teams could not agree on a ball, so Argentina's was used in the first half and Uruguay's in the second.
questions.hook: They played the two halves with different balls because neither side would give way.

questions.question: Which country dominates the sport of table tennis at Olympic level?
questions.explanation: China has won the large majority of Olympic table tennis golds since the sport arrived in 1988, including all five at Paris 2024. Bigger 40mm balls and eleven-point games were partly aimed at making the sport less one-sided.
questions.hook: The rules have been changed several times to make it less one-sided, and China keeps winning.

questions.question: Which Australian city hosted the 1982 Commonwealth Games?
questions.explanation: Sydney hosted in 1938, Perth in 1962, Melbourne in 2006 and the Gold Coast in 2018. Brisbane's Games are remembered for Matilda, a giant winking mechanical kangaroo mascot.
questions.hook: The winking mechanical kangaroo is the most enduring thing about those Games.

questions.question: Which specialist player on an indoor volleyball team wears a different-coloured shirt and cannot attack the ball above net height?
questions.explanation: Six players are on court for each side indoors, while beach volleyball uses two per side. The libero is a defensive specialist who can replace any back-row player without a substitution being counted.
questions.hook: One of the six on court wears a different shirt: the libero.

questions.question: Which nation won the most medals at the 2020 Tokyo Paralympic Games?
questions.explanation: China has topped the Summer Paralympic medal table at every Games since Athens 2004, including Paris 2024. Australia won eighty medals in Tokyo, twenty-one of them gold, finishing eighth on the gold table.
questions.hook: China has topped the Paralympic table at every Games since Athens.

questions.question: Which shape was introduced at the centre bounce in Australian rules football in 1973?
questions.explanation: The diamond had forty-five metre sides and allowed only four players from each team inside at a bounce, to reduce congestion. It became the centre square in 1975, which grew to fifty metres in 2004.
questions.hook: Diamond first in 1973, square from 1975: the square everyone pictures came second.

questions.question: Which Australian city will host the 2032 Summer Olympics?
questions.explanation: It will be Australia's third Summer Games, after Melbourne 1956 and Sydney 2000. Brisbane was chosen in 2021 as the first host picked under the IOC's new process without a competing vote.
questions.hook: Melbourne 1956, Sydney 2000, Brisbane 2032: one every generation or so.

questions.question: Which sport does Australia's national women's team, the Diamonds, play?
questions.explanation: The Diamonds have won the Netball World Cup twelve times, the most of any nation. The Opals play basketball, the Hockeyroos hockey and the Aussie Spirit softball.
questions.hook: Diamonds netball, Opals basketball, Hockeyroos hockey: the gems and the roos.

questions.question: Which country won the 2026 FIFA men's World Cup?
questions.explanation: Spain beat defending champions Argentina 1-0 after extra time in New Jersey, with Ferran Torres scoring in the 106th minute. It was Spain's second title after 2010, and the first 48-team World Cup.
questions.hook: Spain 2010 and 2026: both finals won 1-0 in extra time.

questions.question: Which sport returns to the Olympics at Los Angeles 2028 for the first time since 1900?
questions.explanation: The only Olympic cricket match, in Paris in 1900, was won by Great Britain against a French team made up mostly of British expats. In LA it will be played as Twenty20, and lacrosse also returns for the first time since 1908.
questions.hook: One match in 1900, then a 128-year wait.

questions.question: Which nation won its first Women's Cricket World Cup in 2025, beating South Africa in the final?
questions.explanation: India won by fifty-two runs in Navi Mumbai. Shafali Verma was player of the match, and Deepti Sharma became the first bowler to take five wickets in a Women's World Cup final.
questions.hook: India's women won at home in 2025; the men won the T20 World Cup at home in 2026.

questions.question: Which city hosted the 2026 Commonwealth Games after Victoria withdrew as host?
questions.explanation: Victoria pulled out in 2023, citing costs, and Glasgow stepped in with a smaller program of ten sports. Australia topped the medal table with seventy golds and 171 medals.
questions.hook: Victoria pulled out, Glasgow stepped in, and Australia still won the most.

questions.question: Which team won the 2026 men's T20 World Cup, the first to win the title three times?
questions.explanation: India beat New Zealand by ninety-six runs in the final in Ahmedabad, after also winning in 2007 and 2024. It was the first time a team defended the title and the first time a host nation won it.
questions.hook: India won in 2007, 2024 and 2026: the first T20 champion to defend the title.

questions.question: Which nickname belongs to Australia's national men's rugby union team?
questions.explanation: The name dates back to the early 1900s, when Australian teams toured Britain. The 1908 Olympic rugby gold in London went to a combined Australasia side rather than the Wallabies alone. The Kangaroos is the national rugby league side, while the Waratahs and Brumbies are Super Rugby franchises.
questions.hook: Two marsupials, two codes: the Wallabies play union and the Kangaroos play league.

questions.question: In which sport do competitors use apparatus such as the pommel horse and the rings?
questions.explanation: Men's artistic gymnastics has six apparatus: floor, pommel horse, rings, vault, parallel bars and high bar. Women compete on four: vault, uneven bars, balance beam and floor.
questions.hook: Six apparatus for the men, four for the women.

questions.question: What colour is the centre of a standard archery target?
questions.explanation: The rings run outwards from gold through red, blue, black and white. A gold hit scores ten points, and the innermost part of the gold ring is used to break ties at some events.
questions.hook: Gold in the middle, white on the edge: the colours step outwards from the centre.

questions.question: Which nickname is used for Australia's national women's basketball team?
questions.explanation: The name nods to Australia's national gem. The Opals have won silver or bronze at several Olympics, including silver at Sydney 2000, and the men's team is the Boomers.
questions.hook: Opals for the women, Boomers for the men, and the Diamonds play netball.

questions.question: Which of the four competitive swimming strokes is the slowest?
questions.explanation: Butterfly split off from breaststroke in the early 1950s after swimmers began using an over-the-water arm recovery. Freestyle is the fastest because the front crawl is the most efficient of the four strokes, and nearly all swimmers choose it when they are free to pick any stroke.
questions.hook: Butterfly was born as a cheat in breaststroke, and breaststroke is still the slowest.

questions.question: Which AFL club plays its home games at Kardinia Park?
questions.explanation: Through sponsorship the ground has been called Shell Stadium, Baytec Stadium, Skilled Stadium, Simonds Stadium and GMHBA Stadium, the name it has carried since 2018. Geelong's home crowd is famously loud, and it has been one of the hardest venues for visiting teams.
questions.hook: Geelong's home ground has gone by at least five names.

questions.question: Which team beat the Matildas in the semi-final of the 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup?
questions.explanation: England won 3-1 at Stadium Australia in Sydney. The Matildas had reached the last four by beating France 7-6 on penalties, with Cortnee Vine scoring the winning kick.
questions.hook: The Matildas went out to England after a penalty shootout win over France.

questions.question: Which horse won the first Melbourne Cup in 1861?
questions.explanation: The 1861 field had 17 starters. A popular legend says Archer walked from Nowra to Melbourne, but the Australian Dictionary of Biography cites considerable evidence that he travelled by steamer. Carbine, Peter Pan and Poseidon all won the Cup later.
questions.hook: The first Cup winner has a popular legend about walking to the race.

questions.question: In which city were the equestrian events of the 1956 Melbourne Olympics held?
questions.explanation: Australia's strict quarantine rules for horses made it impractical to hold the equestrian events in Melbourne, so they were held in Stockholm months before the rest of the Games.
questions.hook: The horses were quarantined out of the Melbourne Games and went to Sweden.

questions.question: Which Big Bash League club is based in Tasmania?
questions.explanation: The Hurricanes were one of the eight founding clubs when the league began in 2011-12. They play most home games at Bellerive Oval in Hobart.
questions.hook: Hurricanes blow in from the island state.

questions.question: Which team was the last to beat Australia in a Test at the Gabba before India did in January 2021?
questions.explanation: The West Indies won there in 1988, starting a run of more than three decades without an Australian defeat at the ground. India chased 328 on the last day, with Rishabh Pant hitting the winning runs.
questions.hook: Thirty-two years between Brisbane losses.

questions.question: Which two colours make up the Richmond guernsey?
questions.explanation: The famous yellow jumper with a black sash is Richmond's guernsey, and the club entered the VFL in 1908.
questions.hook: Tigers wear the colours of a warning sign.

questions.question: Which footballer's name is given to the imaginary line separating AFL heartland from rugby league heartland?
questions.explanation: The Barassi Line runs roughly through New South Wales and Queensland, with rugby league dominant to the north and east. The line is named after Ron Barassi, the Melbourne legend.
questions.hook: Barassi's line splits the footy country from the league country.

questions.question: After which Aboriginal Fitzroy footballer and pastor is the AFL's Indigenous Round named?
questions.explanation: The Sir Doug Nicholls Round celebrates Indigenous contributions to football. Nicholls also became Governor of South Australia in 1976.
questions.hook: Footballer, pastor and governor: Sir Doug Nicholls.

questions.question: Which stadium in Perth has hosted West Coast and Fremantle home games since 2018?
questions.explanation: Optus Stadium in Burswood replaced Subiaco Oval as the home of both clubs when it opened in 2018.
questions.hook: Both Perth clubs swapped Subi for Burswood.

questions.question: Chris Judd won a Brownlow Medal at West Coast in 2004 and another at which club in 2010?
questions.explanation: Judd was one of the few to win the award with two clubs. He captained Carlton for years after leaving the Eagles, and he was a premiership player in 2006 with West Coast.
questions.hook: Judd won in the west, then again in navy blue.

questions.question: Which Geelong forward kicked nine goals in the 1989 Grand Final despite losing to Hawthorn by six points?
questions.explanation: Hawthorn won 21.18 (144) to 21.12 (138) in a brutal game. Gary Ablett Senior's son, Gary Junior, later also became a Geelong star.
questions.hook: Nine goals and still a loser: Ablett's bittersweet day.

questions.question: Which club beat Collingwood in the 1977 Grand Final replay after the first game was drawn?
questions.explanation: The first 1977 Grand Final ended in a draw. North Melbourne won the replay under Ron Barassi, giving the Kangaroos the second of their flags.
questions.hook: A drawn final, then a Roos win in the replay.

questions.question: By what team name is the New South Wales State of Origin side known?
questions.explanation: They wear sky blue jerseys and have worn them since the series began in 1980. Their northern rivals are known as the Maroons, the colour of the Queensland jersey.
questions.hook: Sky blue for the south, maroon for the north.

questions.question: Which nation won the first Rugby League World Cup, held in France in 1954?
questions.explanation: Great Britain beat the hosts 16-12 in the final in Paris. It was the first Rugby League World Cup, and the first rugby union World Cup did not take place until 1987, 33 years later.
questions.hook: The league world cup came 33 years before the union one.

questions.question: What is the nickname of Australia's women's national rugby union team?
questions.explanation: The name is a play on the men's Wallabies, since a wallaroo is a large kangaroo-like marsupial. The Jillaroos are the national women's rugby league side, and the Matildas and Opals play soccer and basketball.
questions.hook: A wallaroo is a bigger cousin of the wallaby.

questions.question: Which Pacific nation won the first Olympic gold medal in men's rugby sevens at Rio 2016?
questions.explanation: Fiji beat Great Britain 43-7 in the final, and it was the country's first Olympic medal of any kind. Rugby sevens returned to the Olympics in 2016 after rugby union's last appearance in 1924.
questions.hook: Fiji's first-ever Olympic medal was gold.

questions.question: Australia won the 1991 Rugby World Cup final in London against which opponent?
questions.explanation: The Wallabies won 12-6 in front of England's home crowd, with Nick Farr-Jones as captain. Their second title came in 1999, when they beat France in Cardiff.
questions.hook: 1991 beat England at their own ground; 1999 beat France in Cardiff.

questions.question: What does the T in the rugby abbreviation TMO stand for?
questions.explanation: The Television Match Official uses replays to help the referee decide whether a try was scored or whether foul play occurred.
questions.hook: The TMO watches the replays so the referee does not have to guess.

questions.question: Which Super Rugby club is based in Dunedin?
questions.explanation: The club plays at Forsyth Barr Stadium, the roofed ground known as the Glasshouse. The Highlanders won the Super Rugby title in 2015, beating the Hurricanes in the final.
questions.hook: Dunedin is the Scottish-flavoured city, and the Highlanders are its team.

questions.question: Which Auckland ground hosted the finals of both the 1987 and 2011 Rugby World Cups?
questions.explanation: The All Blacks won both finals there, beating France 29-9 in 1987 and then 8-7 in 2011. Eden Park is also a cricket ground and is the home of the Blues.
questions.hook: New Zealand's two cup wins on home turf came at the same ground.

questions.question: Which country made its Rugby Championship debut in 2012, joining Australia, New Zealand and South Africa?
questions.explanation: The tournament grew out of the Tri Nations, which began in 1996. Argentina was invited after finishing third at the 2007 Rugby World Cup in France, and the Pumas are its nickname.
questions.hook: Three became four when the Pumas joined in 2012.

questions.question: Which Brisbane ground in Herston has long been the home of Queensland rugby union?
questions.explanation: Ballymore is the long-standing home of Queensland rugby union, and it has hosted Wallabies Tests as well as Reds games.
questions.hook: Ballymore is Queensland rugby's old stomping ground.

questions.question: Which nation won its only men's World Cup in 1966 on home soil?
questions.explanation: England beat West Germany 4-2 after extra time at Wembley, with Geoff Hurst scoring the only hat-trick ever in a men's World Cup final, and have not won the trophy since.
questions.hook: Three lions, one trophy, 1966.

questions.question: Which colour of card means a player is sent off in soccer?
questions.explanation: A yellow card is only a caution, though two yellows in one match add up to a red. Cards were introduced at the 1970 World Cup after referee Ken Aston, stopped at traffic lights, came up with the idea.
questions.hook: Traffic lights inspired the cards: yellow for caution, red for stop.

questions.question: Which country won the 2018 men's World Cup in Russia, beating Croatia in the final?
questions.explanation: France won 4-2 in Moscow, with teenager Kylian Mbappe scoring in the final. It was their second title, 20 years after winning on home soil in 1998 under captain Didier Deschamps, who won it as coach in 2018.
questions.hook: Deschamps lifted it as captain in 1998 and coach in 2018.

questions.question: Which team beat the Matildas in the 2023 Women's World Cup third-place play-off in Brisbane?
questions.explanation: Sweden won 2-0 after the Matildas had lost their semi-final to England, leaving Australia fourth, their best World Cup result. The tournament was won by Spain, who beat England in the final.
questions.hook: Fourth place was the Matildas' best ever.

questions.question: In 1948, Ludwig Guttmann organised a sports competition for wounded veterans at which English hospital?
questions.explanation: The Stoke Mandeville Games opened on the same day as the London Olympics. They grew into the Paralympics, with the first official Games held in Rome in 1960.
questions.hook: A hospital in Buckinghamshire started the Paralympic movement.

questions.question: Borobi, the mascot of the Gold Coast 2018 Commonwealth Games, was which animal?
questions.explanation: The blue mascot's name is the Yugambeh word for koala, the language of the area's Aboriginal people. Australia topped the medal table on home soil, as it did in Melbourne in 2006.
questions.hook: A blue koala wore the Gold Coast's local Indigenous name.

questions.question: Which breed of dog was Waldi, the first official Olympic mascot, at Munich in 1972?
questions.explanation: Waldi was a colourful dachshund, chosen as a Bavarian favourite for being tough, agile and resilient. Official mascots have been a feature of every Games since.
questions.hook: Waldi the dachshund started the Olympic mascot tradition.

questions.question: Which Perth venue was the main stadium for the 1962 British Empire and Commonwealth Games?
questions.explanation: Built for the Games at Floreat, Perry Lakes Stadium was the main athletics venue for the 1962 event.
questions.hook: Perry Lakes, Perth's own 1962 Games arena.

questions.question: What colour belt does a beginner in karate usually wear when starting out?
questions.explanation: In most karate schools white is the first belt. Students then move through the coloured kyu grades before reaching the black belt and its dan ranks.
questions.hook: White is the blank page; black is the finished book.

questions.question: At which famous Sydney suburb does the 14 kilometre City2Surf fun run finish?
questions.explanation: The race starts at Hyde Park in the city each August and finishes at Bondi Beach. Runners climb Heartbreak Hill partway along the course before the long descent to the sea.
questions.hook: From the city to the sand, with Heartbreak Hill in between.

questions.question: Which Olympic wrestling style prohibits attacking an opponent's legs and holds below the waist?
questions.explanation: Freestyle allows leg attacks, while Greco-Roman is a pure upper-body contest. It has been on the Olympic programme since the first modern Games in Athens in 1896.
questions.hook: Greco-Roman: from the waist up only.

questions.question: Which Grand Slam tournament insists that players dress almost entirely in white?
questions.explanation: Wimbledon's all-white dress rule is a long-standing tradition, and it is still enforced, down to undergarments. The other three Grand Slams allow colour freely.
questions.hook: Wimbledon keeps its whites and nobody else bothers.

questions.question: What is the name for a tennis score of 40-40?
questions.explanation: From deuce, a player must win two points in a row to take the game. The first point after deuce gives the winner the advantage, and losing the next point sends the game back to deuce.
questions.hook: At deuce, one point is never enough.

questions.question: Which fruit, served with cream, is the classic snack of the Wimbledon crowd?
questions.explanation: Strawberries and cream have been part of the Wimbledon tradition since the early years of the championships, and the pairing is one of the event's best-known sights.
questions.hook: Strawberries and cream: the taste of an English summer.

questions.question: At which racecourse is the Melbourne Cup run each year?
questions.explanation: Flemington sits beside the Maribyrnong River, and the Victoria Racing Club has staged the Cup there since 1861. Caulfield hosts the Caulfield Cup, while Randwick and Rosehill are Sydney tracks.
questions.hook: Flemington: Cup Day's fashions, crowds and racing all sit beside the Maribyrnong River.

questions.question: Which two colours are the flags that mark the safe swimming area on a patrolled Australian beach?
questions.explanation: Lifesavers place the pair of flags so that swimmers can stay between them, where the surf is supervised and the rips are least likely. The same red and yellow colours appear on lifesaver caps.
questions.hook: Between the red and yellow flags is where the lifesavers are watching.

questions.question: Which famous Victorian surf beach hosts the long-running Rip Curl Pro?
questions.explanation: The contest has run there since 1961 and is the world's longest-running surfing competition. The winner receives a bell as a trophy, and the beach is near the Great Ocean Road.
questions.hook: The Bells Beach winner takes home an actual bell.

questions.question: On which Italian make of motorcycle did Casey Stoner win the 2007 MotoGP world championship?
questions.explanation: It was Ducati's first premier-class title. Stoner, from Queensland, later won again in 2011 on a Honda and retired from full-time racing in 2012 at the age of 27.
questions.hook: Queenslander Casey Stoner's title-winning 2007 season.

questions.question: Which nickname do Australia's national men's field hockey team carry?
questions.explanation: The Kookaburras won the men's Olympic gold medal in 2004. The women's national team is the Hockeyroos.
questions.hook: Kookaburras laugh last: the men's hockey side, with the Hockeyroos for the women.

questions.question: In hurling, what is the small ball called?
questions.explanation: The sliotar has a cork core and a leather cover, and players strike it with a stick called a camán, or hurley. A bodhrán is an Irish frame drum.
questions.hook: The sliotar is the ball, and the camán is the stick.

questions.question: In lawn bowls, what is the small white target ball called?
questions.explanation: The jack is rolled first, and players then try to get their bowls closest to it. The mat is where bowlers stand and the rink is the lane they bowl along.
questions.hook: Jack is the target; get your bowls nearest it.

questions.question: Which sport is named after the Gloucestershire country house of the Duke of Beaufort?
questions.explanation: A game with shuttlecocks reached England from India, where army officers played it as 'Poona', and it was popularised at Badminton House in the 1870s. The estate also lends its name to the famous Badminton Horse Trials.
questions.hook: A duke's house gave a shuttlecock its name.

questions.question: On which day of the week is Victoria's public holiday for the AFL Grand Final held?
questions.explanation: The holiday falls on the Friday before the Saturday Grand Final, so Victorian fans get a day off before the game.
questions.hook: Footy fans get Friday off, then the big game on Saturday.

questions.question: In which city is Bellerive Oval, Tasmania's main Test and Big Bash cricket ground?
questions.explanation: The ground sits on the Derwent's eastern shore, across the river from Hobart's city centre. Launceston's York Park, in the state's north, is the other main venue and hosts AFL games.
questions.hook: Across the Derwent from Hobart's centre, but still Hobart's ground.

questions.question: What colour is traditionally worn on day three of the Sydney Test to raise money for breast cancer care?
questions.explanation: The Pink Test began in 2009 as a tribute to Jane McGrath, wife of Glenn McGrath, who died of breast cancer in 2008. Money raised by the McGrath Foundation funds breast care nurses around Australia.
questions.hook: The SCG goes pink for Jane McGrath.

questions.question: Which Australian city hosted the 2018 Invictus Games, the sporting event for wounded service personnel?
questions.explanation: Prince Harry launched the Games after seeing the American Warrior Games. The first Games were held in London in 2014. The Sydney edition ran in October 2018 at the Olympic Park precinct, and the name comes from a poem by William Ernest Henley.
questions.hook: From a London start to Sydney, the unconquered compete.

questions.question: In which sport did Sweden's Oscar Swahn win a medal at the 1920 Antwerp Games aged 72, the oldest Olympic medallist in sporting events?
questions.explanation: He took silver in the team running deer, double-shot event, having won gold in the same event at the 1908 and 1912 Games. His son Alfred also won Olympic medals in shooting.
questions.hook: Seventy-two years old and still hitting a running target.

questions.question: Which band released the album Abbey Road in 1969?
questions.explanation: It was the last album the Beatles recorded together, although Let It Be was released after it in 1970. The zebra-crossing cover was shot in a few minutes outside EMI's studios in St John's Wood, which were later renamed Abbey Road Studios after the album.
questions.hook: The studio was named after the album, not the other way round.

questions.question: Which film won eleven Academy Awards, including Best Picture, at the 1998 ceremony?
questions.explanation: Its eleven Oscars from fourteen nominations equalled the record set by Ben-Hur, later matched by The Return of the King. Titanic was also the first film to gross a billion dollars worldwide.
questions.hook: Three films share eleven Oscars: Ben-Hur, Titanic and The Return of the King.

questions.question: Which Australian band was fronted by Michael Hutchence?
questions.explanation: Their 1987 album Kick sold millions and produced 'Need You Tonight' and 'Never Tear Us Apart'. After Hutchence died in 1997, the band chose a new singer, J.D. Fortune, through the 2005 reality show Rock Star: INXS.
questions.hook: They found their next frontman through a TV talent show.

questions.question: Which superhero is also known as the Caped Crusader?
questions.explanation: Created by Bob Kane and Bill Finger in 1939, he has no superpowers, only money, training and gadgets. Superman is the Man of Steel, and Batman's other nickname is the Dark Knight.
questions.hook: Caped Crusader and Dark Knight are Batman; Man of Steel is Superman.

questions.question: Which 1985 Nintendo game made a plumber and his brother household names?
questions.explanation: Mario had first appeared in the 1981 arcade game Donkey Kong as a carpenter called Jumpman. Super Mario Bros. sold about forty million copies, and The Super Mario Bros. Movie became one of 2023's biggest films.
questions.hook: He started as a carpenter called Jumpman.

questions.question: Which musical features the song 'Defying Gravity'?
questions.explanation: Based on Gregory Maguire's novel, it retells The Wizard of Oz from the Wicked Witch's side and opened on Broadway in 2003. The film version was split in two: Wicked (2024) and Wicked: For Good (2025), starring Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande.
questions.hook: It is The Wizard of Oz told by the witch, who turns out not to be wicked.

questions.question: Which Australian children's music group formed in Sydney in 1991?
questions.explanation: Anthony Field, Murray Cook and Greg Page met studying early childhood education at Macquarie University and teamed up with Jeff Fatt. They topped BRW's list of Australia's richest entertainers several years running, and Emma Watkins became the first female Wiggle in 2013.
questions.hook: Red, purple, yellow, blue: four shirts, one of the most profitable acts Australia has produced.

questions.question: Which film won the first Academy Award for Best Picture in 1929?
distractors: All Quiet on the Western Front
questions.explanation: A silent First World War flying film, Wings was the only silent Best Picture winner until The Artist in 2012. All Quiet on the Western Front won the following year.
questions.hook: The first Best Picture was silent, and the next silent one came 83 years later.

questions.question: Which musician wrote and performed 'Purple Rain'?
questions.explanation: The song and its 1984 film won Prince an Oscar for Best Original Song Score. He played most instruments on his records himself, and in 1993 he changed his name to an unpronounceable symbol during a fight with Warner Bros.
questions.hook: He became a symbol to escape his record contract.

questions.question: Which Australian comedy team drove a fake Canadian motorcade into the APEC security zone in Sydney in 2007?
questions.explanation: Chas Licciardello, dressed as Osama bin Laden, stepped out near the leaders' hotel before police noticed. The stunt was filmed for The Chaser's War on Everything on the ABC, and charges against the team were later dropped.
questions.hook: 'Bin Laden' got out of the car before anyone checked the passes.

questions.question: Which animation studio produced Toy Story?
questions.explanation: Toy Story (1995) was the first fully computer-animated feature. Steve Jobs bought Pixar's forerunner from George Lucas in 1986 for about ten million dollars and sold it to Disney in 2006 for about 7.4 billion.
questions.hook: Ten million from George Lucas, 7.4 billion from Disney.

questions.question: Which sitcom featured the characters Jerry, George, Elaine and Kramer?
questions.explanation: Created by Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David, it was called 'a show about nothing', and the writers' rule was 'no hugging, no learning'. George Costanza was based largely on Larry David himself.
questions.hook: No hugging, no learning.

questions.question: Which Australian film was nominated for the Best Foreign Language Film Oscar in 2017?
questions.explanation: Shot on the island of Tanna in Vanuatu with local villagers as the cast, it tells a true story of forbidden love. It is the only Australian film nominated in that category, and it did not win.
questions.hook: Australia's only nomination in the category was filmed in Vanuatu.

questions.question: Which record label rejected the Beatles in 1962, reportedly saying guitar groups were on the way out?
questions.explanation: Decca's Dick Rowe signed Brian Poole and the Tremeloes instead, a London band. George Martin then signed the Beatles to Parlophone, part of EMI.
questions.hook: Decca declined; Parlophone signed them.

questions.question: Which video game passed 350 million copies sold in 2025, the most of any single game?
questions.explanation: Released in 2011 by Swedish studio Mojang, which Microsoft bought for 2.5 billion US dollars in 2014, it passed 350 million sales in 2025. A Minecraft Movie took nearly a billion dollars that year. Tetris is sometimes given as the answer, but only by counting all its versions together.
questions.hook: Tetris wins only if you add up every version; Minecraft wins as one game.

questions.question: Which Beach Boys album did Paul McCartney name as the biggest influence on Sgt. Pepper?
questions.explanation: Brian Wilson made Pet Sounds (1966) partly in response to the Beatles' Rubber Soul, and McCartney answered it with Sgt. Pepper. McCartney called 'God Only Knows' one of the best songs ever written.
questions.hook: Rubber Soul led to Pet Sounds, which led to Sgt. Pepper.

questions.question: Which Seven Network drama about a Sydney hospital ward ran from 1998 to 2009?
questions.explanation: It began on Ward 17 of the fictional All Saints Western General Hospital and later moved to the emergency department. GP and MDA were ABC medical dramas, and The Flying Doctors was set in outback New South Wales.
questions.hook: Twelve years at All Saints, Ward 17.

questions.question: In which Western Australian city is AC/DC singer Bon Scott buried?
questions.explanation: Born in Scotland, Scott grew up in Fremantle, and his grave there was added to the state heritage register in 2006. A bronze statue of him stands at the Fremantle Fishing Boat Harbour.
questions.hook: The singer's grave is heritage-listed.

questions.question: Which country won its first Eurovision Song Contest in 2026 with DARA's 'Bangaranga'?
questions.explanation: The final was held in Vienna after Austria's JJ won in 2025 with 'Wasted Love'. Bulgaria won both the jury and public votes, by a margin of 173 points, the biggest in the contest's history.
questions.hook: Bangaranga brought Bulgaria its first win by a record margin.

questions.question: Which musician was born Reginald Kenneth Dwight?
questions.explanation: He took his stage name from two members of his early band Bluesology, saxophonist Elton Dean and singer Long John Baldry. He changed it legally in 1972.
questions.hook: His new name was borrowed from two bandmates.

questions.question: Which fictional African nation is ruled by King T'Challa in the Marvel films?
questions.explanation: Marvel's comics place Wakanda as a hidden, technologically advanced country powered by the metal vibranium. Zamunda is the African kingdom from Coming to America, and Latveria belongs to Doctor Doom.
questions.hook: Hidden kingdom, secret metal, and a famous crossed-arms salute.

questions.question: Who plays the cyborg assassin who says 'I'll be back' in the 1984 film The Terminator?
questions.explanation: Arnold Schwarzenegger plays the title cyborg, the role that made him a global action star. The line 'I'll be back' became one of the most quoted lines in film history.
questions.hook: A bodybuilder from Austria played the machine from the future.

questions.question: In The Matrix, which colour of pill does Neo swallow to find out the truth?
questions.explanation: Morpheus offers Neo a choice of two pills: the other one would let him wake up in his bed and believe whatever he liked. The red pill has since become internet slang for accepting an uncomfortable truth.
questions.hook: Red means the rabbit hole; blue means going back to sleep.

questions.question: What is the surname of Vin Diesel's character in The Fast and the Furious?
questions.explanation: The 2001 film began as a street-racing story based on a magazine article, and Dominic Toretto's talk of family became the franchise's catchphrase. O'Conner is the undercover cop played by Paul Walker, and Shaw and Hobbs are later characters.
questions.hook: Family is the one word that fuels every sequel.

questions.question: Which 2001 Ray Lawrence mystery, starring Anthony LaPaglia and Barbara Hershey, won the AFI Award for Best Film?
questions.explanation: Andrew Bovell adapted it from his own play Speaking in Tongues. Lantana is an invasive weed in Australia that tangles over and hides what lies beneath, a fitting image for the film's interlocking secrets.
questions.hook: Named after the weed that hides what's underneath.

questions.question: Which 2016 film stars Dev Patel as an adopted man who uses satellite maps to find his birth family in India?
questions.explanation: Based on Saroo Brierley's memoir A Long Way Home and directed by Garth Davis, it was nominated for six Oscars including Best Picture. The title comes from Saroo's real birth name, Sheru, which means lion.
questions.hook: His birth name meant the film's title.

questions.question: Which 2009 stop-motion clay feature by Adam Elliot follows a lonely Melbourne girl and her New York pen pal?
questions.explanation: Toni Collette voices Mary and Philip Seymour Hoffman voices Max, who has Asperger's syndrome. Elliot had already won the Oscar for the animated short Harvie Krumpet in 2004.
questions.hook: Letters between Mount Waverley and New York, in clay.

questions.question: In the children's series Round the Twist, what unusual building does the Twist family move into?
questions.explanation: The series was based on Paul Jennings' short stories and was made in Australia from 1990. The family's odd happenings include a ghost sailor, a toilet that swallows people and the lighthouse's own spooky history.
questions.hook: The Twists lived in a beacon by the sea.

questions.question: The Logie awards, Australia's TV Week prizes, are named after which early television pioneer?
questions.explanation: The awards began in 1959 and the top prize, the Gold Logie, was added the following year. The awards are named after John Logie Baird, a Scot who gave the first public demonstration of a working television system in London in 1926.
questions.hook: The statuette honours the man who first showed television publicly.

questions.question: Which producer created Prisoner, Sons and Daughters and Neighbours?
questions.explanation: Watson had created the British soap Crossroads in 1964 before creating these Australian shows. Reg Grundy's company produced several of them, but the creative origins were Watson's.
questions.hook: One writer behind three of Australia's biggest long-runners.

questions.question: In which English city is the gangster drama Peaky Blinders set?
questions.explanation: The series follows the Shelby family in the Small Heath district after the First World War. The real Peaky Blinders were a street gang in Birmingham in the late 19th and early 20th century, though the show's version of them is heavily fictionalised, and Cillian Murphy stars as Tommy Shelby.
questions.hook: Flat caps, razor blades and a gang that rules the backstreets.

questions.question: Which dim-witted servant in Blackadder is famous for announcing that he has a 'cunning plan'?
questions.explanation: Tony Robinson played Baldrick through all four series, each set in a different era from the Middle Ages to the First World War. His plans were almost always disastrous, and the last series ended with the characters going over the top in the trenches.
questions.hook: The plan was cunning only in his own mind.

questions.question: Which long-running NBC sitcom, set in a Boston bar, gave rise to the spin-off Frasier?
questions.explanation: Kelsey Grammer first played psychiatrist Frasier Crane as a recurring character in Cheers, then took him to Seattle for Frasier in 1993. The theme song, 'Where Everybody Knows Your Name', is as famous as the show itself.
questions.hook: Where everybody knows your name, and where Frasier began.

questions.question: In which Berkshire town is the paper company of the original UK version of The Office located?
questions.explanation: Wernham Hogg's Slough branch was home to David Brent, played by co-creator Ricky Gervais. The series ran for only twelve episodes plus a Christmas special in 2001 to 2003, yet it was remade in more than a dozen countries.
questions.hook: Brent's corner of the world was a Thames Valley trading estate.

questions.question: Which network rescued Brooklyn Nine-Nine after Fox cancelled it in May 2018?
questions.explanation: Fans ran a strong social media campaign after the cancellation. NBC's rescue led to three more seasons after Fox's five, taking the cop comedy to a total of eight seasons.
questions.hook: Cancelled by Fox, rescued by a rival network.

questions.question: On which Swedish reality format was the American show Survivor based?
questions.explanation: Expedition Robinson first aired in Sweden in 1997 and was created by Charlie Parsons, who later brought the idea to Mark Burnett. The US version launched on CBS in 2000 and was won by Richard Hatch.
questions.hook: Survivor's format came from a Swedish show named after a famous castaway.

questions.question: Which singer had a 1984 hit with 'Like a Virgin'?
questions.explanation: She performed it in a wedding dress at the first MTV Video Music Awards in 1984, famously rolling across the stage. The song was written by Billy Steinberg and Tom Kelly, not by Madonna herself.
questions.hook: A wedding dress, a stage floor and a pop career.

questions.question: What was George Michael's surname at birth?
questions.explanation: He was born Georgios Kyriacos Panayiotou in London to a Greek Cypriot father. He formed Wham! with school friend Andrew Ridgeley.
questions.hook: Greek Cypriot family name, hidden behind Wham!.

questions.question: Just Dance and Poker Face both appear on which 2008 debut album?
questions.explanation: The album made Lady Gaga a global star and was followed in 2009 by an extended edition called The Fame Monster. Both singles reached number one in the US.
questions.hook: Her first album, then the Monster follow-up.

questions.question: What colour was the cover of Charli XCX's 2024 album Brat, which gave rise to a summer-long trend?
questions.explanation: The plain lime-green cover with lowercase text became a viral meme and a social media aesthetic. Politicians and brands even adopted the colour during 2024.
questions.hook: Slime-green, low-fi, and it took over the summer.

questions.question: Which country did Conchita Wurst represent when she won Eurovision in 2014 with Rise Like a Phoenix?
questions.explanation: Conchita was the drag persona of singer Tom Neuwirth, whose bearded look made headlines. The contest in Copenhagen was Austria's first win since 1966.
questions.hook: Bearded diva ends a 48-year drought.

questions.question: Cardi B's 2017 hit Bodak Yellow was the first Hot 100 number one for a solo female rapper since which artist's 1998 hit Doo Wop (That Thing)?
questions.explanation: Cardi B became only the second solo woman rapper to top the chart. Hill's song came from her album The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill.
questions.hook: Nineteen years between solo women rap number ones.

questions.question: Which Brisbane band, built around songwriters Robert Forster and Grant McLennan, recorded 'Cattle and Cane'?
questions.explanation: McLennan died in 2006, and a Brisbane bridge opened in 2010 was named the Go Between Bridge in honour of the band. The Triffids were from Perth and the Saints from Brisbane too, but neither wrote the song.
questions.hook: A Brisbane bridge carries their name.

questions.question: Which keyboard player wrote most of Cold Chisel's songs, including 'Flame Trees'?
questions.explanation: Cold Chisel formed in Adelaide in the 1970s. Walker later led the band Tex, Don and Charlie and is the band's main songwriter.
questions.hook: The quiet keyboard player behind the pub-rock anthems.

questions.question: Which band, led by Iva Davies and originally called Flowers, recorded 'Great Southern Land'?
questions.explanation: Flowers changed its name to Icehouse, and Iva Davies led the band through its best-known hits.
questions.hook: The band that was once Flowers.

questions.question: Which yellow electric mouse is the loyal companion of Ash Ketchum in the Pokémon anime?
questions.explanation: Pikachu was never the original mascot plan, as early marketing focused on Clefairy, but the anime's star turned it into the face of the franchise. It is Pokémon number 25 in the original Pokédex.
questions.hook: Number 25 in the Pokédex took over from Clefairy as the face of Pokémon.

questions.question: In Nintendo's Zelda series, what is the name of the green-clad hero the player controls?
questions.explanation: Despite the title, the playable hero is not Princess Zelda. Link is usually silent.
questions.hook: The game is named after the princess, but you play the one who isn't her.

questions.question: Under what name was Sega's Mega Drive console sold in North America?
questions.explanation: Sega used the name Genesis there because it could not secure the Mega Drive trademark in the United States. The console launched in Japan in 1988 and competed hard with Nintendo's NES and Super Nintendo.
questions.hook: Same console, different continent, different name.

questions.question: Which songwriting duo wrote the scores for both Cabaret and Chicago?
questions.explanation: John Kander wrote the music and Fred Ebb the lyrics. Their partnership also produced 'New York, New York', which Liza Minnelli sang in the 1977 film before Frank Sinatra made it his own.
questions.hook: Willkommen and Welcome to Chicago, courtesy of the same pair.

questions.question: Which spirit is the base of a classic margarita?
questions.explanation: A margarita is tequila, orange liqueur such as Cointreau or triple sec, and lime juice, usually served with a salted rim. By law tequila must be made from blue agave, mostly in the Mexican state of Jalisco.
questions.hook: Salt on the rim, agave in the glass.

questions.question: Feta cheese is protected as a traditional product of which country?
questions.explanation: Since 2002 only brined cheese made in Greece from sheep's milk, with up to 30% goat's milk, can be sold as feta in the EU. Cow's-milk versions elsewhere must use another name.
questions.hook: Real feta is Greek, and made from sheep and goat, never cow.

questions.question: Which meringue dessert is named after a Russian ballerina who toured Australia and New Zealand in the 1920s?
questions.explanation: Anna Pavlova toured both countries in 1926, and each still claims the dessert, with Perth chef Herbert Sachse's 1935 version the best-known Australian claim. Peach Melba, by contrast, honours an Australian opera singer, Nellie Melba.
questions.hook: The dancer got the meringue; the soprano got the peaches.

questions.question: What is the main ingredient of guacamole?
questions.explanation: The name comes from the Aztec Nahuatl word āhuacamōlli, meaning avocado sauce. Botanically, the avocado is a large berry with a single seed.
questions.hook: Guaca-mole is literally avocado-sauce in Nahuatl.

questions.question: Hummus is made mainly from which legume?
questions.explanation: Hummus is simply the Arabic word for chickpea; the full dish name means chickpeas with tahini, a sesame paste. Broad beans are the base of Egyptian ful medames.
questions.hook: Hummus means chickpea, so the name gives it away.

questions.question: Earl Grey tea is black tea flavoured with the oil of which citrus fruit?
questions.explanation: The blend is named after Charles Grey, the 2nd Earl Grey and British prime minister from 1830 to 1834. Most bergamot oil comes from Calabria, the toe of Italy.
questions.hook: Earl Grey is bergamot, and bergamot grows in Italy's toe.

questions.question: Which spirit is distilled from sugar cane juice or molasses?
questions.explanation: Rum was so central to early colonial New South Wales that it served as currency, and the 1808 Rum Rebellion saw Governor William Bligh deposed. Bundaberg Rum is distilled from Queensland molasses.
questions.hook: Sugar cane gives rum, and rum toppled Bligh.

questions.question: South Australia's Barossa Valley is most famous for which red grape?
questions.explanation: Because phylloxera never reached the Barossa, it still has shiraz vines planted in the 1840s, among the oldest producing vines in the world. Penfolds Grange is built mostly on Barossa-style shiraz.
questions.hook: Barossa is old-vine shiraz country, spared the vine louse.

questions.question: Kimchi, spicy fermented cabbage, is a staple of which country's cuisine?
questions.explanation: Kimjang, the annual communal making of kimchi before winter, was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list for South Korea in 2013. Its red heat comes from gochugaru chilli flakes.
questions.hook: Kimchi and kimjang: Korea's winter cabbage ritual.

questions.question: Prunes are the dried form of which fruit?
questions.explanation: Not every plum dries well; prune plums such as the French d'Agen are sweet enough to dry without fermenting around the stone. Sultanas, by contrast, are dried seedless white grapes.
questions.hook: Every prune was once a plum.

questions.question: Which spice is made from the dried stigmas of a crocus flower?
questions.explanation: Each flower yields only three stigmas, all picked by hand, which is why saffron is the world's most expensive spice by weight. Iran grows the large majority of the world's supply.
questions.hook: Three threads per crocus, which is why saffron costs a fortune.

questions.question: Tofu is made by curdling which kind of milk?
questions.explanation: Soy milk is set with a coagulant such as nigari (magnesium chloride) or gypsum and pressed into blocks, a process very like cheesemaking. Silken tofu is set without pressing.
questions.hook: Tofu is cheese made from soy milk.

questions.question: Goulash, a paprika-rich stew, originated in which country?
questions.explanation: Gulyás means herdsman in Hungarian, the cowboys of the Great Plain who cooked it in a cauldron. Paprika, made from dried capsicum, is Hungary's defining spice, and Szeged is its capital.
questions.hook: Hungarian cowboys stirred the first goulash.

questions.question: Which spirit gets its dominant flavour from juniper berries?
questions.explanation: Gin descends from Dutch genever, whose name comes from the word for juniper. London Dry is a style, not a place, and can be made anywhere; aquavit is flavoured with caraway or dill.
questions.hook: Genever, gin, juniper: all the same root.

questions.question: Tzatziki is made from cucumber, garlic and what?
questions.explanation: Strained Greek yoghurt keeps it thick, and the cucumber is grated and squeezed so it doesn't go watery. India's raita and Turkey's cacık are close cousins.
questions.hook: Greek yoghurt, grated cucumber, a lot of garlic.

questions.question: Which French bread was added to UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list in 2022?
questions.explanation: Under a 1993 French decree, a baguette de tradition may contain only flour, water, salt and yeast. The croissant descends from the Austrian kipferl, so it is Viennese pastry rather than French bread.
questions.hook: Four ingredients and a UNESCO listing: the baguette.

questions.question: Which alcoholic drink is made by fermenting apple juice?
questions.explanation: Perry is its pear equivalent, mead is fermented honey and kvass is a Russian drink fermented from rye bread. Distil cider and you get apple brandy such as Calvados.
questions.hook: Apples make cider, pears make perry, honey makes mead.

questions.question: What is the main herb in pesto alla genovese?
questions.explanation: Genoa's pesto pounds basil with pine nuts, garlic, hard cheese and olive oil. The name comes from pestare, to pound, the same root as pestle.
questions.hook: Pesto is pounded, like a pestle, and Genoa pounds basil.

questions.question: Which cocktail is made from equal parts gin, Campari and sweet vermouth?
questions.explanation: The story goes that Count Camillo Negroni asked a Florence bartender around 1919 to strengthen his Americano by swapping the soda water for gin. Swap the gin for bourbon or rye and it becomes a Boulevardier.
questions.hook: An Americano with gin instead of soda is a Negroni.

questions.question: Which spirit is the base of Brazil's caipirinha?
questions.explanation: Cachaça is distilled from fresh sugar-cane juice, while most rum is made from molasses. The caipirinha is simply cachaça muddled with lime and sugar.
questions.hook: Brazil's cane-juice spirit makes Brazil's national cocktail.

questions.question: Calvados, from Normandy, is a brandy distilled from what?
questions.explanation: Normandy's cool climate suits apples better than wine grapes, so cider is distilled into Calvados. A trou normand, a Norman hole, is a glass of it taken mid-meal to make room for more food.
questions.hook: Normandy's apples make cider first, then Calvados.

questions.question: Which white grape makes the Hunter Valley's most celebrated age-worthy wine?
questions.explanation: Hunter semillon is picked early, is low in alcohol and usually unoaked, yet develops toasty, honeyed flavours over a decade in bottle. That toastiness comes from age, not barrels.
questions.hook: Hunter semillon tastes of toast without ever seeing oak.

questions.question: South Australia's Clare Valley is best known for which white grape?
questions.explanation: In 2000 a group of Clare Valley winemakers bottled their riesling under screwcap together, a move that helped make screwcaps the norm in Australia and New Zealand. Neighbouring Eden Valley is the other great Australian riesling region.
questions.hook: Clare riesling pioneered the screwcap.

questions.question: Port wine takes its name from which city?
questions.explanation: The grapes are grown up the Douro Valley, and the wine is fortified with grape spirit mid-fermentation to keep it sweet. It was traditionally aged in lodges at Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river from Porto.
questions.hook: Port is Porto's wine, fortified halfway through fermenting.

questions.question: Which beer style was first brewed in 1842 in a Bohemian city now in the Czech Republic?
questions.explanation: Bavarian brewer Josef Groll made the first golden, clear lager in Plzeň, sold today as Pilsner Urquell. Before then most lagers were dark.
questions.hook: Plzeň gave its name to the first golden lager.

questions.question: Besides carbon dioxide, which gas gives draught Guinness its creamy head?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen barely dissolves in beer, so it forms tiny bubbles that make a dense, lasting head. Canned Guinness copies this with a nitrogen widget, introduced in the late 1980s.
questions.hook: Guinness is nitro, which is why its bubbles cascade downwards.

questions.question: Which pasta's name means little ears?
questions.explanation: Orecchiette come from Puglia, where they are classically served with cime di rapa, a bitter turnip green. Housewives in Bari's old town still shape them by hand in the street.
questions.hook: Little ears from the heel of Italy's boot.

questions.question: Carpaccio, the dish of paper-thin raw beef, was named after a Venetian what?
questions.explanation: Giuseppe Cipriani created it at Harry's Bar in Venice around 1950, inspired by the reds of Renaissance painter Vittore Carpaccio. The same bar named the Bellini cocktail after painter Giovanni Bellini.
questions.hook: Harry's Bar named both a dish and a drink after painters.

questions.question: Nutmeg and which other spice come from the same fruit?
questions.explanation: Nutmeg is the seed and mace is the red lace-like aril wrapped around it. Both came from the tiny Banda Islands, and the Dutch kept the island of Run in 1667 in exchange for giving up Manhattan.
questions.hook: One fruit, two spices: seed is nutmeg, lace is mace.

questions.question: Vanilla comes from the seed pod of what kind of plant?
questions.explanation: Native to Mexico, the vanilla orchid would not fruit elsewhere until 1841, when Edmond Albius, a 12-year-old enslaved boy on Réunion, worked out how to hand-pollinate it. Madagascar now grows most of the world's supply.
questions.hook: Vanilla is an orchid pod, pollinated by hand.

questions.question: Ben Shewry is the chef-owner of which Melbourne restaurant, known for native Australian ingredients?
questions.explanation: New Zealand-born Shewry runs Attica in Ripponlea, a regular on the World's 50 Best Restaurants list since 2010. Vue de monde, in the Rialto tower, was founded by Shannon Bennett.
questions.hook: Attica: a Kiwi chef cooking with Australian bush foods.

questions.question: Barolo and Barbaresco are made from which grape?
questions.explanation: Nebbiolo is named from nebbia, the fog that settles over Piedmont's hills at harvest. Barbera and Dolcetto are also Piedmontese, while Sangiovese is Tuscany's grape for Chianti.
questions.hook: Nebbiolo ripens in the Piedmont fog.

questions.question: Which native Australian tree's leaves are used as a spice with an intense citrus flavour?
questions.explanation: Lemon myrtle's leaves contain more citral, the lemon-scented compound, than lemons themselves. Wattleseed is roasted for a coffee and chocolate flavour and mountain pepperberry comes from Tasmania.
questions.hook: Lemon myrtle out-lemons the lemon.

questions.question: Maggie Beer popularised which sour condiment pressed from unripe grapes?
questions.explanation: Verjuice, from the French for green juice, was widely used in medieval cooking before lemons became common. Beer revived it from her Barossa farm and co-hosted the ABC's The Cook and the Chef with Simon Bryant.
questions.hook: Green juice from green grapes, revived in the Barossa.

questions.question: Noma, named the world's best restaurant five times, is in which city?
questions.explanation: René Redzepi's restaurant defined New Nordic cuisine through foraging and fermentation. It ended regular service at the end of 2024 to become a food lab, then reopened as a restaurant in Copenhagen in August 2026.
questions.hook: Noma is short for nordisk mad, Nordic food.

questions.question: Which publication rates Australian restaurants with hats rather than stars?
questions.explanation: The Good Food Guide, started by the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age, awards up to three hats. The Michelin Guide made its first Australian foray in October 2026 with a South Australia edition.
questions.hook: Australia wears hats; Michelin hands out stars.

questions.question: Which liqueur, made by Carthusian monks, gave its name to a yellow-green colour?
questions.explanation: The monks of the Grande Chartreuse monastery near Grenoble still guard its recipe of 130 plants. It comes in green and a milder yellow version.
questions.hook: The colour chartreuse came from the bottle.

questions.question: Ceviche, raw fish cured in citrus, is the national dish of which country?
questions.explanation: The citrus acid firms the fish without heat, and the leftover marinade, leche de tigre or tiger's milk, is drunk as a hangover cure. Peru celebrates National Ceviche Day on 28 June.
questions.hook: Peru's fish is cooked by lime, not flame.

questions.question: The cashew belongs to the same plant family as which plant, sharing its irritant oil in its shell?
questions.explanation: Cashew shells contain urushiol, the same irritant as in poison ivy, which is why cashews are never sold in the shell. The family, Anacardiaceae, also includes mango and pistachio.
questions.hook: Cashew, mango, pistachio and poison ivy are all relatives.

questions.question: A Harvey Wallbanger is a screwdriver with a float of which Italian liqueur?
questions.explanation: Galliano is a vanilla and anise liqueur in a tall, tapered bottle that is hard to fit on a bar shelf. A screwdriver itself is just vodka and orange juice.
questions.hook: Harvey banged his head, and the tall yellow bottle was to blame.

questions.question: Rutherglen in north-east Victoria is famous for which fortified wine?
questions.explanation: Rutherglen Muscat is classified in four rising levels: Rutherglen, Classic, Grand and Rare. Its sister wine, once called Tokay, was renamed Topaque after an agreement with the EU.
questions.hook: Rutherglen, Classic, Grand, Rare: four steps of muscat.

questions.question: South Africa's Pinotage is a cross between Pinot Noir and which grape?
questions.explanation: Professor Abraham Perold bred it in 1925. Cinsault was then known in South Africa as Hermitage, so Pinot plus Hermitage gave Pinotage.
questions.hook: Pinot plus Hermitage (Cinsault) equals Pinotage.

questions.question: Zinfandel, California's signature red, is genetically identical to which Italian grape?
questions.explanation: DNA testing traced both back to a Croatian grape known as Crljenak Kaštelanski or Tribidrag. Primitivo is grown in Puglia, in the heel of Italy.
questions.hook: Zinfandel and Primitivo: one Croatian grape, two names.

questions.question: The word barbecue came into English via Spanish from which people's language?
questions.explanation: The Taíno of the Caribbean used barbacoa for a wooden frame of sticks for cooking or sleeping. Taíno also gave English hammock, hurricane and canoe.
questions.hook: Barbecue, hammock, hurricane, canoe: Caribbean words.

questions.question: The quandong, or native peach, is related to which tree?
questions.explanation: Quandong is Santalum acuminatum, a semi-parasitic member of the sandalwood family that taps other plants' roots. Its tart red fruit is rich in vitamin C and its kernels were also eaten.
questions.hook: Quandong is a sandalwood that bears peaches.

questions.question: Which fish was confit in Tetsuya Wakuda's famous signature dish at Tetsuya's in Sydney?
questions.explanation: The Tasmanian ocean trout was gently confit in oil and topped with kombu, and was often called the world's most photographed dish. Tetsuya's closed in July 2024 after more than 30 years.
questions.hook: Tetsuya's trout, the most photographed dish in the world.

questions.question: Which cured pork cut does an authentic Roman spaghetti alla carbonara use instead of bacon?
questions.explanation: Guanciale is cured pork cheek, fattier and more deeply flavoured than pancetta, which comes from the belly. A traditional Roman carbonara is made from just guanciale, eggs, pecorino romano and black pepper, with no cream.
questions.hook: No cream and no garlic: Rome's carbonara is cheek, egg, cheese and pepper.

questions.question: Which grape-based brandy do Peru and Chile both claim as their national spirit?
questions.explanation: Pisco is distilled from fermented grape juice and is the base of the pisco sour, made with lime juice, sugar, egg white and bitters. Both countries protect the name and argue over who invented it.
questions.hook: A grape spirit, a diplomatic row, and a sour with egg white on top.

questions.question: Which red grape is the backbone of Chianti, grown in central Tuscany?
questions.explanation: Sangiovese is Italy's most planted red grape and gives high-acid, cherry-flavoured wines. Chianti Classico must contain at least 80 percent of it. Nebbiolo makes Barolo in Piedmont, far to the north-west.
questions.hook: Its name is said to mean blood of Jove, and Chianti is mostly made of it.

questions.question: On a sparkling-wine label, which term marks the sweetest style?
questions.explanation: Doux has more than 50 grams of sugar per litre. Next come demi-sec, sec and extra dry, with brut and extra brut drier still, so extra dry is sweeter than brut, a common trap.
questions.hook: Extra dry is sweeter than brut, and doux is the sweetest of all.

questions.question: Ethiopia's spongy, sour flatbread injera is made from the flour of which tiny grain?
questions.explanation: Teff is among the smallest cereal grains in the world, and the batter is fermented for a few days before cooking, which gives injera its tang. The grain is gluten-free and grows mainly in the highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea.
questions.hook: A tiny grain, fermented for days, becomes the plate and the fork.

questions.question: Which species of coffee, hardier than arabica and with roughly twice the caffeine, is grown widely in Vietnam and used in instant blends?
questions.explanation: Robusta, Coffea canephora, grows at lower altitudes, resists disease and carries about 2.2 to 2.7 percent caffeine against roughly 1.2 to 1.5 percent in arabica. Vietnam grows more of it than any other country.
questions.hook: Arabica gets the cafe menu; robusta gets the kick and the instant jar.

questions.question: Darjeeling, the champagne of teas, is grown in the Himalayan foothills of which Indian state?
questions.explanation: Darjeeling sits in the north of West Bengal, close to Nepal, Sikkim and Bhutan, and was the first product in India to receive a geographical indication. Assam, a different state, makes the stronger malty teas used in breakfast blends.
questions.hook: Darjeeling is a hill town and Assam is a river plain: two states, two kinds of tea.

questions.question: Theobroma, the genus name Linnaeus gave the cacao tree in 1753, comes from Greek and means what?
questions.explanation: Linnaeus joined the Greek words theos, god, and broma, food. Cacao was a sacred and valuable crop for the Maya and Aztecs, who drank it bitter and spiced rather than sweet.
questions.hook: Even the scientific name admits chocolate is divine.

questions.question: What is the Japanese name for the thin slices of pickled ginger served with sushi to cleanse the palate?
questions.explanation: Gari is young ginger sliced thin and pickled in sweet vinegar, eaten between pieces of sushi so the next fish tastes fresh. Umeboshi are pickled plums, takuan is pickled daikon radish and rakkyo are pickled shallots.
questions.hook: Gari clears the palate so the next piece tastes new.

questions.question: Hops, the bitter flavouring in beer, belong to the same plant family as which other well-known plant?
questions.explanation: Hops and cannabis are both in the Cannabaceae family, and both have sticky resin glands on their female flowers. Hops are the cone-like flowers of the climbing vine Humulus lupulus.
questions.hook: Beer's bitter herb and cannabis are botanical cousins.

questions.question: Tequila may only be made in a handful of Mexican states, centred on which state, home to the town of Tequila?
questions.explanation: Most tequila comes from Jalisco, whose blue agave fields and old distilleries around the town of Tequila are a UNESCO World Heritage landscape. Oaxaca, a different state, is the heartland of mezcal.
questions.hook: Tequila the spirit comes from Tequila the town in Jalisco.

questions.question: Which seaweed, pressed into dark sheets, wraps a classic sushi roll?
questions.explanation: Nori is red algae that is shredded, pressed and dried into thin sheets much like paper. Kombu, a thick kelp, is used instead to make dashi stock.
questions.hook: Nori is the seaweed you can roll with.

questions.question: Raisins, sultanas and currants are all dried forms of which fruit?
questions.explanation: Sultanas come from seedless green grapes and currants from tiny Zante grapes, so they are not related to blackcurrants at all.
questions.hook: Every dried vine fruit started on a vine.

questions.question: Which Italian cheese, originally made from buffalo milk, is the classic melting cheese on a pizza?
questions.explanation: Traditional mozzarella di bufala comes from Campania, though most pizza cheese today is made from cow's milk. The curd is heated and stretched, which gives it that famous stringy pull.
questions.hook: Mozzarella is the cheese that stretches.

questions.question: Which spice, a relative of ginger, gives curry powder its yellow colour?
questions.explanation: Turmeric is the ground root of a plant in the ginger family, and its yellow pigment is called curcumin. It also stains benches, plastic containers and tea towels very effectively.
questions.hook: Turmeric stains yellow, ginger stays pale.

questions.question: In Australian fish and chip shops, the fish sold as flake is which animal?
questions.explanation: Flake is usually gummy shark, caught in southern waters and sold skinned as boneless fillets. It is especially popular in Victoria and South Australia, and the sweet, firm white flesh suits battering.
questions.hook: Order flake and you are eating shark.

questions.question: Which fat gives white chocolate its creamy body?
questions.explanation: White chocolate is cocoa butter blended with sugar and milk solids, with none of the dark cocoa solids that give other chocolate its colour. That is why some people argue it is not true chocolate.
questions.hook: White chocolate keeps the butter, drops the brown.

questions.question: Genuine caviar is the salted roe of which fish?
questions.explanation: Beluga, osetra and sevruga are all sturgeon species from the Caspian and Black Sea region. Roe from other fish, such as salmon, is sold as roe rather than true caviar.
questions.hook: No sturgeon, no true caviar.

questions.question: Which bitter compound, long used to treat malaria, gives tonic water its flavour?
questions.explanation: Quinine comes from the bark of the cinchona tree. A popular story says British officers in India added gin and sugar to their quinine drink to make it easier to swallow, giving us the gin and tonic. Historians dispute that account, so the exact origin is uncertain.
questions.hook: Tonic water started out as a malaria medicine.

questions.question: Wilbur Scoville devised his chilli heat scale in 1912 while working for which drug company?
questions.explanation: Scoville worked at the drug company Parke-Davis. He diluted chilli extract in sugar water until a panel of tasters could no longer feel the burn. Modern labs measure the heat chemical, capsaicin, with machines instead of tongues.
questions.hook: The heat scale came from a drugmaker.

questions.question: True cinnamon, the pale curled quills of Cinnamomum verum, is native to which country?
questions.explanation: Most cinnamon in supermarkets is actually cassia, a darker and harsher relative grown in Indonesia, Vietnam and China. True cinnamon is sometimes sold as Ceylon cinnamon, after Sri Lanka's old name.
questions.hook: Ceylon cinnamon is Sri Lankan.

questions.question: Roasted and ground seeds of which Australian native plant give a nutty, coffee-like flavour to bush cooking?
questions.explanation: Aboriginal Australians have long ground the seeds of certain acacia species into flour, and today they flavour ice cream, breads and desserts. Only some of the hundreds of wattle species are safe to eat.
questions.hook: Golden wattle is Australia's national floral emblem.

questions.question: Prosecco, the sparkling wine of north-east Italy, is made mostly from which grape?
questions.explanation: Until 2009 the grape itself was called prosecco, but the name was then reserved for the wine region and the grape became glera. Most Prosecco gets its bubbles in a pressurised tank rather than in the bottle.
questions.hook: Glera is the grape, Prosecco the place.

questions.question: The croissant descends from which Austrian pastry?
questions.explanation: Bakers in Vienna made kipferl for centuries as a plain yeasted roll. The flaky, layered butter version we know today took shape in France in the early 1900s.
questions.hook: The croissant is a Viennese kipferl, remade in Paris.

questions.question: Which hardware chain is best known for the charity barbecues set up outside its stores on weekends?
questions.explanation: Community groups book weekend slots at Bunnings stores to raise money, selling a sausage and onion in a slice of white bread. The sausage sizzle there has become a national ritual and a handy fundraiser for clubs and schools.
questions.hook: Bunnings: hammers inside, snags outside.

questions.question: Which Arnott's biscuit is topped with pink fondant, a stripe of raspberry jam and sprinkled coconut?
questions.explanation: The Iced VoVo is a wheaten biscuit with two strips of pink fondant either side of a raspberry jam stripe, dusted with coconut. It has been a fixture in Australian biscuit tins for generations.
questions.hook: Pink, jam, coconut: that is the Iced VoVo.

questions.question: Which animal is Cadbury's small chocolate Freddo shaped like?
questions.explanation: Freddo is a small, hollow chocolate figure sold in Australia and the United Kingdom, and its full name is Freddo the Frog. It has long been the classic cheap pocket-money treat in Australian milk bars.
questions.hook: Freddo is a frog, ribbit and a chocolate.

questions.question: Which Arnott's baked savoury snack biscuits come in flavours such as Pizza and BBQ?
questions.explanation: Arnott's Shapes are small, crunchy baked snack biscuits sold in packets and boxes, popular in lunchboxes and at parties.
questions.hook: Pizza, BBQ, and a party plate.

questions.question: Which type of pastry sandwiches the custard in a bakery vanilla slice?
questions.explanation: A vanilla slice has a thick layer of set custard between two sheets of crisp, flaky pastry, usually topped with passionfruit or pink icing. Puff pastry gets its flakiness from many thin layers of butter and dough.
questions.hook: Custard in a puffy sandwich.

questions.question: Which Australian chocolate bar has a red fruit and coconut filling under dark chocolate?
questions.explanation: The Cherry Ripe is made from cherries and coconut in a dark chocolate coat, and is a long-running Australian chocolate bar.
questions.hook: Dark shell, red fruit, coconut inside.

questions.question: In New South Wales fish and chip shops, what name is given to a battered, deep-fried slice of spud?
questions.explanation: The potato scallop is a thick slice of potato dipped in batter and deep-fried. It is a fish and chip shop staple.
questions.hook: No shellfish: a scallop is a spud.

questions.question: Which Arnott's biscuit sandwiches raspberry jam and vanilla cream between two coconut-flecked biscuits?
questions.explanation: The Monte Carlo has a rough, golden, coconut-speckled surface and a filling of jam and vanilla cream, which makes it a favourite with morning tea. It is one of Arnott's long-running cream biscuits.
questions.hook: Jam, cream, and a rough coconut top.

questions.question: Weet-Bix is made by which company, owned by the Seventh-day Adventist Church?
questions.explanation: Sanitarium Health Food Company is owned by the Seventh-day Adventist Church. Weet-Bix is also sold in New Zealand.
questions.hook: Church-owned Sanitarium makes the Weet-Bix.

questions.question: In which NSW city did Scottish baker William Arnott start his biscuit business in 1865?
questions.explanation: William Arnott opened a bakery in Newcastle in 1865. The family firm grew into one of Australia's best-known biscuit makers, and its parrot trademark became a household symbol.
questions.hook: Arnott's began life in a Newcastle bakery.

questions.question: Arnott's Scotch Finger is what style of biscuit?
