questions.explanation: The Scotch Finger is a buttery, crumbly shortbread-style biscuit, shaped like a finger and lightly sweet. It is a classic with a cup of tea and is one of the plain biscuits in the Arnott's range.
questions.hook: Scotch finger means Scottish shortbread.

questions.question: Chicken parmigiana is a descendant of an Italian dish built on slices of which vegetable?
questions.explanation: The original dish, parmigiana di melanzane, layers fried eggplant with tomato sauce and cheese. Italian migrants in the United States replaced the vegetable with veal or chicken, and Australia took the idea from there.
questions.hook: The original parma was an eggplant bake.

questions.question: Which French pastry, also called a Napoleon, is the ancestor of the vanilla slice?
questions.explanation: The mille-feuille layers puff pastry with pastry cream, and the Australian vanilla slice is a thicker, plainer relative of it. In Quebec and parts of Europe the same style of dessert is still sold as a Napoleon.
questions.hook: A French mille-feuille, Aussie-style.

questions.question: The Yarra Valley wine region lies on the outer edge of which Australian capital city?
questions.explanation: The Yarra Valley is about an hour's drive east of Melbourne. Its cool climate suits pinot noir, chardonnay and sparkling wine.
questions.hook: Melbourne's wine country is one train-and-drive away.

questions.question: The King Valley in north-east Victoria is best known in Australia for which Italian sparkling white wine?
questions.explanation: Italian-Australian families in the valley planted the glera grape, the base of the wine, and the valley is one of the best-known homes of Australian prosecco. It is usually fresher and lighter than Champagne-style wine.
questions.hook: Little Italy of the Victorian high country.

questions.question: What word on a wine label tells you the year the grapes were picked?
questions.explanation: A wine from a good year is called a great vintage, and a bottle with no year is called non-vintage. The year on a vintage wine label is the harvest year.
questions.hook: Vintage means the harvest year, not the age.

questions.question: Brown Brothers, a family winery founded in 1889, is based in which north-east Victorian town?
questions.explanation: The family has grown grapes at Milawa for more than 130 years and also sources fruit from the cooler King Valley.
questions.hook: Milawa: the Browns' home paddock.

questions.question: Henschke's celebrated Hill of Grace shiraz vineyard is in which region, in the hills east of the Barossa Valley floor?
questions.explanation: The old vines grow at Keyneton on higher, cooler ground than the valley floor. Eden Valley is better known as a riesling region, so a shiraz star from there is a surprise.
questions.hook: A red icon from the white-wine hills.

questions.question: Before founding Lindeman's in the Hunter Valley in 1843, Henry Lindeman worked as what?
questions.explanation: Lindeman trained in England, served as a ship's surgeon and migrated to New South Wales in 1840.
questions.hook: Doctor's orders: plant vines.

questions.question: Italian-Australian families in the King Valley first made their living growing which crop before turning to grapes?
questions.explanation: Post-war migrants from northern Italy grew tobacco in north-east Victoria, and as the tobacco industry declined they turned to planting vines. Families such as Dal Zotto and Pizzini still make wine there.
questions.hook: From leaf to vine in one generation.

questions.question: In Australia, what is a bottle of wine with a plain label and no brand name called?
questions.explanation: Cleanskins began as a way for makers to sell surplus stock cheaply without damaging their brand. The term is mostly Australian and New Zealand.
questions.hook: Naked bottle, anonymous wine, low price.

questions.question: Clonakilla's famous Canberra District red blends shiraz with a small amount of which white grape?
questions.explanation: Tim Kirk's Shiraz Viognier from Murrumbateman was inspired by the Cote-Rotie wines of the northern Rhone. The viognier is fermented with the shiraz skins, adding perfume.
questions.hook: Rhone inspiration in a cold-climate paddock outside Canberra.

questions.question: The old red soils behind Heathcote's shiraz reputation in Victoria date from which geological period?
questions.explanation: The Cambrian greenstone soils are about 500 million years old and hold water well, giving rich, deeply coloured wines. Heathcote sits on the Mount Camel Range.
questions.hook: Half a billion years of soil under the vines.

questions.question: The Hill of Grace vineyard in South Australia is named after a Lutheran church. What is the church's German name?
questions.explanation: The Gnadenberg Lutheran church stands on the hill near the vines, which were planted by German settlers in the nineteenth century. Gnadenberg means hill of grace, the origin of the English name.
questions.hook: A German name that means hill of grace.

questions.question: Which light Italian sparkling wine, made mainly from the glera grape in the Veneto, is the usual base of a spritz?
questions.explanation: Prosecco is cheerful, fruity and best drunk young. Asti is a sweeter, lower-alcohol sparkler from Piedmont, while Franciacorta comes from Lombardy and is made like Champagne.
questions.hook: Veneto's fizz for the Aperol spritz.

questions.question: What is the name for a wine bottle that holds 1.5 litres, the equivalent of two standard bottles?
questions.explanation: A standard bottle holds 750 millilitres, so a magnum holds two. Wine in larger formats tends to age more slowly, which is why collectors prize magnums of fine vintages.
questions.hook: Magnum: double the standard bottle.

questions.question: Chablis, the crisp, flinty white from northern Burgundy, is made from which grape?
questions.explanation: Chablis sits far north of the rest of Burgundy, so its cool climate and chalky Kimmeridgian soils give a lean, steely style of chardonnay. It is typically made with little or no new oak.
questions.hook: Chablis is chardonnay in a steely cool-climate coat.

questions.question: Spain's Rioja region is best known for red wines built mainly on which grape?
questions.explanation: Tempranillo, whose name comes from the Spanish word for early, ripens sooner than most reds. In Rioja it is often blended with grenache (garnacha) and aged in American or French oak.
questions.hook: Tempranillo ripens early, hence the name.

questions.question: Which French word names the trained restaurant professional who advises diners on what to drink with their meal?
questions.explanation: The sommelier curates the cellar, recommends pairings and serves the bottle at the table. The title is protected through qualifications such as the Master Sommelier diploma, one of the hardest exams in hospitality.
questions.hook: The somm pours, pairs and keeps the cellar.

questions.question: Which natural compound, found in grape skins, seeds and oak barrels, gives a young red its dry, mouth-gripping feel?
questions.explanation: Tannins come from grape skins, seeds and stems, and from the oak a wine is aged in. They soften with age, and the same compound is why stewed black tea feels astringent.
questions.hook: Tannin is the grippy feel, like stewed tea.

questions.question: Beaujolais Nouveau, the very young red released with great fanfare, goes on sale in which month each year?
questions.explanation: By French law it is released on the third Thursday of November, only weeks after the harvest. The gamay grapes are fermented for just a few days, so the wine is fruity, light and meant to be drunk quickly.
questions.hook: Third Thursday of November, wine barely out of the vat.

questions.question: Most Prosecco gets its bubbles from a second fermentation in large sealed steel tanks. What is this method called?
questions.explanation: Champagne and Cava ferment a second time inside each bottle, which is slower and costlier. The tank method keeps Prosecco fresh and fruity and much cheaper, and it is named after its inventor, Eugène Charmat.
questions.hook: Tank fizz is Charmat, bottle fizz is Champagne.

questions.question: Which grape dominates the blends of Bordeaux's Right Bank, including the famous names of Pomerol and Saint-Émilion?
questions.explanation: The clay and limestone soils of the Right Bank suit merlot, which ripens earlier and gives plusher wines. The gravelly Left Bank is instead led by cabernet sauvignon.
questions.hook: Right Bank, merlot; Left Bank, cabernet sauvignon.

questions.question: Vouvray and Savennières, white wines of the Loire Valley, are made from which grape?
questions.explanation: Chenin blanc is unusually versatile, producing bone-dry, off-dry, sparkling and lusciously sweet wines. High acidity lets the best examples age for decades, and it has long been South Africa's most planted white grape.
questions.hook: The Loire's shape-shifter: dry, sweet or sparkling.

questions.question: Germany's Mosel is famous for riesling grown on slate slopes above a river that flows into which larger river?
questions.explanation: The Mosel joins the Rhine at Koblenz after rising in France, where it is called the Moselle. The slate soil stores heat on the very steep slopes, helping riesling ripen in a cool climate.
questions.hook: Mosel slate slopes drain to the Rhine at Koblenz.

questions.question: Louis XIV of France is said to have called which sweet wine the wine of kings, king of wines?
questions.explanation: The phrase is traditionally attributed to the Sun King, who is said to have served it at Versailles. Tokaji Aszú is made in north-east Hungary from grapes shrivelled by botrytis, and was also a favourite of Russian tsars.
questions.hook: Louis XIV's drink: Hungary's golden Tokaji.

questions.question: Assyrtiko, a crisp white grown on ancient bush vines in volcanic soil, is the signature grape of which Greek island?
questions.explanation: Santorini's vines are trained into low baskets to shield the grapes from fierce winds. Many vines are ungrafted because the volcanic ash soil defeated the phylloxera pest that wrecked most of Europe's vineyards.
questions.hook: Basket-trained vines on a volcano.

questions.question: Which pink-skinned, lychee-scented grape produces Alsace's most perfumed white wines?
questions.explanation: Alsace, in north-eastern France on the German border, labels its wines by grape. Gewürztraminer gives rich, spicy, rose-petal wines that pair well with Asian food and strong cheeses such as Munster.
questions.hook: Pink grape, white wine, lychee and roses.

questions.question: Which large format, holding six litres or eight standard bottles, is the name of a Champagne bottle?
questions.explanation: Large Champagne formats carry biblical names: Rehoboam is 4.5 litres, Methuselah 6, Salmanazar 9, Balthazar 12 and Nebuchadnezzar 15.
questions.hook: Methuselah lived long; six litres of fizz.

questions.question: Before Argentina made it famous, malbec was the black wine of which south-western French town?
questions.explanation: Cahors reds, made from at least 70 per cent malbec, were once so dark they were called black wine. The grape arrived in Argentina in the 1850s, and thrived at altitude in Mendoza.
questions.hook: Argentina's star grape began in Cahors.

questions.question: On a Rioja label, which ageing term marks wines that have spent at least five years in oak and bottle combined?
questions.explanation: Gran Reserva wines spend at least two years in oak and three in bottle, and are made only in the best vintages. Crianza is the shortest oaked tier and Joven wines see little or no ageing.
questions.hook: Gran Reserva: the longest-aged tier.

questions.question: Bordeaux's Left Bank, home to the Médoc and its great châteaux, runs along the western side of which estuary?
questions.explanation: The Gironde forms where the Garonne and Dordogne meet. Gravelly soils on the Left Bank suit cabernet sauvignon, while the Right Bank lies east of the Dordogne and Gironde.
questions.hook: Left Bank means left of the Gironde.

questions.question: In which German city is the world's biggest beer festival held every autumn?
questions.explanation: The festival began in 1810 as a party for the wedding of Bavaria's Crown Prince Ludwig, and only the six big Munich breweries may serve beer there. Despite the name, it starts in September, not October.
questions.hook: Munich's party starts in September, not October.

questions.question: A shandy is beer mixed with which soft drink?
questions.explanation: The classic shandy is about half beer and half lemonade. It is a long, low-alcohol drink that is popular in Australian pubs.
questions.hook: Half beer, half fizzy lemon, all shandy.

questions.question: Which cereal grain is malted to make the base of most beer?
questions.explanation: Malting means soaking the grain so it sprouts and then drying it in a kiln, which develops enzymes that turn starch into fermentable sugar. Australia is one of the world's major barley growers and exporters.
questions.hook: No malt without sprouted barley.

questions.question: XXXX Gold is a beer closely identified with which Australian state?
questions.explanation: It is brewed in Brisbane, and the brand is a fixture at Queensland pubs and State of Origin nights.
questions.hook: Four Xs mark the Sunshine State's beer.

questions.question: Mead, one of the oldest alcoholic drinks, is made by fermenting what?
questions.explanation: Honey is diluted in water and fermented with yeast, giving a drink that can be dry, sweet or sparkling. Archaeological evidence suggests people have made mead for thousands of years.
questions.hook: Mead is honey wine, with bees to thank.

questions.question: Before yeast turns it into beer, what is the sweet liquid drawn off from the mashed grain called?
questions.explanation: Brewers steep crushed malt in hot water to extract sugars, then boil the wort with hops. Must is the equivalent in winemaking, and trub is the sediment left after boiling.
questions.hook: Wort is beer's sweet start, must is wine's.

questions.question: Which Belgian farmhouse ale was traditionally brewed in the cool months to refresh workers in summer?
questions.explanation: Saison comes from the French-speaking region of Wallonia, and its name is the French word for season. Modern versions are dry, spicy and highly carbonated.
questions.hook: Saison means season: brewed in winter, drunk in summer.

questions.question: The word stout originally described a stronger version of which dark London beer?
questions.explanation: Brewers advertised a stout porter, meaning a strong one, and over time the first word became the name of the style. Porter itself became popular in 18th-century London.
questions.hook: Stout began as strong porter.

questions.question: Little Creatures, known for its pale ale, started brewing in which Western Australian port city?
questions.explanation: The brewery opened in Fremantle around 2000 and became one of the best-known names in Australia's craft beer boom.
questions.hook: Little Creatures began in Fremantle.

questions.question: What does the German word radler, the name of a beer and lemonade mix, literally mean?
questions.explanation: The drink is said to have been created in Bavaria in the 1920s for cyclists who wanted something lighter. It is lower in alcohol than ordinary beer, and shandy is its British cousin.
questions.hook: Radler is the cyclist's beer.

questions.question: Duke William IV of Bavaria issued the 1516 beer purity law at which town?
questions.explanation: The law was proclaimed at a meeting of the Bavarian estates in Ingolstadt, and it applied first to Bavaria. It was adopted across all of Germany only after unification, in the 20th century.
questions.hook: Purity law, Ingolstadt, 1516.

questions.question: At which Brisbane suburb brewery is XXXX brewed?
questions.explanation: XXXX is brewed by Castlemaine Perkins at its Milton brewery in Brisbane, the home of the brand for generations.
questions.hook: XXXX is brewed in Milton, Brisbane.

questions.question: Which red juice gives the Cosmopolitan, the pink cocktail made famous by Sex and the City, its colour?
questions.explanation: A Cosmopolitan is vodka, Cointreau, lime juice and a splash of cranberry juice. It was already around in the 1980s but became a global craze in the late 1990s thanks to television.
questions.hook: Carrie's drink was vodka with cranberry blush.

questions.question: In what metal is a Moscow Mule traditionally served?
questions.explanation: The drink is vodka, ginger beer and lime, and the chilled copper mug is part of its identity. It was popularised in the United States in the 1940s as a way to introduce vodka to American drinkers.
questions.hook: Mule in a mug of copper.

questions.question: Alongside grains such as rye, which vegetable is a traditional base for vodka in Poland?
questions.explanation: Poland and Russia both claim to have invented vodka. Polish written records of the drink go back to the early 15th century, and Russian ones to the 1530s. Potato vodka became common in Poland in the 18th century when the crop spread.
questions.hook: Poland's vodka grew from the potato patch.

questions.question: Laphroaig, Ardbeg and Lagavulin are all distilleries on which Scottish island?
questions.explanation: Islay's malt is dried over peat fires and the island's coastal air and water add a medicinal, briny character. The island has several working distilleries, including Lagavulin and Bowmore.
questions.hook: Islay: peat smoke and sea spray.

questions.question: Bill Lark won the first licence for legal small-scale whisky distilling in over 150 years in 1992, in which Australian state?
questions.explanation: Tasmania had banned small stills in 1839, and the law was only relaxed in 1992. Lark Distillery in Hobart reignited the local craft, using the island's cool climate and pure water.
questions.hook: One man's licence restarted Tasmanian whisky.

questions.question: A Rusty Nail cocktail is Scotch whisky stirred with which Scotch-based liqueur?
questions.explanation: Drambuie is flavoured with heather honey, herbs and spices, and its name comes from the Gaelic an dram buidheach, meaning the drink that satisfies. Legend credits Bonnie Prince Charlie's recipe.
questions.hook: Scotch plus honeyed Drambuie makes the Rusty Nail.

questions.question: In Casino Royale, James Bond's Vesper martini combines gin, vodka and which aromatised wine?
questions.explanation: Ian Fleming's 1953 novel has Bond order three measures of Gordon's gin, one of vodka and half a measure of Kina Lillet, shaken. Kina Lillet's quinine-heavy recipe was later changed, so modern versions use substitutes.
questions.hook: Bond named the Vesper after Vesper Lynd.

questions.question: Sullivans Cove French Oak, named World's Best Single Malt in 2014, is distilled in which city?
questions.explanation: The distillery is in the suburb of Cambridge and draws its name from the cove where Hobart was first settled in 1804. Its win at the World Whiskies Awards stunned the Scotch-dominated whisky world.
questions.hook: A Hobart malt beat Scotland in 2014.

questions.question: In which US city did pharmacist John Pemberton first sell Coca-Cola in 1886?
questions.explanation: Pemberton's syrup was first served at Jacobs' Pharmacy in Atlanta, Georgia, at five cents a glass and sold as a tonic. His bookkeeper Frank Robinson came up with the name and the looping script logo.
questions.hook: Coke began as a pharmacy tonic in Atlanta.

questions.question: Which South American country has been the world's biggest coffee grower for more than a century?
questions.explanation: Brazil took the lead in the 19th century and still grows roughly a third of the world's coffee, mostly in Minas Gerais and Sao Paulo states. Colombia is famous for quality but produces far less.
questions.hook: Brazil grows a third of the world's coffee.

questions.question: In Hindi, what does the word chai mean?
questions.explanation: Chai is simply the word for tea, so ordering a chai tea in a cafe says tea twice. The spiced, milky version is properly called masala chai, and the word travelled with the Silk Road trade into many languages.
questions.hook: Chai tea just means tea tea.

questions.question: Which religious order's brown robes are said to have inspired the name of a popular frothy milk coffee?
questions.explanation: The colour of a cappuccino, espresso with foamed milk, resembled the habits of the Capuchin friars in Italy and Austria. The friars themselves took their name from the capuche, or hood, they wore.
questions.hook: Brown robes and a hood gave us the cappuccino.

questions.question: The lemon-lime soda 7 Up, launched in 1929, originally contained which element, marketed as a health boost and later dropped from the recipe?
questions.explanation: Its first name was Bib-Label Lithiated Lemon-Lime Soda, because lithium citrate was marketed as a health boost. The lithium was later removed from the formula, and the drink was renamed 7 Up.
questions.hook: 7 Up was once lithiated, hence its first long name.

questions.question: Twinings sells tea from a narrow shop that has traded on the same London site since 1706. On which street is it?
questions.explanation: Thomas Twining first bought a coffee house there, then moved into tea when it was still an expensive novelty. The shop at number 216 still trades on the Strand site it has occupied since 1706.
questions.hook: Twinings has poured from the Strand since 1706.

questions.question: Italian gnocchi are soft dumplings most commonly made from flour and which mashed vegetable?
questions.explanation: Potato gnocchi are boiled until they float, then tossed in butter and sage or a tomato sauce. Versions made with semolina, ricotta or bread also exist, but potato is by far the most common.
questions.hook: Gnocchi are potato pillows that bob up when they are done.

questions.question: In Spain, crisp fried churros are traditionally dunked in what at breakfast or after a night out?
questions.explanation: Spanish chocolate con churros uses a drinking chocolate so thick it nearly holds a spoon upright. The ridged shape comes from piping the dough through a star-shaped nozzle straight into hot oil.
questions.hook: Star-piped, fried, then dunked in chocolate you could stand a spoon in.

questions.question: Baklava, the nutty syrup-soaked sweet of Turkey and Greece, is built from layers of which thin pastry?
questions.explanation: Dozens of paper-thin filo sheets are brushed with butter, layered with chopped pistachios or walnuts, baked, then soaked in syrup or honey. Filo is Greek for leaf, a good description of the sheets.
questions.hook: Filo means leaf, so baklava is a pile of buttered leaves.

questions.question: Sicilian cannoli are crisp fried pastry tubes filled with sweetened what?
questions.explanation: The sheep's-milk ricotta is mixed with sugar and often studded with chocolate chips or candied fruit. Cannoli began as a Carnival sweet in Sicily, and the name means little tubes.
questions.hook: Cannoli is little tubes, stuffed with sweet ricotta.

questions.question: Which Mediterranean port is the home of bouillabaisse, the saffron-scented stew of rockfish?
questions.explanation: It began as a fishermen's stew made from bony rockfish too awkward to sell. Marseille restaurateurs later signed a charter to protect the authentic recipe, and the broth is served separately from the fish.
questions.hook: Marseille's fishermen turned unsellable catch into a classic.

questions.question: Under the EU-protected rules for traditional Neapolitan pizza, how must the dough base be shaped?
questions.answer: By hand, with no rolling pin
distractors: By cutting it from a sheet
questions.explanation: The specification requires the dough to be stretched by hand, with no rolling pin or press in the method. The pizza is then baked in a wood-fired oven for only a minute or two.
questions.hook: Hands only: the Neapolitan base is stretched, not rolled.

questions.question: Which Italian region is famed for its dimpled, olive-oil-glossed focaccia?
questions.explanation: Focaccia genovese is dimpled with fingertips and brushed with a brine of oil and water before baking. Liguria also gave the world pesto and farinata, a chickpea pancake.
questions.hook: Dimples, oil and sea air: focaccia is Ligurian.

questions.question: Ricotta, meaning recooked in Italian, is traditionally made by heating what leftover liquid from cheesemaking?
questions.explanation: After the curds are taken for cheese, the whey still holds proteins that clump when reheated and are skimmed off. That second cooking is why ricotta is made from whey rather than from curds.
questions.hook: Ricotta is cheese's second act, cooked again from the leftovers.

questions.question: Turkish delight, or lokum, is a chewy sweet set from sugar syrup and which thickener?
questions.explanation: Traditional lokum is boiled with cornflour or other starch until it forms a firm gel, then flavoured with rosewater, lemon or mastic and dusted with icing sugar. Many cheap Western versions use gelatine instead.
questions.hook: Real lokum sets with starch, not gelatine.

questions.question: Sicilian arancini, fried and crumbed rice balls, get their name from their resemblance to which fruit?
questions.explanation: Arancini means little oranges, after the golden colour and round shape. Fillings include ragù with peas or mozzarella and ham, and in Palermo they are round while in Catania they are cone-shaped.
questions.hook: Little oranges you can eat with a fork.

questions.question: The blue-green veins in Italy's gorgonzola are caused by moulds of which genus?
questions.explanation: Cheesemakers pierce the young wheel with needles so air reaches the interior and the Penicillium spores can grow. The same genus gave us the antibiotic penicillin.
questions.hook: Needle holes let the penicillin-family mould breathe.

questions.question: Savoury Breton galettes, the dark crêpes folded round ham and egg, are made from which flour?
questions.explanation: Buckwheat, called blé noir or black wheat in French, thrived in Brittany's poor acid soil where ordinary wheat struggled. Sweet crêpes are made from wheat flour instead.
questions.hook: Savoury Breton pancakes are buckwheat, sweet ones are wheat.

questions.question: Béarnaise sauce, a buttery cousin of hollandaise, is flavoured with a reduction of vinegar, shallots and which herb?
questions.explanation: The reduction is whisked into egg yolks and clarified butter, and fresh tarragon is stirred in at the end. Béarnaise is the classic partner for steak and chips.
questions.hook: Béarnaise is hollandaise with a tarragon kick.

questions.question: Iskender kebab, sliced doner on pide bread under tomato sauce, hot butter and yoghurt, is associated with which Turkish city?
questions.explanation: It is named after Iskender Efendi, a 19th-century Bursa cook who changed how the meat was cut and served. Diners expect the waiter to pour hot butter over the plate at the table.
questions.hook: Iskender's butter-drenched kebab belongs to Bursa.

questions.question: Egypt's version of falafel, called ta'amiya, is traditionally made from which bean rather than chickpeas?
questions.explanation: Egyptian ta'amiya uses dried split fava beans and a lot of fresh herbs, giving a bright green centre. The Levantine version, found in Lebanon and Israel, uses chickpeas.
questions.hook: Egypt's falafel is green inside, because it is fava.

questions.question: Pandoro, the tall golden star-shaped Christmas cake dusted with icing sugar, comes from which Italian city?
questions.explanation: Pandoro means golden bread, and the soft, buttery, fruit-free cake is baked in an eight-pointed star mould. It is Verona's answer to Milan's panettone.
questions.hook: Golden bread from Verona, panettone's fruit-free rival.

questions.question: Which pungent green Japanese plant, grated from its stem, is served with sushi and is often replaced by dyed horseradish?
questions.explanation: Real wasabi is a fussy water-loving plant that is hard to farm, so most tubes and restaurant dabs are horseradish paste coloured green. Its heat hits the nose and fades within seconds rather than lingering on the tongue.
questions.hook: Real wasabi clears the nose, then vanishes.

questions.question: Naan bread is traditionally baked by slapping the dough against the hot inner wall of which clay oven?
questions.explanation: The tandoor is a deep cylindrical clay oven heated by charcoal or wood, reaching temperatures far hotter than most home ovens. It also cooks tandoori chicken on long skewers and gives naan its blistered, charred spots.
questions.hook: Naan sticks to the tandoor wall like a sticker.

questions.question: Which unsalted fresh Indian cheese is cubed and simmered in spinach dishes such as saag?
questions.explanation: Paneer is made by curdling hot milk with lemon juice or another acid, then pressing the curds. It does not melt when heated, which is why the cubes hold their shape in curries and on skewers.
questions.hook: Paneer holds its shape when the heat is on.

questions.question: Tonkatsu, a Japanese breaded and deep-fried cutlet served with a tangy brown sauce, is traditionally made from which meat?
questions.explanation: The ton in tonkatsu is the Japanese word for pork, and katsu is short for katsuretsu, from the English word cutlet. The cutlet is coated in panko crumbs and usually served on shredded cabbage.
questions.hook: Ton means pork, so the pig is in the name.

questions.question: Which rich Mexican sauce, made in Puebla and Oaxaca from dozens of ingredients including dried chillies, nuts and sometimes chocolate, is poured over turkey or chicken?
questions.explanation: The name comes from the Nahuatl word molli, meaning sauce. Mole poblano and the seven moles of Oaxaca are the best known, and the dark colour comes from toasted chillies and spices rather than chocolate alone.
questions.hook: Mole is Mexico's chocolate-and-chilli sauce.

questions.question: Indonesian satay skewers are traditionally served with a sauce made from which nut?
questions.explanation: Satay is grilled skewered meat, usually chicken, goat or lamb, and the sauce is ground roasted peanuts with chilli, garlic, palm sugar and lime. Botanically the peanut is a legume that ripens underground, not a true nut.
questions.hook: Satay sauce is crushed peanut.

questions.question: Which compound is responsible for the burning heat of chillies?
questions.explanation: Capsaicin is concentrated in the white pith that holds the seeds, not the seeds themselves. Piperine is the pungent compound in black pepper, allicin comes from crushed garlic and gingerol from fresh ginger.
questions.hook: Capsaicin is the C in chilli.

questions.question: Japanese mochi is pounded until smooth and stretchy from which ingredient?
questions.explanation: Despite the name, glutinous rice contains no gluten; it is simply very high in a sticky starch called amylopectin. Steamed grains are pounded in a mortar at New Year to make the cakes eaten in ozoni soup.
questions.hook: Sticky rice with no gluten, pounded smooth.

questions.question: Couscous, the North African staple, is made by rolling and steaming tiny granules of which?
questions.explanation: Semolina is the coarse flour milled from durum wheat, the same grain used for dried pasta. The granules are traditionally steamed in a couscoussier, a pot with a perforated top sitting over the stew.
questions.hook: Couscous is tiny pasta granules of durum semolina.

questions.question: Which rhizome, a ginger cousin with a piney, citrusy bite, flavours Thai tom yum soup and green curry paste?
questions.explanation: Galangal is paler and firmer than ginger and cannot simply be swapped for it without changing the flavour. Thai cooks slice it into soups and pound it into curry pastes with lemongrass and kaffir lime leaf.
questions.hook: Galangal is ginger's sharper, piney cousin.

questions.question: Japanese dashi stock is classically made from kombu seaweed and shaved flakes of which dried fish?
questions.explanation: Skipjack tuna, known in Japan as katsuo and as bonito in English, is smoked, dried until rock hard and shaved into katsuobushi flakes. Together with kombu it gives the savoury umami base of miso soup and countless other dishes.
questions.hook: Dashi: seaweed plus shavings of bonito.

questions.question: Curry laksa, the spicy Malaysian and Singaporean noodle soup, gets its richness from which ingredient?
questions.explanation: The broth is built on a pounded paste of chilli, shallot, lemongrass and shrimp paste, then softened with coconut milk. Asam laksa, a different style, is sour from tamarind and has no coconut at all.
questions.hook: Curry laksa is creamy from the coconut.

questions.question: Which Spanish word names the grill on which an Argentine asado is cooked, and the steakhouses built around it?
questions.explanation: The parrilla is a grate set over glowing embers, with the grill slowly lowered or raised to control the heat. A plancha is a flat griddle, a comal is a flat Mexican griddle and a cazuela is a clay cooking pot.
questions.hook: Parrilla means grill and steakhouse alike.

questions.question: Ethiopian doro wat, a spicy chicken stew, gets its fiery red colour from which spice blend?
questions.explanation: Berbere combines chilli, fenugreek, garlic, ginger, korarima and other spices, and each family has its own recipe. Doro wat is traditionally served with hard-boiled eggs and scooped up with flatbread.
questions.hook: Berbere is Ethiopia's red-hot blend.

questions.question: Boerewors, the spiced coil grilled at every South African braai, is named in Afrikaans for whom?
questions.explanation: Boer means farmer in Afrikaans, and wors means sausage. The coil is seasoned with spices such as coriander, nutmeg and cloves.
questions.hook: Boer is a farmer, wors is the sausage.

questions.question: Egusi soup, a West African staple, is thickened with ground seeds of which plant?
questions.explanation: Egusi are the dried, shelled seeds of certain melons, ground to make a nutty, thick base for soups with leafy greens and meat or fish. The soup is eaten with pounded yam, eba or fufu.
questions.hook: Egusi soup is thickened with melon seeds.

questions.question: South Indian dosa batter is made by fermenting rice with which kind of lentil, also called black gram?
questions.explanation: The rice and urad batter ferments overnight, which gives the thin crisp crepe its slight sourness and its bubbly texture. Urad dal is also the base of idli steamed cakes and vada doughnuts.
questions.hook: Dosa batter ferments overnight, urad dal doing the work.

questions.question: Korean bulgogi, the marinated grilled beef, translates literally as what?
questions.explanation: Bul means fire and gogi means meat. The thin slices are marinated in soy sauce, sugar, sesame oil and garlic, often with grated pear to tenderise the meat, then grilled at the table.
questions.hook: Bul-gogi: fire plus meat.

questions.question: Which banana variety makes up most of the bananas sold in Australian supermarkets?
questions.explanation: Cavendish dominates the world export trade because it travels well, and most Australian crops grow around Queensland's tropical north. Its near-identical clones are vulnerable to disease.
questions.hook: Cavendish: one clone feeding the world.

questions.question: Which part of an egg acts as the emulsifier that holds mayonnaise together?
questions.explanation: Egg yolk contains lecithin, which lets oil and the watery vinegar or lemon juice blend into a stable creamy emulsion instead of separating.
questions.hook: Yolk binds oil to water.

questions.question: Which seeds are blended with basil, garlic and Parmesan in a classic Genoese pesto?
questions.explanation: Pine nuts come from the cones of certain pine trees and are costly because each cone must be dried and the seeds shelled out.
questions.hook: Pesto's pale nutty crunch is pine.

questions.question: Which amino acid, found in tomatoes, Parmesan and kombu, produces the savoury taste known as umami?
questions.explanation: Glutamate is the active part of monosodium glutamate, and ripe or aged foods carry more of it, which is why they taste deeply savoury.
questions.hook: Glutamate: the savoury fifth taste.

questions.question: Which natural gelling substance, found in apple skins and cores, makes jam set?
questions.explanation: Pectin sets into a gel when heated with sugar and acid, which is why citrus pith and pips are boiled with marmalade.
questions.hook: Fruit's own jam glue.

questions.question: Manuka, the shrub behind prized honey, is native to New Zealand and which other country?
questions.explanation: The plant is a tea tree species, Leptospermum scoparium, and grows wild in south-eastern Australia too, though its honey was made famous by New Zealand.
questions.hook: Manuka is a tea tree, shared across the Tasman.

questions.question: Table sugar, or sucrose, is made of one glucose molecule joined to which other sugar?
questions.explanation: Digestion splits sucrose back into glucose and fructose. Fructose is the sweetest natural sugar, which is why honey and fruit taste so sweet.
questions.hook: Sucrose equals glucose plus fructose.

questions.question: Sauerkraut gets its sour tang from which acid made as bacteria ferment salted shredded cabbage?
questions.explanation: Lactic acid bacteria that live on the cabbage thrive in the salty brine and acidify it, which also preserves the vegetable for months.
questions.hook: Salt, wait, and bacteria sour it.

questions.question: Monosodium glutamate was first isolated in 1908 from which Japanese seaweed?
questions.explanation: Chemist Kikunae Ikeda noticed the savoury taste of kombu broth, named it umami, and went on to patent a seasoning from it.
questions.hook: Kombu broth gave us umami and MSG.

questions.question: What name is given to the finest dice in classical French knife work, about three millimetres square?
questions.explanation: It is made by cutting a julienne of matchsticks crosswise. Macedoine is a larger dice, so brunoise is the smallest of the standard dice.
questions.hook: Brunoise: julienne turned to tiny cubes.

questions.question: The sweet orange is a natural hybrid of the pomelo and which other citrus?
questions.explanation: Genetic studies show sweet oranges arose in southern China from crossing pomelo with mandarin, followed by backcrossing.
questions.hook: Orange is mandarin times pomelo.

questions.question: Harland Sanders first sold his fried chicken from a petrol station in which Kentucky town?
questions.explanation: He served meals from a Shell service station in North Corbin during the Depression, and the Sanders Court and Cafe later became a motel and restaurant. The site is now preserved as a museum.
questions.hook: Chicken beside the petrol pumps.

questions.question: Which spice made the tiny island of Run so valuable that the Dutch swapped Manhattan for it in 1667?
questions.explanation: Under the Treaty of Breda the Dutch kept Run, and the English kept New Amsterdam, renamed New York. The Banda Islands were then the only source of nutmeg in the world.
questions.hook: Manhattan was worth less than nutmeg.

questions.question: What sits at the centre of a Jaffa, under its hard orange shell?
questions.explanation: Jaffas are small chocolate balls with an orange-flavoured sugar coating, and they became famous as the lolly rolled down cinema aisles. The name comes from Jaffa oranges, shipped from the port of Jaffa.
questions.hook: Orange outside, chocolate inside, rolling down the aisle.

questions.question: Which bird is the traditional centrepiece of an American Thanksgiving dinner?
questions.explanation: The turkey is a native American bird, which helps explain why it became the festive roast. Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday of November and was fixed by US law in 1941.
questions.hook: Fourth Thursday in November, and a bird from the Americas.

questions.question: On which day of the Easter weekend are hot cross buns traditionally eaten?
questions.explanation: The spiced, fruity buns are marked with a cross for the crucifixion. They are now sold for weeks beforehand, but the custom began as a Good Friday treat.
questions.hook: The cross on the bun marks the day itself.

questions.question: Kit Kat began life in 1935 as Rowntree's Chocolate Crisp, made in which English city?
questions.explanation: It was renamed Kit Kat in 1937, and the factory stayed in York for decades. Nestle bought Rowntree in 1988, and Nestle still makes it across the world.
questions.hook: Kit Kat is York's biscuit and chocolate story.

questions.question: Haigh's Chocolates, Australia's oldest family-owned chocolate maker, was founded in 1915 in which city?
questions.explanation: Alfred Haigh opened the first Haigh's shop in Adelaide, and the company is still run by his descendants. Its chocolate frogs are a South Australian favourite.
questions.hook: Haigh's frogs hop out of Adelaide.

questions.question: Stir-up Sunday, when British families traditionally make Christmas puddings, falls just before which season?
questions.explanation: It is the last Sunday before Advent, and the name comes from a prayer that begins stir up, we beseech thee. Each family member stirs the mix and makes a wish.
questions.hook: Stir the pudding before Advent begins.

questions.question: The English word companion comes from Latin words meaning with and which food?
questions.explanation: A companion was literally someone you broke bread with. The French word copain has the same root, and the term was used for people who shared a meal, including soldiers.
questions.hook: Your companion is whoever shares your loaf.

questions.question: Compared with beef, kangaroo meat is prized for being very low in which nutrient?
questions.explanation: Kangaroo is very low in fat compared with beef, while being high in protein and iron. Because it is so lean it dries out quickly and is best cooked rare to medium-rare.
questions.hook: Lean as a roo, so do not overcook it.

questions.question: The cheese gruyere takes its name from a small town in which Swiss canton?
questions.explanation: The town of Gruyeres sits in the Fribourg canton, and the cheese takes its name from the town. The cheese is aged for months and is a key part of a classic fondue.
questions.hook: Gruyeres is the castle town in Fribourg.

questions.question: The Mars bar was first made in 1932 in which English town?
questions.explanation: Forrest Mars, son of American candy maker Frank Mars, set up in Slough, Berkshire, and launched the bar there in 1932.
questions.hook: Mars landed in Slough in 1932.

questions.question: Which South Australian port is home to most of Australia's southern bluefin tuna fishing and farming industry?
questions.explanation: Young wild tuna are caught in the Great Australian Bight, towed to pens off Port Lincoln and fattened for the Japanese sashimi market.
questions.hook: Tuna ranchers made a fortune at Port Lincoln.

questions.question: The Swiss melted cheese dish raclette takes its name from a French verb meaning what?
questions.explanation: Diners hold a cut wheel of cheese to a heater and scrape off the melted surface onto potatoes, pickles and cured meats. The French verb is racler.
questions.hook: You scrape the melted cheese off the wheel.

questions.question: Which US president joined Washington, Jefferson and Lincoln on Mount Rushmore?
questions.explanation: The faces were carved into the Black Hills of South Dakota between 1927 and 1941. The teddy bear takes its name from Theodore Roosevelt after he refused to shoot a tethered bear on a 1902 hunting trip.
questions.hook: The teddy bear's namesake is up on the mountain.

questions.question: Whose portrait appears on the US $100 bill?
questions.explanation: Franklin and Hamilton ($10) are the only non-presidents on notes in circulation. Hundred-dollar bills are nicknamed 'Benjamins' for him.
questions.hook: 'All about the Benjamins' means all about the hundreds.

questions.question: Which British monarch reigned for more than 70 years, the longest in British history?
questions.explanation: Elizabeth II reigned from 1952 to 2022, passing Victoria's 63 years in 2015. Only Louis XIV of France, at 72 years, reigned longer as sovereign of a recognised state.
questions.hook: Seventy years earned her the only Platinum Jubilee.

questions.question: Who became heir apparent to the British throne when Charles III acceded in 2022?
questions.explanation: William automatically became Duke of Cornwall and was then created Prince of Wales. His eldest child, George, moved up to second in line.
questions.hook: Dad became King, so William became Prince of Wales.

questions.question: Which queen was on the British throne when Australia federated on 1 January 1901?
questions.explanation: Victoria died on 22 January 1901, three weeks after Federation, and Edward VII succeeded her. The first federal parliament was opened in May 1901 by her grandson, the future George V.
questions.hook: Victoria saw the Commonwealth born, then died three weeks later.

questions.question: At which Scottish estate did Elizabeth II die in September 2022?
questions.explanation: Balmoral was bought by Victoria and Albert in 1852 and, like Sandringham, is the family's private property rather than the Crown's. The Palace of Holyroodhouse in Edinburgh is the monarch's official Scottish residence.
questions.hook: Balmoral and Sandringham are the family's own, not the state's.

questions.question: In which city is NATO's headquarters?
questions.explanation: NATO moved from Paris in 1967 after Charles de Gaulle pulled France out of its integrated military command. Brussels is also home to the main EU institutions.
questions.hook: De Gaulle showed NATO the door, so it moved to Brussels.

questions.question: Who proclaimed the independence of Vietnam in September 1945?
questions.explanation: His declaration opened by quoting the American Declaration of Independence. Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City in 1976, seven years after his death.
questions.hook: Uncle Ho quoted Jefferson.

questions.question: Which Tanzanian independence leader was known as 'Mwalimu', or teacher?
questions.explanation: Nyerere translated Shakespeare's Julius Caesar into Swahili and pursued a village socialism called Ujamaa. Unusually for his era, he retired voluntarily in 1985.
questions.hook: The teacher who put Shakespeare into Swahili.

questions.question: Which country's head of government holds the title Taoiseach?
questions.explanation: Taoiseach is Irish for 'chief' or 'leader', and the deputy is the Tánaiste. Ireland's head of state is a separately elected president.
questions.hook: Taoiseach sounds like 'tee-shock': Ireland's chief.

questions.question: Which pope opened the Second Vatican Council in 1962?
questions.explanation: Angelo Roncalli, 'Good Pope John', died in 1963, and Paul VI closed the council in 1965. John XXIII was canonised in 2014 on the same day as John Paul II.
questions.hook: Good Pope John opened the Church's windows.

questions.question: Who was the last emperor of China, a child who abdicated in 1912?
questions.explanation: Puyi took the throne aged two in 1908 and abdicated in 1912 after the Xinhai Revolution. Japan later installed him as puppet emperor of Manchukuo, and after years in prison he worked as a gardener in communist Beijing.
questions.hook: Emperor at two, a Japanese puppet later, a gardener at the end.

questions.question: Which Roman emperor created the Tetrarchy in 293, sharing power among four rulers?
questions.explanation: Diocletian found the empire too big for one man, so he appointed a co-emperor and two junior emperors. He also retired voluntarily in 305 to his palace at Split, which is almost unique among Roman emperors.
questions.hook: Four emperors at once: Diocletian's cure for an overstretched empire.

questions.question: Who proclaimed Indonesia's independence from the Dutch on 17 August 1945 and became its first president?
questions.explanation: Sukarno read the proclamation with Mohammad Hatta, who became vice president. The Dutch fought the new republic until they accepted independence in 1949. Sukarno was pushed aside by General Suharto after 1965.
questions.hook: Like many Javanese, Sukarno had no family name.

questions.question: In which country did Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power in the October Revolution of 1917?
questions.explanation: It is called the October Revolution because Russia still used the Julian calendar, so the date fell on 7 November by our modern calendar. Russia then became the largest republic in the Soviet Union, which was formed in December 1922.
questions.hook: The October Revolution happened in November on today's calendar.

questions.question: Which Carthaginian general led elephants over the Alps in 218 BCE to invade Italy?
questions.explanation: Hannibal crushed a much larger Roman army at Cannae in 216 BCE. The Roman general Scipio Africanus finally beat him at Zama in 202 BCE by taking the war to Carthage's home ground.
questions.hook: Elephants over the Alps, but Scipio beat him at home.

questions.question: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal?
questions.explanation: Mumtaz died in 1631 and the tomb at Agra took about two decades to build. Shah Jahan was later deposed by his son Aurangzeb and held in Agra Fort, with a view of the monument.
questions.hook: Imprisoned within sight of the tomb he built.

questions.question: Who became Rome's first emperor in 27 BCE after defeating Mark Antony at Actium?
questions.explanation: Born Octavian, he was the great-nephew and adopted heir of Julius Caesar, and the Senate gave him the title Augustus. The month of August is named after him, just as July honours Caesar.
questions.hook: July for Caesar, August for his heir.

questions.question: Before entering politics, Ben Chifley worked on the New South Wales railways as what?
questions.explanation: Born in Bathurst in 1885, Chifley rose to engine driver before entering parliament. As Prime Minister from 1945 to 1949 he gave the 'light on the hill' speech that Labor leaders still quote.
questions.hook: The Prime Minister who drove the trains.

questions.question: Which colony held the last of the federation referendums, voting yes in July 1900?
questions.explanation: The gold rush had drawn thousands of migrants from the eastern colonies, and they helped deliver a yes vote of roughly 70 per cent. Western Australia joined only just in time to be an original state of the Commonwealth.
questions.hook: The goldfields voters made Western Australia the last yes.

questions.question: Which private industry did Ben Chifley try to nationalise in 1947, a move that fed the Coalition's 1949 victory?
questions.explanation: The Banking Act 1947 would have put private banks under the Commonwealth Bank. The High Court struck it down in 1948 and the Privy Council upheld that in 1949, while Menzies campaigned against Labor's 'socialism'.
questions.hook: Chifley wanted the banks and lost the election.

questions.question: In which Canberra hotel did Ben Chifley die of a heart attack in June 1951?
questions.explanation: Chifley was Opposition Leader by then and died on 13 June 1951. Even as Prime Minister he had preferred a room at the Kurrajong, a hotel built for public servants and politicians, over living at The Lodge.
questions.hook: The PM who chose a hotel room over the official residence.

questions.question: What title is given to the member who presides over the House of Representatives?
questions.explanation: The Speaker is elected by fellow members at the start of each Parliament and keeps order in debate. The Senate's equivalent is called the President.
questions.hook: The Speaker speaks for the House; the Senate has a President.

questions.question: On which famous Washington street does the White House stand?
questions.explanation: The White House address is 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW. The avenue links the White House with the Capitol, and inaugural parades travel along it.
questions.hook: Sixteen hundred Pennsylvania: the most famous street number in America.

questions.question: Which Wessex king defeated the Danes at Edington in 878 and is the subject of a legend about burnt cakes?
questions.explanation: Alfred is the only English monarch given the title 'the Great'. He built fortified towns called burhs, a navy, and a law code, and encouraged translating Latin works into English.
questions.hook: He burned the cakes but won the war.

questions.question: Which Danish king of England, who also ruled Denmark and Norway, is said to have set his throne by the sea to show courtiers he could not command the tide?
questions.explanation: Cnut took the English throne in 1016 and ruled until 1035, marrying his predecessor's widow Emma of Normandy. In the usual telling of the tide story he was demonstrating humility, not arrogance.
questions.hook: Cnut proved the tide obeys nobody, not even him.

questions.question: Which Roman emperor is blamed in legend for 'fiddling while Rome burned' during the great fire of 64 CE?
questions.explanation: The fiddle is a myth, since the instrument did not yet exist, and Nero was reportedly away from Rome when the fire began. He blamed Christians for it and later died by suicide in 68 CE.
questions.hook: Nero fiddled is a myth; he was out of town.

questions.question: Which pharaoh built the Great Pyramid of Giza, the largest of the Egyptian pyramids?
questions.explanation: Built around 2560 BCE, it was the tallest human-made structure in the world for nearly 4,000 years. Khufu's son Khafre built the second-largest pyramid beside it, while Djoser's step pyramid at Saqqara came earlier.
questions.hook: Khufu built the Great one; his son Khafre came second.

questions.question: In which month of 44 BCE was Julius Caesar assassinated, on the day known as the Ides?
questions.explanation: The Ides fell on the 15th in March, May, July and October. Caesar was stabbed by a group of senators, including Brutus and Cassius, at a meeting of the Senate near the Theatre of Pompey.
questions.hook: Beware the Ides of March: the 15th.

questions.question: Which gladiator led a huge slave rebellion against Rome that began in 73 BCE?
questions.explanation: Spartacus escaped from a gladiator school at Capua and gathered tens of thousands of followers, defeating several Roman armies. Crassus finally crushed the revolt in 71 BCE and crucified about 6,000 captives along the Appian Way.
questions.hook: Spartacus escaped Capua; Crassus lined the road with crosses.

questions.question: Which Persian king ordered a bridge of boats built across the Hellespont for his invasion of Greece in 480 BCE?
questions.explanation: When a storm wrecked the first bridges, Xerxes reportedly had the sea whipped as punishment. His fleet was then smashed at Salamis, and his father Darius had earlier been beaten at Marathon.
questions.hook: Xerxes bridged the sea, then lost it at Salamis.

questions.question: Which Athenian statesman led the city through its golden age and oversaw the building of the Parthenon?
questions.explanation: Pericles dominated Athenian politics for about three decades, strengthening its democracy and its naval empire. He died of plague in 429 BCE, early in the Peloponnesian War against Sparta.
questions.hook: Pericles built the Parthenon and died in the plague.

questions.question: Which Mesopotamian ruler, in legend a cupbearer who became king, founded what is often called the world's first empire around 2300 BCE?
questions.explanation: Sargon united the Sumerian city-states with his own Akkadian-speaking people from his capital Akkad. Hammurabi, famous for his law code, ruled Babylon several centuries later.
questions.hook: Sargon the cupbearer built the first empire.

questions.question: Under which emperor did the Roman Empire reach its greatest territorial extent, in 117 CE?
questions.explanation: Trajan conquered Dacia, in modern Romania, and pushed east into Mesopotamia. His successor Hadrian gave up the eastern gains and focused on defending the borders, including his wall in Britain.
questions.hook: Trajan stretched Rome to its limit; Hadrian pulled back.

questions.question: Which Roman general marched on Rome, became dictator in 82 BCE, then unusually resigned the office in 79 BCE and retired?
questions.explanation: Sulla was the first Roman to lead an army against the city itself, and he posted lists of enemies to be killed, called proscriptions. His retirement was rare, as later dictators such as Caesar clung to power.
questions.hook: Sulla seized Rome, then walked away.

questions.question: Which Roman orator, famed for his speeches against Catiline and Mark Antony, was killed on Antony's orders in 43 BCE?
questions.explanation: Cicero's severed head and hands were displayed on the speaker's platform in the Forum. His letters and speeches survive in large numbers, making him one of the best-documented figures of the ancient world.
questions.hook: Cicero's words cost him his head and hands.

questions.question: Which fifth-century king of the Huns invaded Gaul and Italy but turned back from Rome in 452 CE?
questions.explanation: Tradition says Pope Leo I met him and persuaded him to withdraw, though plague and supply problems probably also helped. Attila died on his wedding night in 453 CE, apparently from a burst blood vessel.
questions.hook: Attila turned back, then died on his wedding night.

questions.question: In the Roman Republic, which office was held by two men at once each year and was the highest elected magistracy?
questions.explanation: The two consuls could each veto the other and commanded Rome's armies. Years were dated by their names, so a date might be given as 'the year Caesar and Bibulus were consuls'.
questions.hook: Two consuls, each able to veto the other.

questions.question: Which Roman general and rival of Julius Caesar was murdered on arriving in Egypt in 48 BCE after losing at Pharsalus?
questions.explanation: Pompey fled to Egypt hoping for help but was killed on the orders of advisers to the young Ptolemy XIII. When Caesar arrived days later he was reportedly shown Pompey's head and wept.
questions.hook: Pompey fled to Egypt and was killed at the shore.

questions.question: Which Zulu king led the army that destroyed a British column at Isandlwana in January 1879?
questions.explanation: The Anglo-Zulu War opened with one of the worst defeats the British army has suffered at the hands of an African force, but British troops won at Ulundi that July. Cetshwayo was captured and later briefly restored to a reduced Zulu kingdom.
questions.hook: Isandlwana: the day spears beat a British column.

questions.question: Which Canadian prime minister's son later also became prime minister?
questions.explanation: Pierre Trudeau governed from 1968 to 1979 and again from 1980 to 1984, bringing home the Canadian constitution in 1982. His son Justin became prime minister in 2015.
questions.hook: Trudeau senior, Trudeau junior, thirty-one years apart.

questions.question: Which province joined New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Quebec as the fourth founding member of Canada in 1867?
questions.explanation: The old Province of Canada was split into Ontario and Quebec at Confederation, giving four provinces. Manitoba joined in 1870, PEI in 1873, and Newfoundland not until 1949.
questions.hook: Four to start, ten provinces now.

questions.question: The 1985 agreement that began abolishing passport checks between European states was signed on a boat on the Moselle river in which country?
questions.explanation: The boat was moored at the village of Schengen, where Luxembourg meets France and Germany. Five states signed first, and the open-border zone that grew from it now covers most of the EU.
questions.hook: Borders were wiped away on a boat at a three-country corner.

questions.question: Which English king was forced by rebel barons to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215?
questions.explanation: John, brother of Richard the Lionheart, had lost Normandy and taxed heavily. The charter promised that even the king was subject to law, though the pope annulled it within weeks and it was reissued under his son.
questions.hook: Bad king John signed away his absolute power, then wriggled free for a time.

questions.question: Which Spartan king led the Greek force that held the pass at Thermopylae in 480 BC?
questions.explanation: He famously held the narrow pass with about 300 Spartans plus several thousand allies against Xerxes' Persian army. A local betrayer showed the Persians a mountain path, and Leonidas died covering the Greek retreat.
questions.hook: Three hundred Spartans, one goat track, and a betrayal.

questions.question: Which Germanic general deposed the last Western Roman emperor, Romulus Augustulus, in AD 476?
questions.explanation: Odoacer sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and ruled Italy as king, ending the line of western emperors. Theodoric the Ostrogoth later killed him in 493 and took control of Italy.
questions.hook: Odoacer ended Rome; Theodoric ended Odoacer.

questions.question: Which Inca emperor did Francisco Pizarro capture at Cajamarca in 1532?
questions.explanation: Pizarro's tiny force ambushed Atahualpa, who then filled a room with gold and silver as ransom. The Spanish executed him in 1533 anyway, and Cuzco fell soon afterwards.
questions.hook: He filled a room with gold to buy his freedom and was killed regardless.

questions.question: What was the name of the warhorse that Alexander the Great tamed as a boy?
questions.explanation: Alexander realised the horse was afraid of its own shadow and turned it towards the sun to calm it. Bucephalus carried him through his campaigns, and Alexander named a city in India after the horse when it died.
questions.hook: A horse afraid of its shadow became a conqueror's lifelong mount.
